#3301. Blue Origin delays New Glenn’s return to flight until January

CEO Dave Limp told staff the rocket will miss its 2026 goal after May's launch pad explosion.

The entrance sign at Blue Origin’s Launch Site One in West Texas.

Blue Origin has pushed New Glenn’s return to flight to January 2027, CEO Dave Limp told staff, Bloomberg reports. The rocket has been grounded since it exploded on its only launch pad in May, delaying Amazon Leo satellites and NASA’s Moon plans.

Blue Origin has pushed back the return of its New Glenn rocket to January, chief executive Dave Limp told staff on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported. The company had pledged to fly again before the end of 2026, after the rocket exploded on its pad in May.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in a memo seen by Bloomberg. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority.”

The Financial Times first reported the delay. Blue Origin declined to comment.

New Glenn blew up during an engine test on 28 May, destroying the rocket and badly damaging Blue Origin’s only New Glenn pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida. The company has spent six months rebuilding it, and Limp said bad summer weather slowed the work. In June, Blue Origin said it had not found the cause yet.

The delay hurts Amazon, Jeff Bezos’ other company. New Glenn was due to carry 48 Amazon Leo internet satellites on its next flight, and the FCC has already cut Amazon’s spectrum priority for satellites launched late.

It also matters for NASA. New Glenn is meant to launch Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander, which NASA plans to use to land astronauts on the Moon under its Artemis programme.

The rocket is years behind schedule and has flown only three times since January 2025, leaving SpaceX far ahead. In July, Blue Origin was reported to be taking outside money for the first time, at a $130B valuation.

#3300. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

#3299. Instagram launches Edits for Mac with multi-track video editing and 4K exports

Instagram users can now download a Mac version of Edits, the company’s free video editing app, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, direct publishing to Instagram, and 4K exports. Here are the details.

Instagram is launching Edits on desktop today, bringing its free video editing app to Mac with a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts that can match those of other video editors.

Like Edits on mobile, Instagram says its desktop counterpart will receive weekly updates and is asking users for feedback to help shape future improvements.

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.

One particularly interesting feature of the new desktop app is the ability to publish videos directly to Instagram, with support for native features such as tagging, location, and trial reels.

Instagram adds that it is expanding Edits to support “multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.”

As for the actual editing tools, Edits for desktop makes basic operations like splitting, cutting, and trimming videos easier, while also offering a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, precise audio waveforms, and advanced color grading tools such as color wheels, curves, and log conversions.

Users can also import their own LUTs and fonts, customize keyboard shortcuts, and access Instagram’s licensed audio library.

Instagram says saved audio and text styles from the mobile app are already available on desktop. However, the ability to seamlessly edit the same project across Mac and mobile is still in development.

Instagram’s desktop Edits app also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages, as well as hundreds of sound and video effects, all for free.

In other words, we reach out to them, and they push a button, and everything pops in. Listings are populated. They see their inventory on Marketplace. They get a reporting, they get a cockpit, they get KPIs, and they are part of our ecosystem. That did not exist.

The way we operated before, and also for larger dealers, is there is a lot of handholding, there is a lot of manual processes in order to connect to the various systems, the dealer-related systems, the MarTech solutions, and so forth. It is a really, truly an innovative new product that the teams have put together, and the amount of time it took to put it together exceeded our own expectations. We are very pleasantly surprised, and we have about 60%-65% of all these new local smaller dealers using it as an auto service jumpstarted, as opposed to a manual process that we need to go through before. That really explains it. That's what we mean by self-service.

Marvin Fong: Great. Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. I would like to also ask about the starter package. Tobi Hartmann: Yeah. Thank you, Marvin. Highly relevant question. I should have mentioned that earlier, so I am glad you picked up on that. One of the dimensions, obviously, is our core currency in terms of leads and the number of leads we are providing, and that also ties to some product work we did, and we have accelerated in the past couple of months, which is the so-called DLE, the dealer lead engine.

We are getting more sophisticated in how we are distributing leads, how quickly we are distributing leads, and if you hop on as a new partner, obviously you would like to have a positive experience very early on. You wouldn't want to wait for three to four weeks for the first lead to come through. Marvin Fong: Got it. If I could do a follow-up, maybe for you, Sonia, just like on the financial impact or how should we think about the impact of the starter program on ARPD? Tobi Hartmann: Yeah. To build on what Sonia stated, we view this from two dimensions. Marvin Fong: No, that was very helpful. Thank you. Sonia, best of luck on the future endeavors. Thanks.

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah, and your question regarding other customer segments and larger dealerships, it's really a different product. That's why we started from scratch. #3297. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3296. WhatsApp adds shareable event invites and a new Events hub

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

When you create an event, you can add a cover photo and share the invite link by text or email. WhatsApp also gives you the option to share a QR code.

WhatsApp says your phone number is hidden from guests you don’t know, and “guests without a WhatsApp account will only see the event address after they RSVP.”

You could already create events in WhatsApp group chats and one-on-one conversations.

With this update, WhatsApp is adding a dedicated Events section in Settings where you can create invites, manage RSVPs, and see past and upcoming events you’ve organized or been invited to.

You can also set custom reminders and give guests the option to bring a plus-one.

WhatsApp says the updated Events feature will roll out to everyone over the next few weeks.

#3295. Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models [U: Now available]

Apple Creator Studio updates were announced late last month, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.

At the time, Apple didn’t give a specific availability date beyond sometime in November, but the updates are rolling out today …

Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.

Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.

Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.

Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.

The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.

Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.

Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.

A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.

In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.

New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.

#3294. Intensity (INTS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Enrollment restarts as cash burn rises and partnership talks advance.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Intensity Therapeutics, Inc. (INTS -11.43%) reported the resumption of clinical enrollment in its late-stage sarcoma and breast cancer programs following previous delays related to funding and protocol revisions. Management reported that the company's phase III INVINCIBLE-3 study is currently enrolling patients at U.S. sites with plans to expand to Europe and Canada in early 2027. The company is operating with $8.5 million in cash and expects a monthly burn of approximately $1 million in the fourth quarter as it advances clinical trials and completes a new manufacturing batch for its lead candidate. Management stated that the pursuit of strategic partnerships with multinational and regional pharmaceutical companies remains a core objective for the coming year.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Intensity Therapeutics Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. Joining the call today is Lewis H. Bender, Intensity's President and CEO, and Joseph Talamo, Intensity's Chief Financial Officer. Shortly before this call, Intensity issued a press release announcing its third quarter 2026 financial results, which is available under the News and Events section of the company website. Shortly after this webcast, a replay of this call will also be posted. Before we begin, the company reminds you that comments made by management during this conference call contain forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties regarding the operations and future results of Intensity Therapeutics.

These statements include, but are not limited to, statements relating to the company's expected future plans, cash runway, development activities, projected milestones, business activities, or results. Forward-looking statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results or events to materially differ from those anticipated. Additional information regarding these risks and uncertainties is included in the company's earnings release issued today. For a more complete list and description of risk factors, we encourage you to review the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including, without limitation, its Forms 10-K, 10-Q, and eight-Ks.

Furthermore, the content of this conference call contains time-sensitive information that is accurate only as of the date of this live broadcast, November 5th, 2026. Except as required by law, the company disclaims any intention or obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements. I'll now turn the call over to Mr. Bender, Intensity's President and CEO.

Lewis Bender: Thank you, Wyatt, and thank you, everyone, for joining us this morning. It is my pleasure to provide the latest update of our company's progress in the INVINCIBLE-3 and INVINCIBLE-4 studies, our publications and presentation strategy, our business development activities, and our plans for the rest of 2026 into 2027. First, I will turn the call over to Joe Talamo, our CFO, to discuss our third quarter financial results. Joe?

Joseph Talamo: Thanks, Lou, and good morning. I'm pleased to join you today and to present a summary of our third quarter 2026 financial results. Our research and development expenses were $2.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $1.6 million for the same prior year period, reflecting an increase of $876,000, or 56%. Clinical trial expenses for our phase III INVINCIBLE-3 study were $1.5 million during the third quarter of 2026, compared with $1 million for the same prior year period. In the current year quarter, we resumed new patient enrollment activities in the INVINCIBLE-3 study in a limited number of U.S. sites after pausing new site activations and patient enrollment in March 2025 due to funding constraints.

During this pause, we continued to treat and monitor patients previously enrolled in the study in cooperation with our CROs. We have prioritized commencing full patient enrollment and site activations once sufficient incremental funding is obtained. Our clinical trial expenses also included $104,000 for our phase II INVINCIBLE-4 study, which also resumed patient enrollment and treatment in the third quarter of 2026. We expect the INVINCIBLE-4 study costs to increase in the coming quarters as we target completing enrollment in this study by the end of 2027. Lou will provide an operational update on both studies shortly. During the third quarter of 2026, we also initiated a new manufacturing batch of INT230-6, incurring $162,000 in higher manufacturing costs.

We expect this batch will be completed in the first quarter of 2027 and will likely be sufficient to fully supply both ongoing clinical studies. Lastly, research and development employee compensation-related expenses were $184,000 higher during the current quarter due to an estimated bonus accrual in the current year period, compared to no bonus accrual in the prior year period. Turning now to G&A. General and administrative expenses were $1.3 million for the third quarter of 2026 and were unchanged compared with the same prior year period. Within G&A, minor increases in employee compensation-related expenses and consulting expenses were offset by minor decreases in insurance costs during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same prior year period.

Overall, net loss was $3.5 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with a $2.7 million loss for the third quarter of 2025, representing an increase in net loss of $873,000, or 33%. Our cash burn from operating activities for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $6.7 million, reflecting an average monthly operating activities cash burn of $741,000 over the first nine months of 2026. We estimate that our operating cash burn will average approximately $1 million per month in the final quarter of 2026 as we continue to advance our clinical studies and manufacture the new INT230-6 batch. Turning now to our balance sheet.

As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $8.5 million. During the third quarter of 2026, we raised $1.5 million in net proceeds from the issuance of common stock under our at-the-market facility. For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we raised $3.2 million in net proceeds under the at-the-market facility. We expect to continue to use this facility opportunistically to raise capital, and we will continue to explore other sources of dilutive and non-dilutive capital as we seek to scale up our clinical activities moving forward. With that, I will now turn the call back to Lou for a discussion on our clinical programs and business development activities. Lou?

Lewis Bender: Thank you, Joe. Well, we are pleased to hold today's earnings call following the positive feedback we received from our stockholders and stakeholders after last quarter's call. Today, as I said, I will discuss the continued progress that the company has made this quarter in more detail and provide an update on ongoing activities. As you just heard from Joe, we ended the third quarter with about $8.5 million. In the fourth quarter, we continue to evaluate the opportunities to raise capital via the ATM and other types of offerings or financings as opportunities present themselves to us.

Well, now I'm going to update on the phase III INVINCIBLE trial, which is our open-label, randomized controlled clinical study that is testing our drug INT230-6 as monotherapy, meaning just our drug alone, compared to the best standard of care drugs in second and third line treatment for three types of soft tissue sarcomas. On last quarter's call, we reported that we had initiated new patient enrollment in terms of starting the process for that in the INVINCIBLE-3 study in a limited number of U.S. sites.

To make this restart happen, this quarter, we added new CROs to help manage this clinical study, including vendors for statistical analysis and a large organization that specializes in receiving computed tomography, known as CT, images from sites around the world electronically during clinical trials. The purpose of this change is to establish consistency of the reads by radiologists across all sites, whether a patient's cancer is progressing or not, or regressing, compared to a patient's prior scan. Our key sarcoma thought leaders made a few important observations and recommendations. One was a central read, and the other was a recommendation to use a different set of criteria to determine whether a patient's disease was progressing.

In the prior version of the amended protocol, we based disease progression on tumor size, which is standard practice for systemic treatments. However, we have learned for our drug, the tumor becomes larger from the injection, from immune cell infiltration, and from the buildup of fluid as the cancer cells die. While changes in tumor size using criteria such as RECIST or WHO may be standard practice for determining progression for systemic treatments because it's based on the size of the tumor, we believe those criteria are unsuitable for our unique intratumoral drug.

Working with the expert radiology group, we finalized a set of criteria to assess whether a patient's cancer is progressing by measuring the tumor's density compared to its baseline. These criteria are referred to as Choi, and they are often used for certain types of sarcoma. While size goes up, density declines using our drug, and using Choi, we think we will have a better assessment of progressive disease. The endpoint remains overall survival. Sites will send their scans for assessment to the central review group, who will return a report on the Choi scores and provide detailed information on density changes for treated and untreated tumors.

Recruitment began in the U.S. in Q3 enrollment, and several sites are activated and seeking patients. We've also filed the needed documentation to restart the phase III in Europe and Canada in Q3. We expect to have approval to begin under the amended protocol in Europe in Q1. As we've mentioned, as incremental capital is raised, we will assess the timing of when additional sites can be activated in the U.S., the E.U., and Canada. Moving to ESMO now. Last month, Kim Guedes, our Vice President of Clinical Operations, and I traveled to Madrid to attend the Annual European Society for Medical Oncology Conference, known as ESMO.

We met with several of the INVINCIBLE-3 investigators who remain excited to resume their participation in the study. The last drug approved for second or third line soft tissue sarcoma of the types in our study was in 2016. It's been a long, dry desert for these patients. The three-year survival for sarcoma patients at this stage with progression, when we will begin to treat, is low. It's in the single digits. The physician investigators told us that there is an opportunity, given the lack of trial options for these patients, for new therapies. We are motivated to activate sites, enroll, and determine whether INT230-6 can help sarcoma patients live longer with improved safety and better quality of life.

Capital is the restriction on speed. Now provide an update on our phase II INVINCIBLE-4 presurgical breast cancer study, which is our randomized, controlled, open-label, multicenter study of INT given before the administration of standard of care neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy regimen in patients with early-stage operable triple-negative breast cancer. The efficacy endpoint is pathological complete response, referred to as pCR, which is the absence of any live cancer at the time of surgery in the tumor, breast, or lymph nodes. Tumor sizes in our trial are more challenging to treat, as our inclusion criteria uses a larger minimal tumor size than what was used for approval of the current regimen. Larger tumors are more challenging to treat.

On October 23rd, we announced new data at ESMO on patients who received our drug, showing an early indication of the potential to improve the percentage of women achieving a pathological complete response, or pCR. Clinical studies have shown that if triple-negative breast cancer patients have no live cancer at the time of surgery, the pCR, the risk of the disease returning in five years after surgery is significantly reduced, from about 50% without having a pCR to about 16% with a pCR. This difference is clinically meaningful, and many regulatory agencies, including the U.S. FDA and the EMA, accept pCR as an endpoint for certain types of accelerated or conditional approvals. There are two cohorts in the study.

The first is one dose of our drug administered prior to the standard of care. This is cohort A. The second cohort B, is the standard of care alone. Patients are randomized one-to-one to each cohort. As reported previously, 71% of patients who received INT230-6 achieved a pCR compared to 42% the standard of care. Very small numbers, it's early data. But these were patients with a median tumor size of 2.6, which is quite large. We also reported that no invasive cancer cells were detected in the axillary lymph nodes in six of the seven patients in cohort A after INT230-6 treatment, despite five of these seven patients, 71%, being initially biopsy-proven node positive. We don't know the nodes.

Results also showed tumor necrosis in all seven cohort A patients. In the pre-surgery MRI, at the completion of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy, four patients in our group had radiological complete response, and three patients, 43%, had partial response. All seven patients met criteria for breast-conserving surgery. These surgical results are consistent with the results from the study in Ottawa, our completed INVINCIBLE-2 study, that the timing of the surgery is unaffected by the use of our drug, which is a very important factor for patients.

We resumed to dose new patients in the third quarter in INVINCIBLE-4 after the study enrollment was paused late last year to revise the dosing regimen for patients receiving our drug because some patients experienced localized skin issues. Our collaborators in the INVINCIBLE study, the Swiss Cancer Institute, have established an IDMB of qualified experts to review safety data and images from these newly treated patients and assess whether the skin issues have been resolved.

The institute team felt, and we agreed, that an independent group of experts reporting that the current dosing regimen had resolved the skin issue would be the best way to assure all the investigators of the safety of this drug with regards to the skin issue. As a side note, we used a higher dose for tumor size in our completed INVINCIBLE-2 study in Ottawa compared to the revised dosing regimen in the ongoing INVINCIBLE-4 study. In the first study, 60 women received our treatment, and no skin issues were reported when injections were made with ultrasound to guide the needle. The INVINCIBLE-4 study uses higher quality ultrasound than was used in the INVINCIBLE-2.

After ESMO, I met and went to Switzerland and met with several of the sites. The meetings included the investigators, the nursing teams, coordinators, pharmacists, and other staff. I presented background data on INT230-6, the data from the Ottawa study, the latest safety and efficacy data from the ongoing phase II INVINCIBLE-4 study, and new results presented at ESMO. I was encouraged by our discussions and the investigators' enthusiasm to enroll their TNBC patients at each site. At ESMO, we also met with our partners at the group managing the French sites, UNICANCER. Along with a couple of French investigators, we discussed the science and study data. Several sites in France have had their site initiation visit and are activated.

We also plan to visit the sites in France, and the remaining sites in Switzerland after the independent safety report is available. We hope to give investigators confidence that a single injection of our drug has the potential to improve efficacy, be safer, and provide patients with the same skin appearance with our drug or without it. These efforts allow us to continue to target completion of enrollment by the end of 2027. It's also important to remember that using today's best immunochemotherapy regimens, only about 50%-63% of TNBC patients achieve a pCR. This depends highly on the size of the tumor. Half a percent of women die from the current approved regimen.

Preliminary findings on safety and efficacy from this randomized control study are encouraging to us and our European investigators. I would now like to discuss our clinical publication efforts. Last quarter, I discussed the 2025 eBioMedicine paper, which focused on translational science of using our drug alone. We continue to pursue additional peer-reviewed manuscript publications from our completed studies to further communicate the important clinical data and results to the oncology community. We have submitted a manuscript to a quality journal from our INVINCIBLE-2 breast cancers trial, and another manuscript from our IT-01 study in metastatic cancer of our drug with immunotherapy to another journal.

The journal's editors accepted each manuscript for peer review, and we have received reviewer comments, which we are addressing. Assuming our responses satisfy the reviewers and editors, we hope to see the papers published next year before Q2. Lastly, we continue to pursue potential partnerships in order to advance our programs more quickly and effectively. While the process is still early, we are pleased with the interest in our science and clinical trials, and discussions continue with several companies. We have also engaged a senior business development consultant to provide supplemental outreach and additional support.

To summarize, our cash position is good, we have options to increase capital, our clinical studies are advancing, and we have reinitiated patient enrollment in both late-stage programs. New peer-reviewed clinical publications are in process, and partnering business development discussions continue. This time, I would like to open the call up to questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, you may press star, then one on your touchtone phone. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, please press star, then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question will come from Kumar Raja with Brookline Capital. Please go ahead.

Kumar Raja: Thanks for taking my questions, and congratulations on all the progress. First, with regard to the INVINCIBLE-4 study, what specific safety endpoints or the metrics will the IDMB looking at in Q1, and what would give confidence that the localized skin irritation has been resolved?

Lewis Bender: Yeah. Thank you, Kumar, for the question. They are looking at the surface of the skin, whether or not there is any irritation over a period of several months. The patients have been enrolled, we are following them for a number of months. We are going to stop after a certain number of patient months. It is coming up very soon. They are just simply going to look and see if the issues that we saw before, and did not see in INVINCIBLE-2, with this new dosing regimen, exist or not. It is that simple.

It is looking at the images of the skin and probably some other metrics that they have, but nothing other than a simple visual, I think, is the key criteria for them.

Kumar Raja: Okay. You also hinted a little bit about business development. Can you provide any color on the nature of this discussion? Anything you can share with regard to that?

Lewis Bender: Well, we have been discussing with regional players, we have been discussing with multinational players. We are still in the evaluation part of this. We have a data room, there are CDAs in place, we are in discussion about the programs. What is of interest to these companies is both programs in some cases, one or the other program in other cases. There are multiple discussions, multiple topics.

We are really in the get to know each other stage right now, but I can tell you that the interest in a phase III program and phase II program in breast cancer, where it is a single dose and a phase III program in a rare disease like sarcoma, which has literally nothing really for 10 years of any consequence, is of interest to these companies.

Kumar Raja: Okay, great. Finally, with regard to the INVINCIBLE-3, what are your expectation in terms of getting additional sites activated? Thank you.

Lewis Bender: Well, as I said, we have opened a number of sites. We are looking for patients. As Joe has said, it will be in a gated way so that we can manage enrollment as we bring in capital. We do not want to get our skis ahead of ourselves and enroll too quickly, which we could possibly do, before we have the adequate cash. Capital will be the gating factor on how quickly we enroll. The enthusiasm is there. We have maintained almost all of the sites over the last, I would say, year and a half since we paused the study. Contracts are in place, budgets are in place.

We had almost 32 sites with contracts agreed and another 30 sites with contracts in negotiation when we paused. We could enroll quickly, or quicker than what we are planning, as we get more capital. It is really going to be definitive on the capital raising that we do.

Operator: Your next question will come from Charles Wallace with H.C. Wainwright. Please go ahead.

Charles Wallace: Hi, this is Charles on for RK. Thanks for taking my question. I guess first from me, for the INVINCIBLE-3 study, you mentioned several sites were active and patients identified. I was just curious if any of the patients have been randomized at this point, and how many sites do you expect to have open by year end?

Lewis Bender: Patients have not yet been randomized. They're going through an evaluation and screening process to make sure they meet all the suitable enrollment criteria that we have. There are a number that have been identified, but that's a process that takes a little bit of time. Ultimately, we will have about 10, we think, initially enrolling, but ultimately, the number of patients we can accept is really going to be dependent on the capital.

Charles Wallace: Okay. Yeah, that makes sense. I guess another question on INVINCIBLE-3. You mentioned the switch to the density-based CT image. Will that just be for the active arm or also the standard of care comparator? Or will the standard of care still use the size-based image?

Lewis Bender: So, it's for both arms. Obviously, it has to be for both. In Choi, there is an element of RECIST, right? So, what you have is, if you're measuring the size increase and the density change. If there's no density change and the size increases, then it's a PD, right? So, it's the same for both groups because they have to use one criteria for both groups. Seeing in our drug a Choi score for the tumors that we've selected for the Choi measurements, a density decrease but a size increase, and the density decrease is above 15%, even if the size increase is really high, it's a PR by Choi.

Because density is really what we're looking at trying to control, because that means that there's no live cancer. If there's a lower density, it's become a sack of water, then even if it gets very big, it's a PR by Choi. Now, we don't know that density change is going to happen in the standard of care, but if it does, and there is an increase, then it's a PR for the standard of care as well. I mean, it's the same criteria, and it is used in sarcoma. Remember, it's only for progressive disease. It is not the endpoint. The endpoint is overall survival, but it is used in both arms.

Charles Wallace: Great. That's very helpful. I guess final question from me. You mentioned the new CRO initiated in the third, or you paid in the third quarter. Does this cover both of the two studies, and does this kind of affect any timelines? Maybe just a little color on why you switched CROs.

Lewis Bender: The new CROs are only for the INVINCIBLE-3, because that's the sarcoma study. We decided to fractionate to different groups to help handle different things. So, we have this CRO that's going to be doing the reads rather than the sites. We have the CRO for statistics. We have the CRO for monitoring. We just felt that it would be better to manage it that way than what we were doing before. For the French and Swiss sites, it's the same group. It's Swiss Cancer Institute in Switzerland. It's the same group, UNICANCER in France. So, that study is separate on the CRO side from the sarcoma study.

Charles Wallace: Great. Then maybe final question from me. So, for the INVINCIBLE-4 study, you mentioned that you expect to complete enrollment by the end of 2027. Does this include any activation of U.S. sites?

Lewis Bender: It does not. It is solely right now going to be in France and Switzerland. That could change, but right now, that is, we believe, unnecessary.

Charles Wallace: Great. Thank you so much for taking my questions.

Lewis Bender: Thanks. Thanks very much, Sean.

Operator: Your next question will come from Ilya Zubkov with Freedom Broker. Please go ahead.

Ilya Zubkov: Good morning, and thank you for taking my questions. First, on INVINCIBLE-4, as the study is a part of phase II/III program, and assuming the amended regimen pCR holds up, could you elaborate on what would the registrational study look like, and roughly what would it cost?

Lewis Bender: Yes. What would a registrational study look like? So, obviously, what we're looking at here is an improvement in pCR, but also because of what we're seeing with regard to the safety, certainly with the immune-related adverse events, what we would do is we would take that data back, analyze how much better, if at all, we're seeing in terms of safety, systemic safety, less grade 3 adverse events, less immune-related adverse events. We'd go to FDA with a trial design sized based on this study for a direct comparison of our drug to the standard of care.

That study cost, obviously, if we're looking for an accelerated approval endpoint, would be costed based on the size of the pCR data. We'll have to run that through FDA. Now, we will have to do event-free survival, which will be a larger study. But the question is, will FDA, if we do see the kind of overall safety in terms of reduced grade 3 systemic adverse events and much fewer immune-related adverse events, and our pCR data is, I'm not going to expect it to be 30% better, but it could be a good 10%-15% or 20% better.

How is the combination of better safety and a pCR, if it's even smaller than what I just said, suitable to the FDA? I think before we really get into any sizing and cost, we have to have the data from this phase II study, or at least close to the data on this phase II study, and then go back to FDA with a discussion on what the appropriate study would be for approval.

Ilya Zubkov: Mm-hmm. Great. Thank you. One more question on the cash spending. I see that cash used in operations was about $2.5 million in Q3, against your $1 million per month second half guidance. What does steady state monthly burn look like for Q4 and 2027 with later sites INVINCIBLE-3 and INVINCIBLE-4, and the new manufacturing batch?

Joseph Talamo: Ilya, so we completed, you're right, about $2.7 million in operating cash burned in the third quarter. We're providing guidance of the same $1 million per month in the fourth quarter, as we exit 2026. The 2027 guidance is going to be largely dependent on bringing in additional capital and how much more we can ramp up enrollment. So, we'll provide what 2027 looks like, but you can get a feel for where we are right now at the current operations, running about $1 million a month. But again, we'll provide better guidance as we head into 2027, once we know what our capital situation looks like.

Operator: Again, if you have a question, please press star, then one. Your next question will come from James Molloy with Alliance Global Partners. Please go ahead.

James Molloy: Hey, guys. Thank you very much for taking my questions. You guys touched on quite a bit the capital issues, and that has certainly been a capital constraint, as everyone's problem, not just yours, of course. Can you talk a little bit about potential out-licensing or partnership opportunities that could offload some of the cash needs to a larger pharma partner?

Lewis Bender: Yes. That would be a key objective for us to achieve, that a partner would come in, fund part or all of the programs, and take a license to it. And those are the kinds of objectives and discussions we have. Sometimes partners want to see for themselves how it works in combination with their drug, and may fund some of those kinds of things. So, there's a lot of discussions and a lot of options on the table for the companies with whom we are in discussion.

But again, it's still a getting-to-know-you type of stage here, where they like the programs, but also potentially will have complementary products that they would want to partner with us to test our drug with their product. So, there's a lot of diverse ideas being discussed between us and some of the parties that we've been talking to.

James Molloy: Thank you for that. Is there any way to give color for us? I was looking in on sort of the number of companies or the size of the companies, or any potential ties or something that could potentially happen in 2027?

Lewis Bender: There are several large multinationals and a number of regional players as well, smaller ones. It is very early in terms of the getting to know you, but we are very pleased with the interest that we have gotten so far.

James Molloy: Yeah. Then I think, was it INVINCIBLE-3 where you mentioned you changed from just the sizing to the density to account for false progression? False progression is certainly not unheard of in immune therapies. What sort of drove that change, and how does that make interpreting the results more or less challenging?

Lewis Bender: Well, what drove the change was the patients were the doctors were seeing on the scans the tumors becoming necrotic and cystic, and then they had to pull them off because the tumor volumes were getting better. So the patients were getting potentially derived benefit, but by protocol, because the size was increasing, they had to pull them off. Then the doctors, they wanted to keep them on, but by protocol, they were obligated to remove the patient. So, that was the primary reason. Then that is when they said, "You got to use this density measurement. We are seeing good results there." Then it was kind of fortunate that we were paused at the time.

But ultimately, this switch was recommended by the doctors.

James Molloy: Okay, great. Thank you. Thank you for taking my questions.

Lewis Bender: Okay. I am going to thank everybody for the call. I just would like to say the following. Look, I believe that to make a real difference in cancer, new and different approaches may be required, even if those approaches go against the current grain of thought. I was recently asked to write a guest column for the October 15th issue of the trade publication, Drug Delivery Leader. In that article, I discussed the long history of attempts to create intratumoral therapies. I also described the common thread for why those prior attempts have really not lived up to expectations. Simply put, the tumor microenvironment is incompatible with water-based drugs.

Water-based drugs must be dosed to patients, and we have made a 100% water-based cancer-killing immune-activating product that is highly compatible with a high-fat, high-pressurized tumor microenvironment. Our phase III INVINCIBLE trial will hopefully show for the first time that a local drug, an intratumoral drug alone, can increase survival in metastatic cancer with fewer side effects. We also hope to achieve improved safety and efficacy for presurgical breast cancer patients with our drug when combined with current treatment. If our trials in sarcoma and triple-negative breast cancer are successful, I believe that this will be a transformational change for cancer patients. I want to thank everybody again for your time today.

Operator: Conference is now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

Knightley and Ben Whishaw return with razor-sharp banter, tangled conspiracies and plenty of bloodshed

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Black Doves" was one of my favorite surprises of 2024. A spy thriller with a panache for murder, double-crosses and dark comedy? Netflix, you really do know me.

Verdict: "Black Doves" season 2 is a thoroughly entertaining return, with plenty of twists, sharp humor and terrific performances from Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw. It occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets, but the show's winning mix of spy games and genuine friendship makes this another binge-worthy winner.

Release schedule: All 6 episodes now streaming

Now, Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw are back for another round as secret agent Helen Webb and her hitman best friend, Sam Young. I've watched all six episodes of "Black Doves" season 2, and I'm happy to report that creator Joe Barton has done it again. This is a terrific installment, with plenty of twists, sharp dialogue and wonderfully messy characters.

So what makes this return such a success? Well, there are a few things, starting with deeper insights into the backgrounds of several major players.

Kelly most recently reviewed "The Gilded Age" season 4, "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

Helen is still feeding government secrets to the Black Doves, the shadowy organization that employs her, while her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) is about to become prime minister. You'd think that would be enough to keep her occupied, but there's another crisis brewing. Her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), is accused of plotting a coup against the organization, putting Helen and Sam in the middle of yet another sticky situation.

It leads to some fascinating revelations about Mrs. Reed's past, including a family connection that turns out to be rather more complicated (and deadly) than anyone expected. I particularly enjoyed the flashbacks to her earlier life; getting a better sense of how Reed became the woman she is today makes her even more interesting. It also gives the world of "Black Doves" a richer history and texture.

The plotting does get pretty convoluted at times. There are a lot of people with competing agendas, and keeping track of who's working for whom and whose loyalties lie where can feel like a full-time job. But honestly, that's part of the appeal. Just when you think you've figured out what's going on, someone turns out to be working for someone else, usually with a gun on hand. It's all very entertaining.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The returning cast is in fine form, particularly Knightley and Whishaw, whose chemistry remains one of the best things about the show. Helen and Sam's friendship is the heart of "Black Doves." You can see their genuine affection for each other, even when they're busy shooting at various foes. Sam has his own demons to contend with this season, and as compelling as that storyline is, the show is strongest when the two of them are in a scene together.

Season 2 also brings in some welcome new faces, most notably Ambika Mod as Laila, an acerbic Black Doves agent who helps Helen with a heist (while toting a big gun, of course). Mod is fantastic, bringing a wonderfully snarky energy to the proceedings and delivering some of the season's best lines.

Not everyone makes quite the same impression. Neve Campbell joins as American envoy Cecile Mason, but her character doesn't get much to do. It's a bit of a waste of an actor and I'm still scratching my head about why someone of Campbell's caliber was cast in such a nothingburger of a role.

There's a lot of competition in the spy thriller department these days, but "Black Doves" continues to hold its own. It's got the action and intrigue you'd expect from the genre, but it also has a sense of humor that keeps things from getting too serious.

Season 2 isn't without its shortcomings. A few characters could use more screen time, and the plot occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets. But those are relatively minor complaints when you've got the kind of cracking cast that could make a dictionary recital work.

Most of all, I'm just glad we get another six episodes with Helen and Sam. Their friendship gives the show something beyond the usual spy-versus-spy shenanigans. If you enjoyed season 1, season 2 is just as good. And there's plenty of story left for "Black Doves" to continue for at least one more outing, but I hope it's more like three or four.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3292. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

CNET built a custom ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that has been folding and unfolding the iPhone Duo 24 hours per day, 7 days a week for over a week now.

When the livestream wrapped up yesterday, iPhone Duo had hit just over 260,000 folds.

So far, the hinge and crease seem to be holding up extremely well. But CNET says it will continue testing daily until at least November 20 to see if anything might change over time.

#3290. SoundCloud lets ElevenMusic users publish AI-made songs directly

Tracks arrive labelled as made with ElevenMusic, and SoundCloud Artist Pro members get three months of ElevenMusic Pro free.

SoundCloud is opening a direct publishing route for music made with the ElevenMusic app, the AI music generation platform from ElevenLabs, allowing creators to send AI-generated tracks to the streaming platform without exporting and uploading them manually.

Previously, users had to download their tracks from ElevenMusic before uploading them to SoundCloud themselves. With the new integration, SoundCloud becomes the first platform outside ElevenMusic where users can publish their creations directly.

Tracks uploaded through the integration will carry a label identifying ElevenMusic as their source, making the use of AI visible to listeners. SoundCloud also prohibits AI-generated content that misleads audiences about its origins or creators, including music that impersonates other artists.

“SoundCloud has always been a place where artists experiment, push boundaries, and turn creative ideas into something bigger,” said Eliah Seton, CEO of SoundCloud.

ElevenLabs, best known for its AI voice technology, entered the music market in 2025 with its first music generation model. In April, it launched ElevenMusic as a standalone app, allowing users to create songs from lyrics, melodies, or moods, as well as remix tracks by other artists.

“We built ElevenMusic to help more artists create, experiment and reach their fans,” said Mati Staniszewski, CEO and cofounder of ElevenLabs. “Music creation and discovery belong together and now, with SoundCloud, that music can reach even more audiences and communities.”

For SoundCloud, the agreement is part of a broader effort to bring AI tools into its platform. Last month, it partnered with Moises, an app used to edit existing music, and it already has an agreement with Google’s Flow Music.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 combines outstanding smart features with solid sports tracking to be one of the best all-round options on the market.

The Pace 4 Pro is a thin, lightweight sports watch with a bright AMOELD display and impressive battery life.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro and Apple Watch Ultra 4 both launched in September this year and both impressed me in my testing overall. I rate the Coros as one of the best sports watches available, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is my favorite sporty smartwatch.

I wore both for my final week of training for the Frankfurt Marathon, and then for race day itself, where I ran 2:25 in my 18th marathon.

With one watch on either wrist, I was keen to see if there were any noticeable differences in their GPS and heart rate accuracy on the day.

I also checked their battery life throughout the weekend to see how fast they were draining, noted any design differences that stood out, and kept in mind how useful they were outside the run itself.

This was a true sports watch vs. smartwatch test, and I’ve picked out the key differences I noticed between the two watches over the marathon weekend below. For more detailed info on either watch, check out our full Apple Watch Ultra 4 review and Coros Pace 4 Pro review.

Before diving into the test, it’s worth noting that the Coros Pace 4 Pro is cheaper than the Apple Watch Ultra 4. It will set you back $449, compared with $799 for the Apple.

Coros rarely reduces its watches, whereas the Ultra 4 is likely to go on sale in time, which will make the gap between them smaller, but the Pace 4 Pro is always going to be the more affordable pick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I love the look of both watches, but they have a different feel on the wrist. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has a full titanium case and is more robust and heavy — it’s a more premium look for sure.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is delightfully light and slim, and has a sapphire crystal case and a titanium bezel, so it’s also going to be durable.

Both watches have three buttons, one of which is a dial, and bright displays that are easy to read in all conditions, including the wet and windy day we had in Frankfurt.

In the rain, the fact that you have to use the touchscreen on the Ultra 4 to navigate its apps and menus is a little annoying compared to the buttons on the Coros.

Importantly, you can do all the key actions you need during runs, like pause and lap, using buttons on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but you have to use the screen to actually end your run.

The Frankfurt Marathon is a tough test for GPS accuracy because the first and final 5K of the race involve twisting around the skyscrapers in the city center. In between, it’s easy enough for watches, with a big loop out to the suburbs.

On the day, the Coros Pace 4 Pro logged a total distance of 42.52km (26.42 miles) and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 logged 43.07km (26.76 miles).

The official marathon distance is 42.19km/ 26.21 miles, and although you never run exactly this distance in an event because of weaving around crowds, I certainly think the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more accurate.

I noticed it was closer in line with the kilometer markers on the course, and because I was in the first 100 runners, I was able to stay pretty close to the most direct racing line throughout the event, so the Ultra 4’s total distance seems too much (it also read long for my colleague Jane at the event).

Looking at the GPS tracks of the watches, you can see they both went wrong at various stages in the city center under the tall buildings there, but the Ultra 4 cut corners and tracked me off the road more often.

This was unexpected for me, as I’ve run marathons with every Apple Watch Ultra and generally they have been pretty good on GPS accuracy in city centers.

I actually used the pacer mode on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it logged me finishing the marathon in 2:23… if only.

Concerning heart rate accuracy, I’m not going to be too hard on either watch because I didn’t wear a chest strap to get a reading to compare them to, and I wore arm sleeves during the marathon, which had watch holes but might have impacted the sensor accuracy.

Looking at the graph of the readings from the two watches, I’d say two things stood out to me when comparing them with past marathons and what I know my heart rate tends to do during them.

One is that the Coros had a consistent reading, but it looks too high compared with my max heart rate of around 176, and it doesn’t trend up throughout the event, which always happens during marathons in my experience.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4’s readings look more accurate to me, aside from the long section from the one-hour to two-hour mark where it didn’t take a reading, greying out the number on the watch because it wasn’t confident it had it right.

I’ve done a lot of testing of the heart rate sensors on both watches outside the marathon (when not wearing arm sleeves), and both are pretty good, but if you want the most reliable results, I’d always say using a chest strap is better.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro certainly wins the battery life battle between these watches, lasting up to seven days on a charge with the screen always-on, compared with 50 hours on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

I used the marathon weekend away as a chance to test the real-world battery life performance of the two, taking both off the charger early Friday morning when I flew to Frankfurt.

After short runs with both watches on Friday and Saturday, the Coros was down to 75% on Sunday morning, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 was at 41% (note that I didn’t sleep with them on, so that saved some battery life).

At that point, I got nervous about the Ultra 4 lasting the marathon and charged it to 75% to match the Coros, which didn’t take long thanks to the fast charging on the Apple.

During the race, I did listen to music on the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for about an hour, which increased how much battery it used, but even so, I could have got by with the 41% it originally had left, as it only drained by 16% in the race.

The Coros only lost 10% of its battery in the race, though, and is certainly the better option for battery life, but the Ultra 4 did impress me over the course of the weekend, and still had 32% of its battery left when I got home on Monday, with only that one short charge over the whole marathon weekend.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is clearly a better smartwatch than the Coros, with a full App Store, easy music storage through streaming services and NFC payments. The Coros can store MP3 files for Bluetooth playback, but that’s about it.

This did come across on a weekend away, where the Ultra 4 could do things like show boarding passes for my flights, and I could wirelessly adjust my running playlist on the watch pre-race and listen to music during the event.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also has more customization options, especially on watch faces. If it’s smarts you want, it’s definitely the better pick.

The weekend trip showcased the pros and cons of both sports watches and smartwatches, and there still isn’t one device from any brand that manages to nail both sides of the coin.

During the marathon, the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more reliable for GPS accuracy and pacing, which is absolutely crucial for me, and it offers much better battery life than the Ultra 4.

However, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is certainly a more useful smartwatch, and it does still offer good sports tracking and a very attractive, robust design.

As someone who has made running most of my job and personality, the superior sports tracking of the Coros Pace 4 Pro is what I’d go for, and I love its lighter design too, but the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a well-rounded pick that handles sports and smarts better than most.
