#3226. MacBook Pro OLED Review: The best display we've ever tested

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display impresses thanks to its astonishing touchscreen OLED display that’s the brightest we’ve ever seen on a laptop. On top of that, it has a thinner, lighter design, punchy speakers, and super-long battery life. Plus. Apple finally ditches the notch. While it’s very expensive, this marvelous laptop will floor you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ($2,899 to start) is the finest laptop I’ve had the pleasure of testing. There’s a lot of hype around Apple’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook, and I can tell you it far surpasses it. Though it commands a steep asking price, I’d argue that this laptop is worth every penny for the pros thanks to the excellent experience you get.

The tandem OLED panel is a stunner, delivering inky blacks and scorching bright whites. You instantly notice the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, which also makes colors pop. Then there’s the touch functionality, which is the most responsive I’ve used on any touchscreen laptop. Combine these features with the Dynamic Island (finally) replacing the notch, and you have the best display ever on a MacBook. This is especially true for models with the optional anti-glare nano-texture display.

Apple didn’t stop with the upgraded display, as this MacBook Pro also has a thinner, slimmer design than its siblings. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display weighs just a little more than a MacBook Air! You also get nearly 17 hours of battery life, blowing away the Windows competition. The cherry on top with the new design is the return of the iconic glowing Apple logo on the lid. In short, Apple somehow perfected its already stellar MacBook design.

While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is decidedly expensive with the same performance as the MacBook Pro laptops released in March 2026, it’s easily one of the best MacBooks and best laptops you can buy. If you can afford it, you won’t be disappointed. Find out more in my full review of the 14- and 16-inch OLED MacBook Pros.

14.2-inch PROLED XDR (3024 x 1986 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

16.3-inch PROLED XDR (3472 x 2266 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

M5 Pro (15-core CPU / 16-core GPU / 16-core Neural Engine)

M5 Pro (18 CPU cores, 20 GPU cores/ 16-core Neural Engine)

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display offers a premium laptop experience, with a magnificent tandem OLED panel, elegant yet utilitarian design, and intuitive touchscreen controls. There’s a lot to love here.

MacBook Pros have used the same design since late 2021. Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the MacBook Pro OLED, retaining the sturdy, squared-off aluminum chassis with rounded edges. However, the new laptops are thinner and lighter than previous models—the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros weigh 0.5 and 0.7 pounds less, respectively, than their predecessors. If you use MacBook Pros as often as I do, you’ll feel the weight difference the instant you pick up either new laptop.

As before, you can open the lid with one hand. This is especially noteworthy because Apple redesigned the lids to better withstand constant tapping and swiping. The lid is also noticeably thinner yet remains very sturdy and doesn’t wobble. Apple has reduced the border size by 15%, resulting in thinner bezels. Lastly, the lid features the glowing Apple logo with a dedicated backlight, signaling to everyone that you’re using a PROLED MacBook Pro.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The keyboard looks and feels the same as on other MacBook Pros I’ve tested, which is great since they’re among the best laptop keyboards. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch model, the keyboard deck is spacious, and the keys are highly responsive, with excellent travel and just the right amount of resistance when pressed. The huge touchpad is also as great as ever, never failing to respond to my gestures. Speaking of touch, the Touch ID button is still here for easier logins. Unfortunately, Face ID is still not supported.

You get the same array of ports here, including three Thunderbolt 5/USB-C ports, an HDMI port, a 3.5mm headphone jack, an SD card slot, and a MagSafe charging port.

Pardon the cliché, but the panel on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a feast for the eyes. Even our lab tester, who tests the best TVs for a living, said he has never seen a lovelier display! I wholeheartedly agree.

The latest trailer for Dune: Messiah showcases what makes the PROLED’s panel such a marvel. The superb contrast renders nighttime scenes appropriately dark, while Arakis’ scorching sun makes you squint during daytime sequences. I’m also impressed by the level of detail on the characters’ dusty faces, thanks to the sharp resolution of both models.

549.8% (SDR) | 1949 (HDR, 10% of display)

Our lab tests confirmed what my eyes saw. Apple claims the PROLED MacBook Pros can reach 2000 nits of brightness, and our display benchmarks were just a hair under that mark. The brightest laptop displays we’ve tested topped out at 1600 nits, but Apple’s notebooks go well beyond that. It’s even more impressive when you consider that images remain clearly defined even when portions of the display are set to maximum brightness.

Color reproduction (sRGB and DCI-P3) is identical on the two PROLED laptops. Color accuracy (Delta-E) is slightly better than on most of the laptops I’ve tested. Combined with the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, you get truly exceptional display quality.

Moving away from benchmarks, let’s discuss the other major display upgrade—the removal of the notch at the top center. While I’ve never been too bothered by the notch, I’m not sad to see it replaced with the Dynamic Island, which makes it easy to access Live Activities. I like how the Dynamic Island expands when you’re playing videos and music, and how you can use the touchscreen to stop playback, fast-forward, and rewind.

The PROLED MacBook Pro with M5 Pro supports up to three external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or one display up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz paired with a second up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz. The M5 Max model steps this up to four external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or two displays up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz.

Both chips can power the laptop's built-in PROLED XDR screen at full resolution at the same time. Thanks to Thunderbolt 5’s native DisplayPort 2.1 bandwidth, you can connect three or four external monitors through a single port using compatible docks or daisy-chaining.

As we detailed in our 10 things you need to know about the MacBook Pro OLED, most laptops use a separate, distinct digitizer to support touch input. Apple found a way to integrate the touch silicon directly into these laptops’ tandem OLED displays. The result? A super precise touchscreen experience.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro. I didn't notice any input lag. Menu bar items expand under your fingertip, and window controls get bigger, making things easier to see and interact with.

So far, I haven’t encountered any compatibility issues with third-party apps. Google apps, such as Docs and Drive, work well with touch based on my testing. And naturally, Apple’s own apps work seamlessly. I’ll keep testing to see if I run into any issues, but so far macOS seems like a natural fit for touch.

I don’t often use touch controls on laptops with touchscreens because they can feel clunky, but I found myself using the MacBook Pro’s touch controls more than I expected. That’s a testament to how well touch is implemented on these laptops.

MacBook Pros have always featured excellent speakers that deliver incredible sound, but even that experience didn’t prepare me for how amazing the speakers are on the new MacBook Pro OLED laptops.

Apple says the enhanced six-speaker sound system now delivers 50 percent deeper bass. And that’s not just marketing bluster. It was the first thing I heard, or rather, felt, when I fired up Tommy Johansson’s cover of Black Sabbath’s “Headless Cross.” The rumbling bass notes beneath the ripping solos and soaring vocals made it feel like a live performance—and no doubt annoyed my neighbors when I had the volume cranked up.

The movie trailer for the latest Godzilla Minus Zero also sounds spectacular on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Explosions, screams, and Godzilla’s iconic roar all came through loud and punchy. And naturally, voices in dialogue-heavy content like the Triple K.O. podcast also sound impressive.

Speakers can almost feel like an afterthought on some laptops, but that’s certainly not the case here. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch MacBook Pro, your ears won’t be disappointed. The sound system on these laptops is every bit as impressive as the display.

Even if the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in the new OLED MacBook Pros aren’t technically new like the Apple M6 chip, they’re still the most powerful M-series chips available for MacBooks. Since these are the same chips we’ve already tested on the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros from March, these laptops deliver comparable performance.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display Apple sent us (valued at $3,699 as configured) has an M5 Pro chip with an 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, 48GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and a glossy display.

Meanwhile, the 16-inch model I reviewed (valued at $8,549) packs an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU / 40-core GPU, 128GB of RAM, a 4TB SSD, and a nano-texture display. Thanks to those specs, both laptops pack a serious performance punch.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

On the Geekbench CPU benchmark, both the 14- and 16-inch PROLEDs delivered strong single- and multi-core scores. They also scored well in Geekbench’s AI benchmarks.

As you can see above, OLED touchscreen competitors like the Dell XPS 16 (currently $2,469) and Lenovo Yoga 9n (currently $2,999) don’t come close in performance. For your reference, the XPS 16 packs an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, while the Yoga 9n has an Nvidia RTX Spark N1X chip, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

Surprise, surprise, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also crushed it in our other benchmarks. Disk speeds are extremely zippy, and the same is true for video transcoding. In fact, the new MacBook was more than 2x as fast as the Dell XPS 16.

Apple’s MacBook PROLED laptops are also more than capable of handling tasks in Adobe creative apps like Photoshop and Premiere Pro. Again, the competition can’t keep pace with Apple’s notebooks.

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

The PROLEDs aren’t slouches at gaming. On the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited GPU benchmark, the laptops scored well, with the M5 Max model performing significantly better thanks to its beefy 40-core GPU. The RTX Spark-powered Yoga 9n didn’t do badly, but Apple’s Pro laptops still outclassed it in this benchmark.

For real-world gaming, I tested Cyberpunk 2077 on both PROLED models. With the “For This Mac” graphics setting, the game ran at 85 fps and 95 fps, respectively. Cyberpunk 2077 is a graphically demanding game that pushes even powerful PCs to their limits, so these results are very impressive.

MacBooks with M-series chips are among the longest-lasting laptops we’ve ever tested. But I wasn’t expecting this kind of endurance, since there appears to be no “power penalty” for Apple adding an OLED touchscreen.

In Tom’s Guide’s battery life test, which involves continuous web surfing over Wi-Fi with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the 14-inch MacBook Pro PROLED lasted 16 hours and 56 minutes, while its 16-inch counterpart endured 21 hours and 24 minutes. The previous non-touch 16-inch MacBook Pro M5 Pro lasted 21:10. This is yet another test in which Windows laptops are handily outclassed.

We always run three battery tests to calculate an average time, but we could only run one test in time for this review. I’ll update once we’ve completed the full testing, but based on my experience, the final results will be just as epic.

The webcam on the new PROLED MacBooks is mostly the same as before, only with a new stabilization feature to prevent screen wobble if you’re actively using the touchscreen display. As before, the camera can record 1080p video and also has Desk View.

The 12-megapixel Center Stage camera is as great as ever. This photo I took in my apartment late at night captures all the details on my face, clothing, and even in my background. During a Google Meet session, colleagues on the call also said my video looked sharp.

The new MacBook Pros come with macOS Golden Gate installed. Like I said in my macOS Golden Gate review, this update isn’t a complete overhaul like macOS Sequoia, but it brings a slew of new and enhanced AI features and smoother overall performance that make using MacBooks feel more personal and streamlined.

macOS Golden Gate now includes a dedicated Siri AI app that works like a typical chatbot. In a dedicated chat window, you can ask Siri AI questions or talk to it about whatever’s on your mind. Siri is baked into the OS, so it can recognize what’s on your screen and do things like add items to your calendar or create shortcuts by speaking what you want instead of building them manually.

A new Liquid Glass UI slider lets you adjust the effect’s opacity more precisely. You’ll also notice that complex background visuals appear more diffused, improving text readability. Icon edges are more pronounced so they stand out more. This feature should have been in Sequoia, but at least it’s here now in Golden Gate.

Another highlight of macOS Golden Gate is Spatial Reframing, which is also available on iOS and iPadOS. Reframe lets you reframe existing photos and adjust the perspective to your liking. If you’ve taken a lot of photos with your iPhone or iPad, this feature is a great way to make them look exactly how you want.

macOS Golden Gate goes big on AI, especially with the new and improved Siri. If that doesn’t matter to you, you’ll still enjoy a smooth, stable macOS experience overall.

The new OLED MacBook Pros are easily the most impressive laptops I’ve ever tested, but all those amazing features come at a steep cost.

I wasn’t expecting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display to be cheap, given all the high-end components it uses. That said, I can’t help but wonder how much these laptops would have cost without RAMageddon inflating electronics prices. I suppose that doesn’t matter, because in this reality, you’ll have to pay a premium for Apple’s high-end touchscreen laptop.

Tech enthusiasts or anyone who can be more productive with a touchscreen laptop will get their money’s worth with the PROLED MacBook Pros. If you want to save money on a MacBook Pro and don’t need the performance of the M5 Pro/M5 Max chips, or if an OLED touchscreen isn’t important to you, the new M6-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. That’s also expensive, but still $900 less than the entry-level MacBook Pro PROLED.

Since the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the regular MacBook Pros we’ve tested, performance gains are negligible at best. This matters if you're considering upgrading from those MacBook Pros to the new touchscreen laptops.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

I selected some benchmarks I discussed earlier to show you how these MacBook Pros compare in performance. As you can see, the gains are minor at best. So unless you are set on owning a touchscreen OLED MacBook, it might be wiser to save your money for future iterations that deliver a substantial performance boost over what you currently own.

I thought the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display could be amazing, but it shattered and exceeded my expectations. The new tandem OLED display raises the bar for laptops in brightness and color reproduction. Smooth touchscreen controls, a lighter design, and booming audio take Apple’s new machine to the next level. Yes, it’s very expensive, but it’s a brilliant laptop that makes competitors pale in comparison.

Apple’s first attempt at a touchscreen MacBook is mostly a success, but I’m already curious to see what future iterations bring to the table. If this initial laptop is anything to go by, we’re in for some truly fantastic devices. For now, Apple has made good with these laptops. They truly are the best of the best.

#3225. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3224. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

#3223. Docusign vs. Monday.com: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Docusign's eSignature empire faces a new test as Monday.com's double-digit growth challenges it on valuation and momentum.

Deciding between an established market leader and a high-growth challenger is a common challenge for investors. Today, we compare whether Docusign Inc. (DOCU -1.96%) or Monday.com (MNDY -3.06%) is the better long-term choice.

Docusign pioneered the e-signature category and now seeks to automate the entire contract lifecycle for businesses of all sizes. Meanwhile, Monday.com provides a highly customizable work management platform that helps teams streamline complex workflows. Both companies compete for enterprise budget in the software space, though they currently occupy very different stages of business maturity.

Docusign provides Intelligent Agreement Management, including its eSignature and contract lifecycle management solutions. The company operates in the broader tech stocks landscape, serving over 1.8 million customers globally through various digital tools. Major strategic technology partners include Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -3.58%), Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM -2.07%), SAP SE (SAP +1.45%), ServiceNow Inc. (NOW -5.93%), Workday Inc. (WDAY -0.83%), and Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -1.93%).

According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached $3.2 billion. This represents an 8.2% increase compared with the prior fiscal year, showing steady expansion in its core markets. Net income for the period was $309.1 million, resulting in a net margin of 9.6% for the latest fiscal year.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is 0.7x and the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, which measure short-term liquidity and total debt levels. Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, reached $1.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Monday.com offers an AI work platform designed to manage and automate work across CRM, service, and development segments. The platform is currently used by approximately 250,000 customers worldwide who utilize its flexible Work OS to build custom applications. By focusing on a no-code interface, the company targets a wide range of departments that need to consolidate disparate work processes.

According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached $1.2 billion. This marked a significant increase of 26.7% compared with the prior fiscal year. Net income for the period was $118.7 million, while the net margin improved to 9.6% as the company scaled its operations.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is 2.5x, and the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.3x, tracking liquidity and total debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, reached $309.9 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC for short) represented roughly 53% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Docusign faces significant revenue concentration, as it relies on its eSignature product for the majority of its total sales. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence could lead to increased competition from general-purpose providers or disrupt the core agreement market. The company also depends on third-party cloud infrastructure from Microsoft and partner platforms to deliver its various services to users.

Monday.com faces intense competition in the productivity and collaboration market from established giants like Microsoft and Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE -0.82%). It must also compete with specialized players like Atlassian Corp. (TEAM -3.47%), Asana Inc (ASAN -4.04%), and Smartsheet for limited enterprise software budgets. The future success of the company depends on its ability to maintain high growth rates while successfully cross-selling its newer customer relationship management (CRM) and service products.

Based on current Forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics, Monday.com appears more attractively priced relative to its growth profile. The P/S ratio measures market capitalization against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Monday.com is undergoing a bit of a reset. In July, it fired 20% of its workforce. It's part of an effort to redirect more capital to AI services for its platform.

In its second quarter, revenue grew 22% year-over-year to nearly $365 million, but net income was $3.64 million, representing a net profit margin of barely 1%.

Still, there were some bright spots. Management touted a record net addition of $100,000-plus and $500,000-plus (client spending) customers, saying they reflect the continued strength of Monday.com's push to go upmarket. In July, the business crossed $1.5 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR), a milestone the company says reflects the durability of its core business even as it reshapes the company around AI.

For the full year, sales should rise nearly 20% to $1.47 billion, but net income should weaken to about $68 million.

For Docusign, sales in its current fiscal year are seen growing by nearly 9% to $3.5 billion, with a slightly better percentage gain in net income to $346 million.

Docusign's launch and global expansion of the IAM platform with the introduction of AI-powered tools should position the company for future growth. However, the not-so-great projected revenue growth rates suggest that Docusign may be entering a phase of more mature growth and a landscape of increasingly competitive digital agreement and contract management software. In particular, news reports OpenAI would launch a ChatGPT product that would compete head-on with Docusign in the document summary field caused some investor fears. Right now, however, the signature and identity verification part of Docusign's business appears unthreatened by ChatGPT.

The choice here is to go with the faster-growing business, sales-wise. In the long term, sales growth is the basis on which businesses can generate profits for investors, so given the two stocks' roughly comparable valuation ratios, Monday.com is the choice.

#3222. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

#3221. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3220. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

Coty Inc. (COTY +12.68%) reported first-quarter results that exceeded management's internal expectations for sales and adjusted EBITDA, despite a modest reported revenue decline of 1%. Management characterized the current period as a transition year focused on the Coty.Curated strategic framework, which prioritizes resources toward 10 core brands that represent the majority of segment revenues. The company reported a narrowing of like-for-like sales declines in its Consumer Beauty division and growth in its primary Prestige brands, particularly in the U.S. and China. Strategic focus remains on organizational simplification, debt reduction, and identifying fixed-cost savings to fund disciplined reinvestment in brand advocacy and influencer marketing.

I would like to remind you that many of the comments today may contain forward-looking statements. Please refer to Coty's earnings release and the reports filed with the SEC, where the company lists factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from these forward-looking statements. In addition, except where noted, the discussion of Coty's financial results and Coty's expectations reflect certain adjustments as specified in the non-GAAP financial measures section of the company's release. With that, we will now open the line for questions.

Could you share what you have built into your budget for the next quarter and over the full year? Secondly, thank you very much for providing all the details on the performance of your 6 core Prestige brands and 4 core consumer brands. Does this give us an indication of the portfolio you intend to retain as part of your strategic review?

And given the absence of skin care brands from this list, should we interpret this as a potential intention to exit the skin care category at some point? And lastly, on the impact of the Gucci license exit, I get the impression that there is a very wide range of estimates for the EBITDA impact next year. Even so, I assume that this impact will be relatively mechanical. Could you please help us quantify it more precisely? And I see the consensus on EBITDA [indiscernible] at $680 million next year. Does that seem reasonable to you considering the impact of the license exit?

Soraya Benchikh: I'll take the first part of the question. This is Soraya Benchikh. I'll take the first part of the question and then pass it over to Markus for the second part. Firstly, let me start with the gross margin and where we landed for the first quarter. Our gross margin declined, as you saw in our statement, by 120 basis points. About 50 basis points of this came from the headwinds from the Middle East freight and material costs, and the rest was basically down to unfavorable mix and excess and obsolescent stock. We're very focused on the controllable drivers that impacted excess and obsolescence stock.

And we're working through these through better planning basically to reduce this because we've had a scattered -- a more scattered approach to innovation with smaller innovations that weren't successful. So as we concentrate and you rightly highlighted in our statement that we've concentrated behind our 6 brands, we will shift to fewer and bigger launches, and that will also help us in terms of the planning and having less obsolescence stock. So this should reduce -- a better S&OP, better demand planning and forecasting and fewer bigger launches will reduce our E&O as we work the inventory down.

Markus Strobel: As for portfolio, first of all, we are very pleased with our top 6 brands growing 5% in the first quarter. Still more work to do because we need broader growth, we need faster growth, and we're working on that. But we are pleased with that. And we are also pleased with the progress we're making in our consumer business where decline was 8% in first half of fiscal '26 is now down to 3%, and we're catching up with market share. And on skin care, actually, we have very much improved profitability, and we are pretty happy with that, too.

Now what this means for your question, it is important for us that all of our business units do well, be it Prestige, be it consumer business, be it skin care, and we are on the way of doing that because it will also give us the strategic optionality of the future. Soraya Benchikh: Okay. This is the strategic review or the Gucci? No, Gucci.

Markus Strobel: I mean to say the impact of the Gucci exit.

Soraya Benchikh: Sorry, can you remind me what the impact of the exit? Okay. We're at the moment in the middle of transitioning the Gucci business. And in terms of the value, have we communicated the value?

Soraya Benchikh: No, the value of the impact.

Markus Strobel: No, I can -- yes, we have -- I can step in here on the value of the impact. Sydney Wagner: Congratulations on the Marc Jacobs license extension and just the success of that makeup launch. Markus Strobel: I think there's a couple of principles that make this launch very successful initially, and we're going to keep it up. So we're going to be much more focused on like which is Gen Z in the Sephora case. And you see the Marc Jacobs proposition really fits to it, thanks to that collaboration.

I -- if you take out -- on Prestige, you take out the Marc Jacobs Beauty pipeline because obviously, the shelves had to be filled in the first quarter. Sydney Wagner: Okay. And if I can just squeeze one more in there. With the greater share of A&CP now concentrated behind the top 6 brands in Prestige and top 4 in Consumer, where the incremental investment be most visible? And which areas do you expect to have the biggest near-term impact there?

Markus Strobel: I think you will see the biggest impact in -- so we have allocated a lot of the incremental investment to improve our capabilities and our impact in advocacy. Operator: We'll move next to Olivia Tong with Raymond James.

Olivia Tong Cheang: I wanted to ask you a couple of questions. First, if you wouldn't mind sort of expanding on what you see as the mile markers of success in this -- in what is clearly a transition year. I know the performance won't be linear. But Markus, can you help us understand how you gauge whether the plan is proceeding as expected? And Soraya, I'm interested in your thoughts on KPIs as well. And then specifically for Soraya, we talked a lot about what you can deploy within this organization when we met. And I wanted to focus on forecasting accuracy, specifically on inventory. And how far through the inventory cleanup are you?

Because excess and obsolescence is still a headwind even though sales drag was at the more favorable end of your guidance range. And just understanding what's going to change or has changed in forecasting and innovation planning to help that?

Markus Strobel: All right. So let me take the first part of the question. I think we are making good progress in our Coty.Curated strategy. You see this in the results of the first quarter. You see this in the concrete share of A&CP that we have increased behind the core brands. And I always talk about focus and sharper priorities, that's what we're doing. And an important element is also innovation. We have launched 4 bigger innovations in this quarter, BOSS Bottled Beyond for Her, the Mood Stones by Kylie, the Marc Jacobs Beauty and the Burberry Amber Vanilla.

And all of these launches are tracking ahead of their objectives, which tells us that disciplined initiative management and fewer, bigger, better is starting to work for us. So I've seen a lot of good green shoots here. We are not there, and we fully admit that because it takes time to make all these changes stick with the organization to embed them in the organization. But we're on our way. Would we like our progress to be faster? Yes, and we're fully working on it. And we will -- we can give you full guidance how this whole thing is going to look, come together once we complete our strategic review.

Soraya Benchikh: Yes. For -- so thank you for the question. So the forecasting reliability and our inventory -- working through our inventory. Olivia Tong Cheang: Got it. Just following up a quick one. If you could give any early thoughts on holiday either in the Western markets or 11/11 in the East?

Markus Strobel: Holiday is just starting. What I can say about holidays, especially in the U.S., is that retailers are starting earlier with their holiday activities, and we're obviously actively participating in these activities because last year, the main activities happened very late in the quarter. And people don't like to wait for that. You want to have more security on your sales and your shipment, also from a retailer perspective. So holiday is starting earlier and earlier. That's the trend that I'm observing this year.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Jonna Kim with TD Cowen.

Jungwon Kim: First one on CoverGirl, you've seen nice improvement there. How sustainable do you think that growth improvement is just going forward? And what are key strategies that you have to improve the performance? And then just the second one, overall in the U.S. Prestige returned to growth in the quarter. How much of that is innovation versus the underlying trends in the core portfolio? And what gives you confidence that you can sustain or accelerate growth from here?

Markus Strobel: Okay. On CoverGirl. CoverGirl is under a program we are calling Color the Future, which is also like part of Coty.Curated. And we are very pleased with CoverGirl almost now catching up with the market in terms of consumption. Net sales are down just 2% this quarter versus almost like 8% in the first half of fiscal '26. And we've seen a gradual improvement quarter-by-quarter. And we hope this will expect -- this will go on like this.

What makes us very confident about this is that we have on CoverGirl, we have smaller innovation bundles, but more powerful innovation bundles, better innovation, more incremental innovation, innovation that needs to earn its place on the shelf and not just being thrown out there. And we already see early success in Q1 because the innovation we launched in spring, we're having actually lower returns than we had the year before. So that means things have been selling out better. Things have been more productive on the shelf, number one. Number two, we are very disciplined to supporting with media our 2 biggest properties like Simply Ageless and Lash Blast to not deviate into smaller things.

We're always on for our biggest properties that really drive the business and that are really liked by consumers. And number three, we have very exciting innovations going in the market right now and innovation coming up. You may have seen the new Showstopper Mascara of CoverGirl, which is a very exciting innovation with a proprietary mascara brush technology and a very luxurious packaging. So sharper bundles, more consistent advertising over time and better innovation makes us confident that we can sustain this trajectory.

On Prestige, I mentioned before that we are pleased with the 5% growth of the top 6 brands and even without the major launch of Marc Jacobs Beauty, which was the main launch, it would still be up 3%. And we have the innovations that we brought out now that looks strong. And these are innovations that I believe have staying power, and we can support as we go on. So we haven't seen the best of the innovation yet, especially if you consider that on BOSS Bottled Beyond for Her, we have not launched it yet in the U.S. and in the U.K. That's going to happen in spring. So still a lot of mileage in that innovation.

And ever since we've put out BOSS Bottled for Her, we have share growth on Hugo Boss in Germany, which is the biggest market for Hugo Boss after a long time. So we see not only shipment and sales growth, but we see sellout and share growth behind these innovations. So we are confident we can keep that up, and we have a fairly good pipeline on Burberry, on Boss, and on new brand Etro that we're going to bring out in the beginning of 2027. So we're fairly confident that our innovation will keep driving our business.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Javier Escalante with Evercore ISI.

Javier Escalante Manzo: Congratulations on the extension of Marc Jacobs. And this is basically my question, Markus. I believe that you managed this business with Procter a long time ago, and it was a very different view of the industry itself and the business model with licenses. I would like to hear your view, your strategic view about this license model, how it's evolving? 40 years to me qualify as a perpetuity. We see -- we saw something similar with Kering Beauté. Is this where the business is going? Like to unlock co-investment, you need these very long licenses to derisk situations like Gucci happening. Will you seek similar long-term partnerships with core brands like Burberry and BOSS? And I have a follow-up.

But this is -- if you can keep it very kind of like strategic, what's happening? This is 40 years is a long time. Tell us what's happening.

Markus Strobel: I think what's happening in the industry is the industry has become -- fragrances has been a growing category for the last couple of years, and it's still growing very nicely. It was just like 5% up globally in the first quarter. So there is a lot of activity. There's a lot of competition, and we launch things, we need investment and we need security that this investment is going to pay off and that we can continue to reinvest to drive these brands. So the longer the license contract, the better it is.

It's not only for us from an investment point of view, but often also better for the licensee because there's a royalty stream that they can bank on in the future. And interestingly enough, a lot of our contracts today are already brands that we either own or we are on almost perpetual licenses. So we feel good about the longevity of our fragrance, and we will be striving with all of our licenses and also new licenses to extend licenses as long as possible and as early as possible so that we all have security to invest.

Javier Escalante Manzo: So Markus, I take your response. I mean, you can agree or not, that, yes, you would be -- your inclination would be to go back to Burberry and to go back to BOSS and say, "We would love to continue the partnership. We are increasing our investment behind it, but we also need longer durations to derisk that investment and make this a true partnership for a long term." Is that a good characterization of what you just said?

Markus Strobel: That sums it up pretty well.

Javier Escalante Manzo: Okay. And then -- so basically, could you tell us what happened to -- because there were a lot of licenses prior. How many licenses are in Prestige? And in your curated approach, would you think that the idea would be to approach these licensees and unwind so that you have a more curated, but at the same time, a more sustainable, say, equity story proposition for minority shareholders?

Markus Strobel: I think when you look at the licensed fragrance portfolio, duration is one question. The other question is also like you want to have a portfolio that goes for the right target groups, if it's Gen Z, Gen X, probably a stronger region in North America. Some brands might be stronger in China, in Asia, in Europe. So you need to have a pretty good balance. What we're also striving for in the -- when we drive brands in the more uber-prestige market, uber-prestige, high prestige, super high prestige, no matter how you want to call it, is a growing part of the business.

We are just increasing our investment behind Atelier des Fleurs of Chloé, which is very successful in this investment -- in this area. We will be launching Etro in spring in the super premium segment. And we're just coming out with the Burberry Prorsum Collection also in the super premium segment. And the marketing in the super premium segment is slightly different than from the non-super premium segment because you've got to be strong in-store. So all of these brands have in terms of curation, have different KPIs that we need to respect. And we think we have a fairly balanced portfolio with world-class licensees and licensors.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Anna Lizzul from Bank of America.

Anna Lizzul: I was wondering if we could discuss more the outlook within the different geographies. There's certainly some encouraging results here from the Americas with improvements in innovation. But it looks like in Europe, a bit of a different dynamic given the softer market consumption there. I was wondering if you could touch on the broader political environment and the impact to sales? And also, how should we be thinking about the cost outlook, just given the pressures you're seeing from freight in the Middle East and what your level of confidence is on delivering on cost management to mitigate this in the near term?

Markus Strobel: Okay. Let me just go on what I see in terms of market development and our development in these markets, and then Soraya can add some color when it comes to costs out of the Middle East and how we're dealing with that. Again, yes, we are pleased with our progress in the U.S. It's the biggest fragrance market. So it's important for us to win. So not there where we need to be, but the progress and we will behind Coty.Curated make this stronger as we move along. We're also very pleased with our development in Asia. We have -- China had a particularly strong quarter in Q1. So our total Asia business is up 8% in net sales.

Europe is the area that we need to focus on fixing. We have good market growth in Spain, Italy. And we have a fairly soft market growth in Prestige in Germany and France. So the market growth in Europe is on average lower than in the other geographies, but it's a big part of our business. So we are very aware of that. We are making progress on Hugo Boss, which is our biggest brand in Europe. I just mentioned the BOSS Bottled for Her launch, which comes fully incremental because obviously, it's a female launch and BOSS is mostly a male brand. And this is our #1 target is to make Hugo Boss grow again in Europe.

And I think we're in a good way. We just signed a partnership. You may have seen that with HYROX in a lot of geographies. We're working together with HYROX in big events, which is going to increase our advocacy, our influencer and creator standing. So we are pleased with that. And then we also curate our portfolio in Europe. Hugo Boss important, Burberry important and the other brands, the regional brands that are important in countries like Germany, we're not neglecting. So we are not there where we need to be in Europe, but we're on the way.

Soraya Benchikh: Okay. When it comes to the outlook and looking at cost pressures, we really -- the Middle East headwinds that I outlined in describing the margin, we expect them to persist for the rest of the year. Currently, what we've built into our forecasting is particularly on oil that has impact our input costs, $30 million to $40 million impact. And we think that now if the barrel price stays above $100, we're going to be in the upper range of this. But generally, with the macro pressures, if they do continue at this level or intensify, we're looking to pull productivity and fixed cost levers first to preserve the room to invest behind the brand.

Productivity is happening on all lines of the P&L, not just on fixed costs. We're also looking at the ROI threshold on our marketing investments. We've rolled out tools to several markets to measure the effectiveness of our spend. So yes, this is a transition year. There's lots of moving parts, but we are going to work productivity really hard to preserve the investment behind our brands because our priority is still to achieve the quality growth that we're pursuing on the top line. I hope that answers it.

Operator: At this time, this concludes -- oh, I'm sorry, go ahead.

Markus Strobel: No, there's no more questions, let me just conclude the call, right?

Markus Strobel: Or do we have more questions?

Operator: We have no more questions at this time.

Markus Strobel: Okay. Okay. Let me just conclude it then. So to summarize it all, Q1 came ahead of our expectations, but it's obviously not where we want to be. We want to be better. Fiscal '27 is a transition year for us. And as we mentioned a couple of times, the recovery will not be linear. Still, we have very encouraging early signs. Our top 6 core Prestige brands grew 5% like-for-like, and we expect growth on our top 6 core Prestige brands in Q2 as well. We will keep investing behind our core brands, turning stronger performance into cash, and we also reduce debt. And we remain on track to complete the strategic review by the end of calendar 2026.

We know that your confidence is earned through consistent delivery, and we will be transparent and accountable along the way. So thanks for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect. Thank you.

#3218. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3217. Football Manager, Warhammer Survivors and More Land on Xbox Game Pass Soon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Microsoft on Tuesday announced the games it’s adding to its Xbox Game Pass service in the first half of November. Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most anticipated game of the year, which Rockstar Games will release on Nov. 19, so GTA 6 may consume your playtime from then on. But that still leaves plenty of time to give these upcoming Game Pass titles a shot. I know I’m particularly excited about Warhammer Survivors. I really enjoyed Vampire Survivors, and I can’t wait to play as Fo’Baran, the chaplain of my beloved Salamanders from Warhammer 40K.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award winner, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 per month. With a higher-tier Game Pass Ultimate subscription ($23 per month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones on release day, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass soon.

Class is back in session in this puzzle game. This sequel to the award-winning Escape Academy brings you more puzzles to solve and a series-first open-world format. That makes the campus one big puzzle room filled with secrets, traps and more. If you get stuck, you can always chill with your friends and enjoy student life away from the classroom. The choice is yours.

Poncle, the creator of the indie hit Vampire Survivors, teamed up with Auroch Digital to let you bring your favorite Warhammer primarchs and champions into bullet-heaven action. Each character has their own special ability to help you defeat waves of enemies. Every stage is a new arena full of enemies and secrets to uncover. So grab your chainsword and whirlwind axes, because there are pixelated enemies to destroy.

Get ready for the most immersive matchday experience yet in the latest installment of the long-running Football Manager series. You’ll shape your club and define your team’s style, and you can get lost in the wider football universe thanks to smart news and events that mirror the drama of the football calendar.

While Xbox is bringing those titles to Game Pass soon, it’s also adding these games to the service in the first half of November, too.

Game Pass Essential costs $10 a month and offers access to a relatively small library of games compared with Game Pass Premium and Ultimate. While Microsoft doesn’t regularly add many games to Essential’s library, it’s adding these eight titles to this Game Pass tier on Nov. 15.

While Microsoft is adding several games to Game Pass soon, it’s also removing over a dozen games on Nov. 15. So you’ll have to buy these games separately if you still need to complete your main campaign or any side quests after they’re removed.

For more, here’s our Xbox Game Pass review and other titles you can play on the service. You can also read our recent review of the Xbox Nano Controller.
