#3216. Comstock Resources (CRK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Stake sale and Jones venture aim to cut debt roughly in half.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Comstock Resources, Inc. (CRK -0.45%) reported production growth driven by its development programs in the Haynesville and Bossier shales while announcing strategic partnerships to deleverage its balance sheet. Management highlighted the execution of a $1.65 billion divestiture to SOCAR and a $450 million drilling venture with the Jones family, which are intended to fund the continued delineation of the Western Haynesville acreage. The company stated it expects to generate free cash flow in the fourth quarter and has extended its credit facility maturity to Nov. 2028, with a further extension to Nov. 2031 contingent on closing the SOCAR transaction.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q3 2026 Comstock Resources Inc. earnings conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star 11 on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star 11 again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Jay Allison, Chairman and CEO. Please go ahead.

Jay Allison: Thank you. I know that there are several companies presenting at the same time, so those of you that have joined this call, we're always appreciative and thankful. Welcome to the Comstock Resources Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results Conference Call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly result presentation. There, you'll find a presentation entitled Third Quarter 2026 Results. I am Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer of Comstock, and with me is Roland Burns, our President and Chief Financial Officer, Dan Harrison, our Chief Operating Officer, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations.

Please refer to slide two in our presentations and note that our discussions today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws. While we believe the expectations in such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. If you would turn to slide three, we summarize the highlights of the third quarter. Our production grew 9% from 2025 and was 8% higher than the second quarter, driven by new wells turned to sales from our drilling program.

In the quarter, 16 legacy Haynesville wells were turned to sales, with an average lateral length of 10,812 feet and an average per-well initial production rate of 25 million cubic feet per day. Six of those were horseshoe wells. We also turned six new Western Haynesville wells to sales in the third quarter, with an average lateral length of 9,829 feet and an average per-well initial production rate of 33 million cubic feet per day. The higher production drove our financial results, which Roland will go over in a few minutes. Starting September 1, we entered into a drilling venture with Jerry Jones covering 27 wells.

18 of the wells are in the Western Haynesville, with nine in the Legacy Haynesville. The new venture will allow us to generate free cash flow in the fourth quarter while also allowing us to continue our development and delineation program in the Western Haynesville. On November 9, yesterday, we entered into a definitive purchase and sale agreement with SOCAR for a $1.65 billion divestiture. The proceeds from the transaction will substantially improve our balance sheet. We also just extended the maturity of our bank credit facility by a year, which will further extend an additional four years after closing the SOCAR transaction. I will cover all of those strategic transactions in the next slides. Turn to slide four.

We summarize the drilling venture with Jerry Jones. Beginning September 1, 2026, Arkoma III, a partnership owned by the Jones family, will fund the drilling and completion costs of 85% of 18 Western Haynesville wells and 80% of nine Legacy Haynesville wells. Arkoma III will fund an estimated $300 million of capital expenditures in 2026 and an additional $150 million in 2027 on these 27 wells. Prior to September 1, Comstock had spent $180 million on these wells, which will be recovered by Comstock from 100% of the net revenues from the first production of these 27 wells.

Arkoma III will receive the net revenues after the pre-venture costs are recovered until Arkoma III has recovered its cost and a 15% return. After the return on investment is achieved, 50% of the interest in the 27 wells revert to Comstock. The drilling venture allows us to generate free cash flow in the fourth quarter while supporting the continued development and delineation of our 547,000 net acres in the Western Haynesville, as well as providing volumes to Pinnacle Gas Services. If you will turn over to slide five, we will summarize the strategic partner with SOCAR.

SOCAR is purchasing a 20% interest in our Legacy Haynesville, a 15% interest in our Western Haynesville, and 15% of our interest in Pinnacle Gas Services for $1.65 billion. We recently executed the definitive purchase and sale agreement and expect the transaction to close by year-end 2026. Proceeds from the transaction will be used for debt repayment. Comstock will remain the operator of the properties, and Comstock and SOCAR will jointly participate in further leasing and acquisitions in the Haynesville. SOCAR will offer Comstock future LNG marketing opportunities. SOCAR's 15% interest in the Western Haynesville reduces to 7.5% after five years, and once SOCAR has achieved a 15% return on investment in those assets.

As a result, Comstock will have an increased participation in the future upside of the Western Haynesville assets, creating a balanced structure that aligns both parties around the long-term performance of those assets. Slide six shows the ownership interest in the Legacy Haynesville, the Western Haynesville, and Pinnacle Gas Services upon closing of the SOCAR transaction. As previously mentioned, after five years and upon SOCAR achieving a 15% return on the investment in the Western Haynesville upstream assets, Comstock's interest in the Western Haynesville assets will increase from 85% to 92.5%. Sixth Street owns the remaining 27% of Pinnacle Gas Services, which reduces to 19.5% after certain return hurdles are met.

At that point, Comstock's interest in Pinnacle Gas Services will increase to 69.5%. Please turn to slide seven. I will show you the key partnership impact of the SOCAR transaction to Comstock. The $1.65 billion purchase price provides strong validation of the value implied by the quality and longevity of Comstock's upstream assets in the Legacy Haynesville and Western Haynesville, while reaffirming our significant midstream value embedded within Pinnacle Gas Services. SOCAR's investment-grade balance sheet and global LNG marketing operations should help create value for Comstock shareholders.

Comstock will use the proceeds from the SOCAR transaction to repay the outstanding balance in our Comstock revolving credit facility, with pro forma net debt decreasing to about $1.7 billion compared to $3.4 billion at the end of the third quarter. The stronger balance sheet will support continued delineation and development of Comstock's 547,000 net acres in the Western Haynesville. Comstock remains operator of the properties and retains further upside in the Western Haynesville through the reversion provisions. On slide eight, we will show you the benefits of the strategic partnership with SOCAR. The partnership with SOCAR combines Comstock's Gulf Coast location, access to significant gas reserves, and midstream operations with SOCAR's LNG and trading platform.

The scaled footprint across both the legacy and Western Haynesville provides decades of drilling inventory. As a result, Comstock is positioned to maximize natural gas pricing netbacks across domestic and international markets while mitigating volatility via strategic partnership in power supply and midstream investments. Both the Jones family and SOCAR are aligned as long-term strategic stakeholders. Lastly, the delevered balance sheet provides development flexibility across our asset base. I will now turn it over to Roland Burns to discuss the third quarter financial results. Roland?

Roland Burns: All right. Thanks, Jay. On slide nine, we cover the third quarter financial results. Our production in the third quarter averaged 1.3 BCFE per day, which was up 8% from the second quarter of this year, and was 9% higher than the third quarter of last year. Oil and gas sales after hedging were $359 million, reflecting the impact of the higher production being offset a little bit by lower natural gas prices in the quarter. EBITDAX in the quarter was $266 million, and we generated $208 million of cash flow, or $0.71 per share, before any working capital changes during the quarter. We reported a $22 million profit for the quarter, or $0.08 per share.

Included in that number was a pre-tax $35 million mark-to-market unrealized gain related to our future hedges. Excluding the mark-to-market gain, exploration expense, and other non-recurring items, and the related income tax impact of those, we reported net income of $6 million for the third quarter, or $0.02 per share. Slide 10 covers the year-to-date financial results. Production in the nine months of the year averaged 1.2 BCF per day. Oil and gas sales after hedging were $1 billion in that period, and EBITDAX was $763 million, and we generated $588 million of cash flow, or $2.02 per share. We reported a $138 million profit for the first nine months of this year, or $0.47 per share.

That number included $119 million mark-to-market unrealized gain on our future hedges. Excluding that mark-to-market gain, exploration expense, and other non-recurring items, and the related income taxes, we reported adjusted net income of $54 million for the first nine months of this year, or $0.18 per share. Slide 11 breaks down our natural gas price realizations in the quarter. The quarterly weighted average NYMEX settlement price averaged $2.95 in the third quarter, and the weighted average Henry Hub spot price averaged $2.87 in the quarter. We sold a third of our gas in the spot market, so an appropriate NYMEX reference price for our quarter would be about $2.93.

Our realized gas price averaged $2.61 in the quarter, reflecting a $0.34 basis differential compared to the NYMEX settlement price and a $0.32 differential compared to the reference price. In the third quarter, we were 59% hedged, so that increased our realized price to $2.93. We also made an additional $0.02 per Mcfe from our third-party marketing activities. Slide 12 details the operating costs per Mcfe and our EBITDAX margin. Our operating costs per Mcfe averaged $0.80 in the third quarter, up $0.03 from our second quarter rate. Lifting costs were down $0.02. G&A was down $0.01, both attributable to that higher production level we had in the quarter.

Production and ad valorem taxes increased by $0.03 in the quarter, really due to prior period true-ups, and gathering costs were up $0.03. Overall, our EBITDAX margin was 73% in the third quarter. Slide 13, we recap the spending so far this year on our drilling activity and other development activity. We spent a total of $383 million on development activities in the third quarter and $1.1 billion during the first nine months of this year.

In the first nine months of this year, we drilled 39 wells, or 28.6 net to our interest, operated wells, and those were in the Haynesville Shale formation, and then we drilled another 16 or 10 net wells in the Bossier Shale formation for a total of 55 wells or 38.7 net wells. We turned 52 wells or 44.7 net operated wells to sales so far this year with an average overall IP rate of 29 million cubic feet per day. Slide 14 summarizes our capitalization at the end of the third quarter. We ended the quarter with $800 million of borrowings outstanding under our upstream credit facility.

Our upstream borrowing base is $2 billion under the credit facility, and the elected commitment under that facility is at $1.5 billion. All of that was recently reaffirmed in our early November bank meeting. The maturity date of our facility was recently extended also to November 2028. After closing the SOCAR transaction, the maturity will further be extended on our bank credit facility to November 15, 2031. Our last 12 months leverage ratio was 3.2 times, and we ended the third quarter with over $850 million of financial liquidity.

Pro forma for the SOCAR transaction, our debt will be reduced by half, and our leverage ratio improves to two times. Given the impact of the Jones drilling venture on the fourth quarter capital spending, we anticipate generating free cash flow in the fourth quarter, which will further reduce our debt before closing the SOCAR transaction. Dan Harrison: Okay. Thanks, Roland. On slide 15, this is our updated overview of our total acreage footprint in the Haynesville and Bossier Shales, East Texas, and North Louisiana. We have 899 gross operated locations with a 78% working interest, or 698 net locations. Roughly 40% of our 3,255 gross operated locations, or 1,317 locations, have laterals exceeding 10,000 feet. 61% of our gross operated locations have laterals exceeding 8,500 feet. The average lateral in our Western Haynesville inventory is 8,884 feet.

Our Western Haynesville drilling inventory is more weighted to the Bossier formation, with nearly two-thirds of the inventory in the Bossier, and one-third of our inventory is in the Haynesville. We currently have five rigs running on our Western Haynesville acreage today. Slide 18 is an overview of our horseshoe well drilling program, which allows for extended reach and reentry opportunities for higher return drilling locations. The improved drilling economics of the horseshoe wells unlocks previously stranded acreage by converting two sectional laterals into a single two-mile lateral. Since starting the horseshoe program, we have turned 17 horseshoe wells to sales with an average IP of 29 million cubic feet a day and an average lateral length of 10,223 feet.

The two most recent horseshoe wells have an average lateral length of 13,518 feet. As mentioned on the previous slide, we have 108 remaining horseshoe locations as of the end of the third quarter. In addition to the drilling of horseshoe wells, we have identified a number of enhancements to further improve returns, including the rotary steerable technology, redevelopment opportunities, the longer laterals, up to 15,000-20,000 foot, and drill-through applications. Slide 19 outlines our average lateral length drilled based on the wells that we drilled to total depth. The average lateral lengths are shown separately for our legacy Haynesville area and our Western Haynesville areas.

In the third quarter, we drilled 16 wells to total depth in the legacy Haynesville area with an average lateral length of 11,905 feet. The individual laterals range from 6,050 feet up to a max of 15,923 feet. The longest lateral drill to date in the legacy Haynesville area still stands at 17,409 feet. In the third quarter, we also drilled five wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville, with an average lateral length of 8,587 feet. The individual laterals range from 6,936 feet up to a max of 10,920 feet. Our longest lateral drill to date in the Western Haynesville is 14,783 feet. To date, we have drilled 54 wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville.

23 of these 54 wells have laterals exceeding 10,000 feet. Slide 20 summarizes the 38 wells that we have turned to sales in our legacy Haynesville area so far in 2026. The average lateral length was 11,530 feet, and the individual laterals ranged on the low end from 8,497 feet up to a high of 15,772 feet. The average IP for the 38 wells is 28 million cubic feet per day, and included in these 38 wells is 14 horseshoe wells. Slide 21 outlines the 17 wells that we have turned to sales on our Western Haynesville acreage so far in 2026.

These 17 wells had an average lateral length of 10,153 feet and an average initial production rate of 31 million cubic feet per day. Since our last call, we have turned six additional wells to sales with IP rates ranging from 26 to 40 million cubic feet per day and an average IP of 33 million cubic feet per day. We have a total of 47 wells currently producing on our Western Haynesville acreage. Slide 22 highlights our drilling efficiency in the legacy Haynesville area. This is for our benchmark long lateral wells that have laterals over 8,500 feet long.

In the third quarter, we drilled 14 of our benchmark long lateral wells to total depth in the legacy Haynesville and averaged 22 days to total depth. Correspondingly, we averaged 1,156 feet drilled per day on our legacy Haynesville acreage, and this represents a 14% increase versus the second quarter of 2026. Five of the wells we drilled in the third quarter were horseshoe wells. Slide 23, this highlights our drilling progress in the Western Haynesville. During the third quarter, we drilled five wells to total depth. This gives us a total of 52 wells drilled to total depth through the end of the third quarter.

We averaged 56 drilling days for the five wells drilled to total depth during the quarter. This is a decrease of three days compared to the second quarter. The drilling speed of 461 feet per day during the third quarter was 2% lower than the second quarter. The main reason the drilling speed decreased from the second to third quarter was the Dollie Jones. That was our first big hole lateral we drilled during the second quarter, and this well drilled 25% faster than our other wells. If we'd taken the Dollie Jones, it would have been excluded. Our drilling speeds would have improved in the third quarter.

Slide 24 details our D&C costs through the third quarter for our benchmark long lateral wells in the Legacy Haynesville area. These costs reflect all of the wells with laterals over 8,500 foot long. The drilling costs are based on the quarter in which the wells were reached TD, and the completion costs are based during the quarter on the wells that were turned to sales. During the third quarter, we drilled 14 of our benchmark long lateral wells to total depth, including five horseshoe wells. Our third quarter drilling costs averaged $634 a foot. This is an 11% decrease compared to the second quarter.

Our improved drilling performance in the third quarter can be attributed to having much stronger lateral drilling performance compared to the second quarter, which outweighed the impacts of the slightly higher service costs we did experience during the quarter. The rotary steerable drilling technology being deployed in our Legacy Haynesville area, especially in our horseshoe wells, has continued to deliver superior results. It is driving our drilling efficiencies higher. During the third quarter, we also turned 15 of our benchmark long lateral wells to sales on our Legacy Haynesville acreage, of which five were horseshoe wells. The third quarter completion costs came in at $715 a foot. This is a 5% increase compared to the second quarter.

The higher completion costs in the third quarter is partially the result of completing three single well pads during the third quarter, compared to nine during the second quarter. We also experienced the higher service costs during the third quarter. On slide 25 is a summary of our D&C costs through the third quarter for all wells drilled in the Western Haynesville. During the third quarter, we drilled five wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville. Average lateral length was 8,587 feet. The third quarter drilling cost averaged $1,934 a foot. This represents an 11% increase compared to the second quarter.

The biggest factor in our higher drilling costs for the third quarter was the shorter average lateral length of 8,587 feet for the wells in this quarter. To a lesser extent, the higher service costs we experienced also contributed to the higher drilling costs for the quarter. During the third quarter, we drilled our second big hole lateral. This time we drilled it to a more challenging lateral target in the Haynesville, but again, our results met our expectations. During the third quarter, we also turned six wells to sales in our Western Haynesville acreage that had an average lateral length of 9,829 feet. The third quarter completion cost averaged $1,959 a foot.

This is a 22% increase compared to the second quarter, and we had several drivers affecting the higher completion costs during the quarter. The primary drivers have been the transition to pumping the larger fracs. This led to we had a 12% higher proppant loading in the third quarter compared to the second quarter. Couple that with the higher service costs that we had. We also tubed up all but one of our third quarter wells, as opposed to only tubing up one of our wells in the second quarter.

Back to the drilling side, we have been very pleased with the results of our first three big hole lateral wells, and we are planning more of these wells for the future. The bigger hole in the lateral creates the lower downhole temperatures, and we are seeing longer, more reliable runs from our downhole drilling assemblies, and it has also provided us with much better steering ability so that we can keep our laterals on target. One last item I want to update from our last call, we should be deploying our first 10,000 PSI rig in the Western Haynesville towards the end of this month, which we fully anticipate will lead to faster drill times.

We are planning to upgrade two more of our rigs to 10K capability in the second quarter of next year. I will now turn the call back over to Jay.

Jay Allison: Dan, great job. Roland, great job. If you will go over to slide 26, we will summarize our outlook for 2026. Where our Haynesville Bossier leases are located is the sweet spot for demand. With the addition of NextEra, Sixth Street, and SOCAR, I believe we have the winning team.

Operator: Okay, thank you. At this time, we will conduct the question-and-answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star 11 on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star 11 again. We ask that everyone limit to just one question and one follow-up question. Please stand by while we compile the roster. Our first question comes from the line of John Annis with Texas Capital. Go ahead, your line is open.

John Annis: Hey, good morning all, and thanks for taking my questions. For my first one, the Dollie Jones well delivered a 40 million a day IP using the big hole design, and I think you are now drilling your fourth well with that design. What have you learned about the repeatability of results on drilling and well performance, and then ultimately, what portion of the Western Haynesville inventory could ultimately be developed this way?

Dan Harrison: That is a really good question. We are drilling our fourth well at the moment with the big hole design. We have not seen anything to date that tells us that we have any concerns with that design. We really need to drill more wells to just hone in on where the breakover is between drilling a slim hole versus a big hole design. Right now, I would probably just say it is somewhere between 10,000 and 11,000 foot lateral length.

Our goal is, of course, we had the shorter average lateral lengths that we reported for the quarter, and that is just due to where we are trying to hold acreage, and the acreage layout and geology and some other things. But in the future, we will definitely be getting the laterals longer in the years ahead. I would say probably the majority of all our future wells, maybe not within the next year or so, but further out, I would say the majority of the wells will be drilled with the big hole design. We just need some more data to just hone in on really just kind of where that crossover mark is.

But we have been super pleased with it. You asked about the Dollie Jones. That was the first one. That thing really drilled incredibly fast. That was drilled to the Bossier. Our second big hole that I kind of mentioned on one of the slides was drilled to the Haynesville. The Haynesville, just on average out here, is a little bit harder digging than it is in the Bossier. The results from the second well were about right on par with what we expected. But I think maybe one of the things to drive home is the intangible benefit of drilling the big hole.

We can steer and keep the laterals on target much more easy than we can than when we are drilling with the slim hole. When staying on target, this directly correlates to the performance of these wells. You want to keep that lateral right there in the best rock where you want it. Not only can we drill long, but even when we are drilling long, we can still keep that thing on target way out there at the end, which the slim holes, they will start walking, and we have a lot more difficulty keeping them on target when the wells get long. Then that just leads to other issues that add drilling days. Happy with the big holes.

John Annis: Got it. I appreciate all that color. Maybe staying on completion design. Last quarter, you noted the 2Q wells were the first full batch completed with 5,000 to 6,000 pounds of proppant per foot, and said their early pressures look encouraging. With another quarter of production history, are you seeing a measurable improvement in expected EURs, and is that uplift, in your view, sufficient to justify the 12% or so higher proppant loading?

Dan Harrison: Definitely. Absolutely. We actually transitioned our standard frac design when we started out, and really for a lot of early wells, was 4,000 pounds per foot. We did have one big job we pumped back early on, one of the Robertson County wells, but other than that, they were all 4,000 pounds per foot. We transitioned to the bigger fracs really starting in December of 2025 when we started popping them. Every well in 2026 has either been 5,000 or 6,000 pounds per foot. When you run the math on the economics, I mean, you only need maybe an incremental like 0.2 BCF per 1,000 to justify adding another 2,000 pounds per foot.

When you look at the well performance we have today, which it's early on some of these wells, but they do look really good. When you take that early data and combine it with the modeling and stuff that the reservoir group has done, we easily should surpass that 0.2 BCF per 1,000 incremental. That's definitely the direction we're going.

John Annis: Got it. I appreciate the time. I'll turn it back.

Dan Harrison: I think Jay and Roland gave you a pretty good answer. I do not really have a lot to add to that. We are blending in some infill development wells a little bit in 2027, which allow. Carlos Escalante: Sure. No, thank you to the three of you. That sounds like a solid answer, I think. On productivity, just going a step further perhaps on the prior question. If I look at your, particularly one of the Craig Smart, and I am sure I am butchering that name, Craig Smart wells, your normalized initial production rate as a very quick and dirty metric, looks to have jumped and actually posted one of the highest numbers in the two years you have been doing a lot of the drilling.

Just wondering, that is obviously just one piece of the puzzle, initial production, but what steps are you taking or what of the completion design tweaks you have done give you confidence that you can flatten the decline rate, or said another way, can lead to maximization of your EUR and really keep that production up the same way that you perhaps did with some of the earlier wells alongside that Circle M trend line?

Dan Harrison: Yeah. You got the names right, Crutchmore. I think everybody struggles with that a little bit. The answer, without making it real complicated, is the larger fracs. Definitely believe in the larger fracs like we talked about earlier. It just takes a minimal incremental EUR, which we should easily surpass, and the conservative drawdown strategy. You are contacting a lot more rock, you are creating a lot more, stimulating a lot more reservoir volume, and with the conservative drawdown, you keep that open. That is going to lead to the bigger EURs.

The early data that we have got on the wells that we have fracked in the last year with the larger fracs are showing that we are heading in that direction. We do need longer-term production to prove that out, but it is all pointing to where we expect it to go.

Jay Allison: I think the good thing on your question is, if you go probably 90 miles north to south, that is kind of a guess number, but the rock that we have found, I mean, it is consistent quality resource rock. It is not the inventory, the 2,500 locations, it is not the rock. It is now really, with Dan's program, that is, we are getting to the point where we can have some repeatability.

Jacob Roberts: Okay. I appreciate that. Then maybe just to follow up on that performance comment. The 2025 and 2026 vintages, we are starting to see that longer production history. Jack Kavanaugh: Morning, team. Thanks for taking my question. I would love to focus on the costs in the Western Haynesville. Dan Harrison: I think if you take inflation out of the mix, the cost and the change in the frac design, basically, I think our costs have been pretty flat if you normalized all of that and took it out. I think when the 10K rigs come, we definitely feel like we're going to shave some days off. That's going to drop our cost a little bit. I think in the future, long term, we are looking at some rotary steerable technology, but that's a little bit further out in the future. Roland Burns: Yeah. The major driver of cost on these shale wells is lateral length. You've seen the legacy Haynesville achieve these great cost levels because we're now just drilling 15,000 plus wells. So, the Western Haynesville's going to get there, but it's going to take a longer period to get there. So, I think the overly focused on the cost of short laterals in the legacy is expensive too. I think, as we improve these drilling and completion techniques and we get the laterals long, which is going to happen in the future, the costs are going to start to look more similar to the legacy. So, I think that the overall focus of the cost is a little bit, you have to have a little patience. There's a lot of exploration costs. There's a lot of single well pad. There's a lot of things in the Western Haynesville in its early development stage that the legacy Haynesville had the exact same thing, and they're just at different time stages. But it's trending there, and all the initiatives for the higher-powered rigs, the higher-powered completions, the better motors, development infill drilling, those are all going to drive those costs way down from where they are today. The best thing is that the large reserves in place in the Western Haynesville make it all worth it.

They are definitely much higher than the legacy Haynesville across the board, usually twice as much.

Jay Allison: We went back to 2008, 2009, 2010, and compared the core, which was iffy in 2008, 2009, 2010, and the results, and you had to have $5.15 gas to have a 30% IRR. Those were 4,500-foot laterals. I mean, we really didn't start drilling extended laterals even in the core till probably 2015, and it's only been the last several years that we've been able to drill 15,000-foot laterals in the core.

So to Roland's point, if you compare where we were in the core, they called it the core back in 2008, 2009, 2010, in the first three or four years of the core versus where we are in the first few years of the Western Haynesville, we are light-years ahead in the Western Haynesville where we were in the core to create value with the reserve potential that you have maybe 200 feet of pay in the core, and you may have 1,500 to 2,000 feet of prospective pay in the Western Haynesville. So it's a completely different game, and the prize is multiple times more valuable in the Western Haynesville.

So the question is, do you have the 1,100 penetrations for that 90 miles? Do you have the seismic? Do you have the balance sheet and the partners in order to de-risk this? Unlike, it didn't happen in the core. There was recklessness when gas hit $6, $8. We've not been reckless in the Western Haynesville. We have exemplary partners, and we didn't have back then, we didn't have LNG and demand for natural gas to power the turbines. That is the game changer. That 30, 40, 50 BCF a day that they've spent trillions of dollars investing in takeaway infrastructure, we didn't have that back then. We have it today.

Jack Kavanaugh: Got it. That's all super helpful color, so appreciate that, team. Maybe for my follow-up, just maybe following up on the earlier kind of gas marketing discussion. With the SOCAR relationship obviously gives that access to international LNG markets. Just kind of how meaningful could you see that exposure become relative to kind of the current domestic marketing portfolio?

Roland Burns: Well, obviously today, there's a significant premium to those markets compared to our domestic markets. There's a very wide, huge margin there. You don't know what the future looks like if those are going to more align with each other. I think having that optionality with a strong partner will be a great asset to our overall marketing portfolio opportunities. Today, we're putting in place several long-term arrangements where we're going to supply natural gas to power generators, and those create much higher margins for us because we're able to get those contracts done with much better prices and also have a very long-term great customer. I think that it's a balance of those two.

Those are the two trends in our gas marketing, to be able to sell more directly to power generators, including the Anderson County power generation hub that the federal government is putting in on our Western Haynesville footprint, in addition to other long-term power generation deals that we're going to supply directly to other power generators. The combination of those two will be kind of a great add to our marketing portfolio.

Jay Allison: For LNG, you need really, if you can have it, you really want location closer to the Gulf Coast, and that's just a transportation cost issue. You want that, and we have it. You want an established production base. We have that. You want a balance sheet because you can't do it without a balance sheet, and you need decades upon decades of inventory. We have all that. You got to check those off, and most of them don't have that, and we have all that. They need to bring a SOCAR in. We have everything plus a big plus sign on it.

Jack Kavanaugh: That's all very helpful. Thanks, team.

Operator: Thank you. One moment. Our last question comes from the line of Tim Moore with Clear Street. Your line is now open.

Tim Moore: Hey, guys. This is Paul on for Tim. Just want to go back to the balance sheets. It is great that you have SOCAR signs, and you are taking net debt down to around $1.5 billion once that closes. But I am just curious how you are thinking about the dividend from there. What leverage level would you want to see before bringing it back?

Jay Allison: Yeah. Let me think about this question that you just asked. Now, think about this. I mean, this is like capturing, what is it, the end of the rainbow, which is a pot of silver, gold, whatever. Could be a big pot of natural gas if prices are high. Now, just think, this is the most reverberating question I have ever had lately, because we had three plus times the leverage ratio coverage, and now we have got 1.5, 1.7, a dividend. That tells you that you see that we have controlled this balance sheet properly, and you are just asking if we are going to continue to do that.

Roland Burns: Yeah, and I think that is a great question.

Roland Burns: I think our target leverage is to be below 1.5x leverage. We would have to look over the horizon, do we have a stronger gas price market than we have right now? Do we have the hedge position that secures that prices? Our number one priority, as we've said always, is to continue to advance the Western Haynesville and advance the relationships we have that we're building out, our midstream, supporting the Anderson Power Hub, et cetera. Those are our top priorities. Then if they're all met and there's a great gas price environment and our leverage can stay below our targets, then the dividend can come back. But we're not going to bring it back early.

We're going to be very responsible to all our stakeholders, because majority of our stakeholders and partners are focused on the long-term future versus short-term return of capital.

Jay Allison: I think you add this fifth rig and you get infill drilling, and you get very comfortable of repeatability, which is going to happen. Remember, you've got two Haynesville zones and you've got two Bossier zones. It's not that we're trying to complete the same zone, that 90 miles. We've got maybe three or four different zones that we're completing. I think as Dan Harrison has told you for the last hour, they're getting better and better and better at what they're doing, and you can see the top partners that we have now.

I do believe that the demand for natural gas is real because the investment has been spent, and I believe that we're in the sweet spot for that demand. The future has never looked better for us, period.

Tim Moore: Got it. That's very helpful. Thank you. For my follow-up, I'd just like to shift back to the Power Hub. In your 10-K, you talked about an initial capacity of around 2 GW, and the Anderson County Hub could go up to 5.2. I guess your supply is reaching close to 1 BCF a day by 2031. Is 2 GW still the right way to think about that and how the volumes could start to grow from that point?

Roland Burns: Well, the very first stage of operations that comes in is a 1 GW power facility, and then the longer-term facilities they're building will be 5.2 GW to 5.3. That is the plan, and that is what's being all designed. It's just a staging. There's the possibility that they expand beyond that if they want to. But that is the initial plans that are in the engineering phase right now. A lot of money is All the equipment's been ordered, so it's off and going. The first phase, that will be sometime in 2028 is when we'll start providing gas under that contract, and they will be constructing the facilities next year, especially on our midstream.

We'll be constructing all the gas facilities for them that we'll need to hook up to the power generation facilities.

Jay Allison: Yeah, you'll see first production early 2028, and it'll strengthen toward the latter part of 2028. They own the acreage, they're spending the money, like Roland Burns said. Really, the goal is to have the 5.2 GW position to have that, if that demand is there.

Tim Moore: Got it. That's helpful. Thanks, guys.

Operator: Thank you. This does conclude the question and answer session. I would now like to turn it back to Jay Allison for closing remarks.

Jay Allison: Again, I know there were several competing companies out there, all great companies that you could have listened to, so we're always thankful if you listened to the full hour and five minutes of this. And I always want you to know that whether you're SOCAR or Sixth Street or NextEra or the Joneses, we as a management group, there's about 255 of us, we will always give you our very best, and we'll always be very honest with you, and we expect to always deliver. So, thank you.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

#3215. OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs – here’s when, and what to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

On the heels of Anthropic's similar move, the change will be tested among select users before being rolled out.

OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs starting in December, according to a post on OpenAI’s website.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

Currently, ChatGPT’s desktop app features a ChatGPT and Codex section, and within the ChatGPT section, you can find the Chat and Work tabs. It’s not especially easy to navigate, and OpenAI is looking to change that.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

“Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans’ usage allowance will be shared across ChatGPT and Codex as we bring the agentic capabilities of Work into the main ChatGPT experience,” OpenAI detailed in its note entitled “Understanding ChatGPT and Codex usage limits.”

An email was also sent to current users, sharing similar information, according to TechCrunch. The email confirmed the merger of the Chat and Work tabs, adding that the integrated experience will be available to select users for feedback before it is made more widely available.

Also: How ChatGPT helped me fix a corrupted gaming PC

“This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said.

OpenAI said the transition will allow both ChatGPT and Codex to draw tokens from the same allowance pool. While most customers won’t be affected, depending on usage and model, some users may need to wait for resets more than usual.

“Your usage for ChatGPT and Codex will be measured in tokens, the units of information a model processes and generates. How much of your allowance you use will depend on the model you choose and the task you ask it to do. More advanced models and complex tasks generally use more of your allowance. Instant chat will not draw from your usage,” OpenAI said in the online note.

In September, rival Anthropic merged Claude‘s chat and Cowork functions into a single screen. OpenAI said that they don’t expect the upcoming change to disrupt users’ current experience.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“We’re preparing carefully for this transition to help prevent disruption to your workflows. We expect most users won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do now,” OpenAI said.

#3214. I put Apple's new MacBook Pro with M6 through its paces — and it's a portable powerhouse

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 is a relatively modest update, but it still packs plenty of performance for power users. It delivers strong image quality on its sharp 14-inch display and long battery life to get you through a full day and then some. Though it costs $400 more than the previous model, it’s worth considering if you don’t want to shell out nearly $3,000 for a PROLED MacBook.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 ($1,999 to start) won’t grab headlines like the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, but it’s still a great laptop for power users who don’t want to pay the latter’s steep asking price.

This year’s MacBook Pro retains the same sleek design and 14-inch Liquid Retina XDR display as the MacBook Pro M5, but it now packs the new Apple M6 chip, which delivers about 10-15% faster performance and better efficiency than the M5. There’s also the Apple N1 chip, which adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support for faster wireless connectivity.

While the 14-inch MacBook Pro M6 is a modest spec bump over last year’s model, it’s still one of the best MacBooks thanks to its elegant design, gorgeous display, fast performance, and epic battery life. It costs $400 more than before thanks to Apple’s price hikes, but you’re still getting your money’s worth if you just want a powerful MacBook. Find out more in my full review.

MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 (starting & tested)

14.2-inch (3024x1964) Liquid Retina XDR, 120Hz

16 hours wireless web (rated) | 19:05 hours wireless web (tested)

1x MagSafe, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB-C, 1x SDXC card slot, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

The MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 is a fantastic laptop, delivering strong performance and long-lasting battery life in a sleek aluminum chassis.

Our review unit has the same specs as the $1,999 starting model. This includes an Apple M6 chip with 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, 16GB of unified memory (RAM), and a 1TB SSD.

The M6 chip is built on TSMC’s 2nm process. It features hardware-accelerated mesh shading, ray tracing, and Dynamic Caching. These are also M5 features, but M6 handles everything faster and more efficiently.

This MacBook Pro handles my typical workload with ease, including dozens of open Chrome tabs, Slack, and the occasional YouTube video. I also had no issues cropping and resizing photos in GIMP.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

As expected, the M6-powered MacBook Pro performed well across our lab tests. On the Geekbench 6 CPU test, it scored well in both single- and multi-core performance. As you can see above, it is 18.17% faster in multi-core performance than its predecessor. It also crushes the Dell XPS 14 (currently $1,699), which features an Intel Core Ultra x7 358H CPU and 32GB of RAM.

In our Handbrake video transcoding test, the M6 MacBook Pro converted a 4K video to 1080p in a zippy 2 minutes and 50 seconds. The laptop also delivered strong results in the PugetBench Photoshop test. SSD speeds on the M6 MacBook Pro aren’t much different from those of the previous model, but both notebooks far outperform the XPS 14.

The M6 MacBook Pro is also pretty adept at gaming. In the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited GPU test, it scored much higher than the M5 model and the XPS 14 and also saw higher frame rates. When I tested Cyberpunk 2077 on the “For this Mac” graphical setting, performance was generally smooth at around 53 frames per second. Games optimized for Apple silicon will run marvelously on this machine.

The M6 MacBook Pro keeps the same design Apple introduced for the line back in 2021. Though I’m now kind of spoiled by the thinner and lighter PROLED MacBook Pros, I can’t knock Apple for keeping a winning design. This is still the same sturdy, functional, and elegant slab of machined aluminum I’ve come to love.

Opening the lid with one hand is easy, and it glides smoothly on its hinge. I also like how smooth the chassis feels when I’m holding the MacBook Pro. On that note, this laptop measures 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches and weighs 3.4 pounds. Since it’s not that large or heavy, it’s easy to carry around in your backpack — as I experienced firsthand when I commuted to and from work.

You get the same number of ports as before, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SD card slot, an HDMI port, and a headphone jack. There’s also a MagSafe port on the left-hand side, though you can charge the laptop using any of the available USB-C ports.

The keyboard deck is another highlight for me because it fits my large hands perfectly. The keys have excellent travel and just the right amount of resistance when pressed. I’m also a fan of the large touchpad, which consistently and accurately registers my gestures. The haptic feedback is great, too. The Touch ID button makes it easy to log in to the MacBook Pro or bypass passwords, though I wish this laptop also included Face ID.

Even if the speakers on this MacBook Pro aren’t as punchy as those on the PROLED laptops, they still deliver clear and loud audio. Whether it’s audio-focused podcasts, movies, or music, your ears won’t be disappointed.

While the MacBook Pro M6’s 14-inch 3024x1964 display isn’t as awe-inspiring as the OLED panel on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the Liquid Retina XDR Display is as gorgeous as ever.

When playing Cyberpunk 2077, I was amazed by the contrast between shadows and light. The game’s bold colors also stood out, and the sharp resolution makes it easy to see even the smallest details in the environment and on characters.

Since this is still the same display as last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, its test results are identical. Color reproduction (sRGB and DCI-P3) is slightly oversaturated but not overly so, resulting in more realistic hues. The excellent color accuracy (Delta-E) also helps. Brightness levels are fantastic with both SDR and HDR content.

I now have mixed feelings about the notch at the top center of the display. It didn’t bother me before, but it now stands out more, especially after testing the OLED MacBook Pros that ditched the notch for the Dynamic Island. While I understand the notch houses the FaceTime camera and ambient light sensor, it has become an eyesore.

The MacBook Pro M6 supports up to two 6K external displays at 60Hz, or one display at up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and another at up to 4K resolution at 165Hz, using any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI ports. You can also connect to a single 8K 60Hz display, a 5K 120Hz display, or a 4K 240Hz display via HDMI or Thunderbolt.

Apple says the MacBook Pro M6 has up to 16 hours of battery life when web surfing. If this laptop met that claim, we’d be impressed. However, our lab testing shows Apple’s notebook can last much longer.

On the Tom’s Guide’s battery test, which involves continuous Wi-Fi web surfing with the display set to 150 nits, the M6 MacBook Pro lasted a mind-boggling 19 hours! That’s an hour longer than last year’s model, which also had epic battery life. While the Dell XPS 14 has admirable endurance for a Windows laptop, it can come close to matching Apple’s.

The MacBook Pro has the same 12MP Center Stage camera as last year’s model, so you’ll look your best during video calls. Thanks to the “Center Stage” feature, you’ll always be perfectly framed.

As you can see in the photo above, the webcam captures all the details on my face, clothing, and background. If you’re in a well-lit area, you’ll almost always have great image quality.

Though the MacBook Pro M6 has many strengths, it’s not a perfect laptop.

Last year’s MacBook Pro started at $1,599, a reasonable price for an entry-level premium laptop. However, thanks to RAMageddon, this year’s M6 MacBook Pro now costs $400 more. And that’s before accounting for component upgrades that could drive the price even higher.

If you don’t need the strong processing power but still want a high-performing machine, you can get the MacBook Air M5 for $1,299. But if this MacBook Pro sounds right for you, prepare to pay a pretty penny.

Like the MacBook Pro M5 before it, the new M6 MacBook Pro is a modest update. That’s not entirely bad, as it delivers fast performance for everyday work, video editing, and gaming. However, given the modest performance gains and higher asking price, it might make folks think twice about getting this laptop.

As I always say about refreshes like this, if you’re happy with your current MacBook Pro, you don’t need to upgrade. However, if you have a machine with anything older than an M3 chip, you should take a serious look at this one. And if your wallet can handle it, the MacBook Pro OLEDs offer stronger performance and OLED touchscreens.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip is the odd duck of the current MacBook lineup. Those who prioritize affordability will likely look to the MacBook Air or even the MacBook Neo for work or watching videos. Conversely, folks who want the most powerful MacBooks available have the new PROLED laptops to consider.

So where does that leave the M6 MacBook Pro? After all, it’s still a stellar laptop that is as elegant as it is fast and efficient. It can still outpace even the most powerful Windows laptops. Yes, the PROLED MacBooks have newer features and are more powerful, but the M6 MacBook Pro is still a valid machine.

Ultimately, the MacBook Pro M6 is for those who want a pro-grade MacBook that’s $900 less than the entry-level MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Sure, it lacks a touchscreen and an OLED display, but for demanding tasks like video editing and gaming, this MacBook Pro won’t let you down. Taken on its own merits, the MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 is still a phenomenal laptop.

#3212. Microsoft Teams Hack Report Shows Old-School Attacks Are Still a Thing

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

By impersonating help desk personnel, hackers were able to infiltrate corporate systems.

Over the last year, the public has been trained to view the biggest new wave of emerging cyberthreats as AI-driven. In fact, frontier AI models accelerating the pace of cyberattacks — and even jumping ahead so far that the models have to be paused in the case of Anthropic’s Mythos — have driven the cybersecurity conversation recently.

But a recent report from Microsoft detailing how hackers used its Teams software to infiltrate corporate systems shows that human hackers are still using social engineering scams to fool other humans into doing their dirty work.

According to the report, “threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist.” Once they were granted access by unsuspecting workers, the hackers were able to set up software using Python, Bun or Java runtimes, open up networks and grant themselves authentication, giving them free rein over corporate systems.

In order to open the door to all that activity, however, a human had to grant access to the intruder. “Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel,” the report stated. “The social engineering persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session, primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation.” Presumably, the employees who granted access thought the people on the help desks reaching out were just doing their jobs to keep their workplaces safe and operations running smoothly.

In an email to CNET, a representative for Microsoft said the company is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that it says “uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users.”

The change was listed as part of Microsoft’s roadmap for the software, which was revealed last month. Teams will also add ways to report suspicious guest invitations and blur QR codes sent by external senders, according to that roadmap.

However, a lot of the burden of making sure these hackers don’t get through falls to companies and their employees. “Users should exercise caution with external connection requests and messages, including verifying a sender’s identity and requests before acting on them,” Microsoft’s spokesperson said. “Administrators can also block external Teams users and specify which users in their organization are permitted to chat or meet with people outside the enterprise.”

Yu Cai, associate director of the Institute of Computing and Cybersystems at Michigan Tech, said social engineering attacks are definitely still widespread. “AI may be changing the cybersecurity landscape, but it hasn’t replaced the human hacker. Human-led social engineering attacks remain a major cybersecurity threat, even as AI cyber attacks continue to get the bulk of today’s headlines,” he said.

But Cai said AI attacks and human-led attacks aren’t necessarily in separate buckets. AI can help make social engineering hacks more convincing by providing tools like voice cloning or deepfake videos.

In the case of the Microsoft Teams hacks, Cai said that what was most surprising was how simple the approach was to gain access. “This is a great reminder that sophisticated attacks don’t necessarily have to begin as sophisticated hacks,” he said. “This Microsoft incident wasn’t caused by any vulnerabilities in the Teams software, but by employees naturally placing trust in communications that come through the tools they use each and every day.”

#3211. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

#3210. Why IonQ Stock Just Fell 10.5% Today

IonQ stock got hit hard in Thursday's AI and chip rout, a reminder that quantum stocks can get swept up in a big AI sell-off.

IonQ, Inc. (IONQ -10.53%) stock fell 10.5% on Thursday, Nov. 5, amid a post-election sell-off in chip and AI stocks that spread to the riskiest corners of tech.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -4.36%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.52%) fell 4.4% and 5.6%, respectively.

The company reported sales of $173.8 million, up 336% from a year earlier -- a big chunk of this was from IonQ's acquisition of SkyWater -- and handily beating Wall Street's target of $141 million. #3209. These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Several creative apps are ready to take advantage of the iPhone Duo's many display configurations, with more to come.

In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, the iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But this early into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

#3208. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.
