#3206. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3205. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3204. Disneyland Is Training a Class of AI Robot Interns

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Pixar robots to help you park your car to droids roaming Star Wars land, physical AI is popping up all over Disneyland.

If you’ve ever driven to Disneyland, you know that parking is a challenge. When the parks open each morning, long lines clog the nearby streets as engines idle, families waiting anxiously to enter the parking structure so they can start their day at the parks.

Parking attendants can only do so much to handle the tens of thousands of cars arriving every day at the Disneyland Resort. But what if a cutesy autonomous robot from Pixar’s Cars series could help direct traffic flow and guide you right into your parking spot?

That’s a project being tested with FieldAI, a company that builds the AI brains for robots. In a demo video at the Disney Accelerator Demo Day on Tuesday, Disney and FieldAI showed footage of robots that would assist with guiding cars through the parking process.

“Imagine if a character from Cars or robots from Wall-E direct you where to park when you arrive,” Gary Daniels, senior vice president of products and experiences at Disney Experiences Technology, said. “The work we are doing now is a great way to see how the robots function, and, as important, how people respond.”

Other companies build the robots; FieldAI slaps its physical AI solution in a box on top of them, having worked so far with around 30 different robot types, shapes and sizes. The box is equipped with multiple cameras that serve as the robot’s “eyes and ears,” helping the AI model process what it’s experiencing in real time. The robots also collect data while operating.

During the event at Walt Disney Studios, FieldAI showcased a Boston Dynamics robot dog and a miniature version of the BBX droids from The Mandalorian and Grogu that roam Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge at Disneyland. FieldAI-enabled robots have already been deployed in Disneyland at Galaxy’s Edge on the BBX droids, though they hedged that this is in its early stages.

“Our intelligence is on the bigger version and operating in the park already,” FieldAI CEO Ali Agha told reporters.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me it could also be used on characters that interact with guests at parks, naming Olaf and The Hulk as examples.

Another project with Disney involves getting multiple robots to talk to each other to coordinate missions.

Headquartered in Irvine, California, with offices in the San Francisco Bay Area, Boston and Pittsburgh, FieldAI primarily works in construction environments and energy facilities to complete tasks like inspections, material transport and supporting construction. But this is easily translated to a theme park environment, where paths and crowds are constantly changing, and autonomous robots need to account for that without needing mapping or GPS.

“Our BBX proof of concept explores how to bring that navigation together with Disney character performance,” said Doug Fidaleo, lab director, Disney Research, Walt Disney Imagineering R&D. “That’s what drew us to FieldAI: deep experience deploying robots in demanding, unstructured environments with uneven terrain, changing layouts and unexpected obstacles.”

Some of the use cases Agha gives include robots supporting security, perimeter patrols, helping cast members backstage and enabling more in-park experiences — even delivering items to people waiting in line for a ride.

“This is a highly self-autonomous system that operates without a positioning system,” Agha said.

Physical Intelligence (Pi) is another company that builds AI brains for robots. Also showcased during Disney’s Accelerator Demo Day, Pi is focused less on roaming droids that can help or entertain guests and instead on robots helping Disney cast members with backstage tasks.

Namely: picking up, folding, cleaning and sorting the 3D glasses used for rides like Toy Story Midway Mania and shows like Mickey’s PhilharMagic.

It’s an unpleasant task that’s a major pain point for cast members who have to spend a long time in a small room completing it several times a day. It also requires “dexterous manipulation,” with Pi previously working on general-purpose robots that perform tasks like folding and stacking, using robots that have grippers rather than five-digit hands.

Sourish Jasti, a technical staffer with Pi, said the company recently spent 12 days at Disneyland between midnight and 6 a.m. collecting data, testing logistics and moving its robots in and out of the park to see whether it could help with sorting the 3D glasses.

“This was like a robot internship,” Jasti said, adding that physical AI is like a toddler, in that it learns from actually doing things.

The robots — which, much like FieldAI, Pi doesn’t build but instead installs the brains for — could be either a humanoid on wheels or just a mechanical arm. There are cameras on the base and cameras on the wrists to help the AI model “see” what it’s doing as it picks up and sorts the glasses.

“We intend to have robots interning in many different spaces with Disney,” Jasti said, pointing to not only the theme parks but also Disney’s studios, hotel rooms and cruise liners, which he calls “mini cities.”

For both Pi and FieldAI, Min said the benefit is that using AI can train the robots much faster to do the tasks Disney needs them to do — and that going to companies like these, which are already well-established in fields like construction and manufacturing, makes it easier to transfer those skills to the theme parks.

Whether they’re roaming around parking structures or lands, or backstage helping workers, the AI-equipped autonomous robots are solving problems for Disney.

“The connection is through the core capabilities that we’re developing for our robots,” Fidaleo said. “Robots that can perceive the world around them, can act in the physical world and adapt when things change.”

Disney is continuing to push technology from the audio-animatronic figures used on rides like Pirates of the Caribbean, making them more sophisticated to build an immersive experience.

“From the expressive Na’vi shaman to a robotic Spider-Man flying through the air, to a walking baby Groot, each advance changes how we can experience a character in the physical world,” Fidaleo said. “The park of the future will be teeming with robot characters.”

#3203. Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver – but you have alternatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

One of Roku's most popular screensavers is about to make its last splash. Here’s how to switch before Dec. 1.

A fan-favorite Roku screensaver is going away, and users aren’t happy.

Over the last several days, users with the Aquatic Life aquarium screensaver set as the default have noticed a message appearing when the screensaver opens. “Starting Dec. 1, 2026,” the message reads, “the Aquatic Life screensaver will no longer be available, and your screensaver will switch to Roku City.”

Also: The free Roku City screensaver game has me hooked

The screensaver, which displays a digital aquarium with tropical fish swimming back and forth, was available as a downloadable theme pack and was a popular pick for many years.

Users on Reddit quickly lamented the loss in many posts, with dozens noting that the aquarium was part of their daily routine. Roku responded to one post, saying, “That makes sense, and we hear you. Aquatic Life has a lot of loyal fans, and we’re passing your feedback along to the team.” The post noted that when “the fish swim off,” Roku devices with Aquatic Life will switch to Roku City.

You can browse to Settings > Theme > Screensaver to find another theme.

Several online reports indicate that the removal is a licensing issue and that the creator of the screensaver posted on Reddit that he removed the license after Roku’s sale to Fox. That thread has now been deleted, so the comment is unavailable. Roku hasn’t issued any statement of its own about why, but I have reached out to ask. I’ve also reached out directly to the screensaver’s creator.

If you’re looking for the exact screensaver, it’s still available as a 2-minute clip on Roku’s YouTube channel. It takes a few extra steps, but if you want to keep the screensaver running on your TV, you can create a YouTube playlist with just that video, set it to loop, and use the YouTube app on Roku whenever you want to see it.

Even though the announcement of the screensaver’s departure happened less than 24 hours ago, the comments section of that video is packed with users begging Roku to keep Aquatic Life.

Also: I started clearing my Roku cache, and it fixed my biggest TV complaint

Alternatively, you could open one of the many YouTube videos that have aquarium displays and let one of them run for as long as you want.

There are also several dozen aquarium apps for Roku. I checked out several of them, and while they don’t look exactly like the Roku one, they do fill the void. Note that if you opt for one of these, most of them do have ads that play before the aquarium starts.

Lastly, you can download the original app for your phone or computer from SereneScreen.

#3202. Brookfield Business (BBUC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Asset sales and a shifting battery mix shaped the quarter's results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Brookfield Business Corporation (BBUC -2.29%) reported a return to profitability in the third quarter, supported by a significant acceleration in capital recycling and resilient performance across its core Industrials and Business Services segments. Management reported generating $1.4 billion from asset sales and distributions year to date, which has strengthened the balance sheet and provided liquidity for over $500 million in new investments across the freight, industrial distribution, and plumbing sectors. The company stated that its strategic focus remains on acquiring essential products and services businesses where operational improvements can drive margin expansion and long-term value compounding. While certain segments faced headwinds from softened demand and contract implementation costs, the ongoing mix shift toward high-margin advanced batteries at Clarios and technology modernization at CDK continue to underpin the company's growth profile.

Operator: Welcome to Brookfield Business Corporation's Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call and Webcast. As a reminder, all participants are in listen-only mode, and the conference is being recorded. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To join the question queue, simply press star one on your touchtone phone. Now, I'd like to turn the conference over to Alan Fleming, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, Mr. Fleming.

Alan Fleming: Thank you, operator, and good morning. Thank you everyone on the line for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that in responding to questions and talking about our growth initiatives and our financial and operating performance, we may make forward-looking statements. These statements are subject to known and unknown risks, and future results may differ materially. For further information on known risk factors, I encourage you all to review our filings with the securities regulators in Canada and the U.S., which are available on our website. We'll begin today's call with Anuj Ranjan, our Chief Executive Officer, who will provide an update on the progress we're making in executing against our strategic priorities.

Anuj will then turn the call over to Mark Wallace, Chief Executive Officer of Clarios, who will discuss the business performance and the growth opportunities we see ahead. We'll conclude our prepared remarks with Jaspreet Dehl, our Chief Financial Officer, who will review our financial results. We'll then open the line to your questions. With that, I'd like to pass the call over to Anuj.

Anuj Ranjan: Thanks, Alan. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on the call today. We've had a busy few months. We're making great progress across our business. We agreed to sell an additional 20% interest in La Trobe Financial, our Australian asset manager and lender. We've now realized a 2x cash multiple and a 35% IRR on our investment, and we still own more than half our original ownership in the business. In addition, last week, we closed the sale of Multiplex for over $600 million. These realizations tell us something about the market. Buyers are increasingly willing to pay for more critical cash-generative industrial and services businesses.

In total, we've generated $1.4 billion from capital recycling since the start of the year, which puts us well on our way to exceeding the $2 billion target we set at our investor day last year. But these two sales are just the latest examples of our strategy in action. We acquire high-quality businesses at attractive values, making them stronger through operational improvements and recycling capital when the time is right to redeploy into new opportunities. We've been doing just that. We closed new investments in World Freight Company and Gregg Distributors and reached an agreement to acquire Reliance Worldwide Corporation, a global leader in plumbing products with category-defining brands, resilient demand, and significant opportunities for operational improvement.

Together, these three investments represent more than $500 million of capital from BBUC. These investments are great examples of the opportunities we're seeing in today's market. They are high-quality businesses with strong competitive positions and durable cash flows. What really excites us is the opportunity to make them even better. Around the world, companies are rethinking how they operate in response to changing supply chains, cost pressures, and advances in technology. These shifts are creating significant opportunities to improve productivity, reduce costs, and make businesses more competitive. We've spent decades making businesses better, and we believe that experience gives us a distinct advantage.

Over the past two years, we've committed more than $1.2 billion to acquire seven market-leading industrial and services businesses. We see significant opportunities in manufacturing efficiency, procurement, commercial execution, and technology to grow earnings and cash flow at these businesses. We're still in the early stages of executing our value creation plans, so much of the opportunity is still ahead of us. Remember, we have a long track record of turning these operational improvements into real cash for our shareholders. Since creating BBUC, we've sold about 30 businesses, generating roughly $9 billion in proceeds and a 19% realized IRR. In aggregate, these monetizations were done at about a 12% premium to our NAV.

Looking ahead, we have a strong pipeline of new investments, a lot of upside in what we already own, and significant capital coming back to us from monetizations. This puts us in an excellent position to continue compounding value for our shareholders. One of the best examples of our approach in action is Clarios. Since acquiring the business, we've significantly grown its earnings, strengthened its operations, and positioned it for the next phase of growth. Today, Clarios is our largest investment, and honestly, we believe the best is yet to come. I'm very pleased to have Mark Wallace, Clarios' CEO, joining us today to share more about the business, the progress we're making, and the opportunities ahead.

Mark Wallace: Thank you, Anuj, and good morning, everyone. It's great to be back with you. I'd like to spend a few minutes providing an update on Clarios, including the strength of our core business and the opportunities we are pursuing that will accelerate our growth and expand our addressable markets, from supercapacitors that help stabilize power demand in artificial intelligence data centers to connected services that help commercial fleets reduce downtime while creating new recurring revenue streams. I'll also touch on how our recent portfolio actions support our long-term strategy. Let me start with our performance. We finished fiscal 2026 with our fourth consecutive year of record financial results.

That performance underscores the strength and earnings power of our core business and provides a strong foundation for long-term growth. At the center of the foundation is our highly resilient business model. Clarios is a global leader in low-voltage energy storage, approximately four times the size of our nearest competitor. We power roughly one in three vehicles on the road, and we sell more than 150 million batteries annually. Approximately 80% of our sales are in the stable aftermarket, where battery replacement is essential and recurring. This scale is supported by a well-established circular model that recovers and reuses critical minerals across the battery life cycle. That aftermarket exposure provides significant stability while also creating meaningful long-term growth potential.

One of the most important drivers is the continued shift towards higher-value advanced batteries, which we expect to be a multi-decade tailwind. Advanced batteries now represent 35% of our units sold, up from just 10% in fiscal 2015. More than 70% of the batteries we sell into the original equipment channel today are advanced batteries. While the aftermarket penetration remains significantly lower, over time, we expect the aftermarket to naturally follow as those vehicles move through the replacement cycle. Because advanced batteries generate greater revenue and profit per unit than conventional batteries, that mix shift creates an attractive long-term growth opportunity. At the same time, the role of the low-voltage power in vehicles is becoming more important.

Vehicles are becoming more electrified, connected, software-defined, and automated. That evolution requires more sophisticated low-voltage power systems to support electronics, critical vehicle functions, and safety redundancy. Importantly, that trend is largely powertrain-agnostic. Internal combustion, hybrid, and fully electric vehicles all require reliable low-voltage power. With more than 620 xEV platform wins to date, we have established a strong position as these architectures continue to evolve. For Clarios, that creates an opportunity to provide greater value to our customers and increase our dollar content per vehicle. This is the strategy behind the Clarios Power Management System, or CPMS.

By bringing together advanced batteries, supercapacitors, electronics, software, and monitoring capabilities, we can address a broader portion of the vehicle's low-voltage architecture and solve more of our customers' power management needs. More broadly, our $6 billion U.S. investment plan supports advanced battery production, critical mineral processing and recovery, next-generation technology, and state-of-the-art manufacturing. These investments strengthen our core while building the capabilities needed to support future growth. Alongside these investments, we remain intensely focused on driving operational efficiency across the business. We're utilizing AI and machine learning, advanced automation, and robotics to improve productivity, optimize our supply chain, and enhance our customer service. Continuous operational improvement is an important lever to support margin expansion and long-term value creation.

Beyond driving growth and efficiency in our automotive business, we also see opportunities to extend power management technology into new attractive markets. A great example is supercapacitors. Our acquisition of Maxwell Technologies added a complementary fast-response power technology to our portfolio. Within automotive, supercapacitors support peak power requirements, stabilization, and redundancy. Beyond automotive, we see applications in data centers, grid infrastructure, industrial applications, and renewable energy. Data centers are particularly interesting. AI workloads are creating increasingly volatile power demands that constrain existing infrastructures. Supercapacitors can respond almost instantly, helping smooth power spikes and bridge short-duration gaps between primary and backup power. We see an attractive opportunity as AI computing drives demand for fast, reliable power.

We are pursuing a similar opportunity through our connected services. By combining battery data, analytics, and our deep expertise, we can help fleet customers identify potential battery issues before they result in vehicle downtime. Today, our connected services solutions support approximately 20 commercial fleets across North America. These deployments validate the need for actionable battery intelligence that can improve uptime and maintenance planning. Over time, connected services can create reoccurring revenue opportunities, deepen customer relationships, and generate valuable insight to inform future innovation. As we pursue these opportunities, we remain focused on allocating capital to strengthen our competitive position and create shareholder value. Our recent portfolio actions are good examples.

Our planned acquisition of Ecobat U.S. operations includes three critical mineral recovery and processing facilities that together process more than 40 million batteries annually. Bringing these capabilities in-house advances our vertical integration, reduces reliance on third-party suppliers, and strengthens access to critical minerals, reinforcing both our closed-loop model and the security of domestic battery supply chains. It also allows us to benefit from greater vertical integration, creating an opportunity to improve margins over time. At the same time, we monetized our non-controlling economic interest in an equity stake in a large battery distributor while preserving our long-standing commercial relationship.

Taken together, these actions reflect a disciplined approach to managing the portfolio, investing in strategic assets and capabilities while maintaining financial flexibility for future growth and long-term shareholder value creation. As we look ahead, I am excited about where Clarios is positioned. We have a resilient cash generative core business. We are strengthening our automotive leadership as vehicle architecture has become more complex, while extending our capabilities into attractive new markets and recurring revenue opportunities. Together, we believe these growth platforms expand the markets we can address by approximately $32 billion today to an estimated $52 billion by 2040, supported in part by the growing demand for advanced power management solutions in data centers.

This strategy gives us multiple avenues to grow while continuing to drive operational efficiency, deploy capital, and with a discipline and create long-term value. Thank you, and I will turn it over now to Jaspreet.

Jaspreet Dehl: Thanks, Mark, and good morning, everyone. We generated third quarter Adjusted EBITDA of $594 million compared to $575 million in the prior period. We have two factories that are being retrofitted as we speak, and those will start, like I said, production in 2028.

When it comes to the, let us call it the non-automotive space, especially data centers, with the acquisition of Maxwell, there is quite a high demand for our supercapacitor systems for data center utilization. We're going to be bringing on two new factories over the next 18 months just to support what I call the near-term demand that we're seeing in data centers. Those two businesses combined, we're expecting our addressable market to grow by 50%. We definitely see those having a more larger impact in our earnings profile and our revenue growth closer to the end of this decade.

Devin Dodge: Okay. That's interesting. Thanks for that. Okay. I'm not sure who wants to take this, but it's another one on Clarios. We've seen financial leverage, I think it's down to the low fours if you back out the credits, and you should decline further once more credits are received. It just seems like you're likely nearing another decision for how to monetize this business. I was just wondering if you could talk about your exit options that you're considering. You've also owned this business for nearly eight years, and I'm not sure if there is a need to return capital to Brookfield's private fund investors plays into the exit options being considered.

Anuj Ranjan: Yeah, I'll take that. I think, look, Clarios is an amazing business. It's highly, highly cash generative. In the future, when we look forward, the potential, the power of that cash flow for BBU is incredible. I'd say just starting with, we're very, very pleased. I'm really excited about what Mark and the team have done and what's actually, frankly, what's ahead, as in my earlier comments, is probably better than what we've seen in the past.

That being said, obviously, we're always open to opportunities to crystallize value, and there's a lot of ways that we can look to crystallize value, which could include, of course, selling the business, but it could also include ways to capture some sort of value at the parent with maybe partial sales or other kinds of opportunities without necessarily needing to sell the entire business. All of these various, we want to retain optionality. The nice thing is when you got this highly cash-generative of a business, that will pay a very stable and growing dividend over a long time, we have all kinds of alternatives at our disposal.

It frankly will come down to in coming time as to what is the best value that we can achieve compared to the cash yield that we're getting. But again, with that sort of a cash yield, we're not in any hurry.

Devin Dodge: Okay, makes sense. Thanks for that, Anuj. Okay, and just one last one. I was going to ask about Nielsen. It is a business we do not talk very much about. Just wanted to know if you could give an update, a high-level update, how the business is performing, and just any color on why Brookfield elected not to participate in the recent acquisition there, and what that pro forma ownership will look like?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah, I can answer maybe the last part and then hand it over to Adrian to maybe just talk about what we are seeing in the business. I think you are referencing the DoubleVerify transaction that Nielsen recently announced. That transaction is primarily debt-funded and with a little bit of equity. As you know, we have got a pref investment in Nielsen, so convertible pref. The, you know, we are quite excited about the transaction, and we think it will be very accretive to the business and continue to kind of set it up for growth, and it will add value to our kind of converted share of the business.

The business was able to do that without requiring additional equity from us, and it really does not kind of impact our overall return profile. That is kind of the approach that we took on it.

Adrian Letts: Just to comment on the performance of the business, we are getting through all the large renewals now, and we are seeing upticks in the value of those renewals as we start to include other products and services, particularly around streaming. The Gracenote business is improving. If you look into the new products and services that we are launching, we are starting to see strong momentum on that. Look, overall, look, we remain very optimistic in terms of the opportunity of the business.

I think to Jaspreet's point, the DoubleVerify acquisition really adds to the portfolio of products and services that we can offer to our customers on either side of the marketplace, and it is a business that is performing well.

Devin Dodge: Okay, good color. I appreciate it. I will turn it over.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star 11 on your telephone. Our next question comes from the line of Jaeme Gloyn with National Bank.

Jaeme Gloyn: Yeah, thanks. Good morning. Just a few questions on some of the company performance. First, Sagen, just wanted to get a sense as to the breakdown of what's driving the reserve build this quarter. Is it entirely macro-driven, or is there something you're seeing with either loss curves or just the underlying performance?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah, it's Jaspreet. I'll take that. I'd say the overall, what you're seeing in the losses is really a normalization towards the long-term, long range. I think we've said this before, but the long-term loss expectations are in that 15%-25% range, and we're seeing a normalization. Since we bought the business kind of late 2019, going through COVID and the home price appreciation, we've seen abnormally low loss ratios over a large period of time that we've held this business. Our expectation has always been that losses will increase and head more in that 15%-25% range. That's what we're seeing now.

In the quarter in particular, and kind of this year, we've seen continued downward pressure on home prices in Canada. I'd say, as you'd expect, the Ontario, GTA, those markets where we saw a substantial increase in home prices, that's where we've seen the largest correction, and I'd say the largest pressure. The loss ratios that we're seeing come through, part of it is the actual kind of experience, and then part of it is just shoring up reserves as we look forward, and we're looking at economic uncertainty. Rates went up, so just making sure that we've got that resilience in our reserves, given kind of the broader macro.

Jaeme Gloyn: Yeah. Okay, understood. Mostly severity from house price decline. The next one would be CDK, showing in growth and Adjusted EBITDA. Anything to draw out from that quarter's performance? The debt markets are obviously one thing, but the operating performance, the cash flow of the business continues to be positive and to grow on a year-over-year basis. Maybe just sort of talk through some of the initiatives that are still rolling through there at CDK?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah. Maybe I'll just make an opening comment and then hand it over to Adrian to talk about operating performance. I'd say the business had a good quarter this year. We have annual price increases, there's cross-sell, and the overall performance has been better. Churn in the business is still elevated, and we are kind of managing through that. What I would say is, you know, while the business is on the right path, and I'll let Adrian talk to everything that we're doing in the business, one quarter, we shouldn't extrapolate that as the trend. We are kind of proactively working on debt. The business just does generate a positive free cash flow.

It continues to invest in its modernization efforts, so the cash flow profile of the business is still good. But we are in active dialogue and looking at the debt maturity.

Adrian Letts: Just to build on operational performance, Jaspreet commented on this quarter's Adjusted EBITDA. Look, continued cross-selling and upselling initiatives, coupled with the appointment of a new CEO who brings deep operational experience in building and scaling large-scale technology and new products, the business is continuing to focus on executing its technology modernization program. That will also underpin CDK's product capabilities. It also improves customer support, improved retention, which gives us a really strong basis to drive cross-selling. It's important to remember, look, CDK's platform is deeply embedded into customer workflows.

It's one of the largest, it remains the largest dealer management software provider in North America, and has a really strong market position, and draws on 40 years of proprietary data, which we think, as you go through the ongoing modernization efforts, the business is really well-positioned to leverage AI as an opportunity to deliver much more value to customers.

Jaeme Gloyn: Okay. Then, last one, maybe similar to an earlier question. Elections in Brazil, a couple of Brazilian assets, obviously the market's maybe not as well received, but anything to draw out from an impact or effect that might affect those businesses on a go-forward basis?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah. Look, I'd say our two largest assets in Brazil, BRK Ambiental, our wastewater business, and Unidas, which is our fleet management and car rental business. Both of those businesses, operating performance has been very good. I think we called out that BRK Ambiental had double-digit EBITDA growth. We continue to optimize the operating costs in that business. We've recently bid on and acquired a new concession, so we're in the process of rolling that out. So business and operating performance has been excellent. But for both businesses, as with any business, extended periods of very high interest rates aren't really constructive.

So, we have seen high rates in Brazil for a long period of time, which has curtailed capital market activity. The rates have been coming down. I think the punchline from the elections is that the expectation is still that rates will come down, maybe a little bit of moderation on how quickly they come down. So I'd say our focus continues to be on operating these businesses well, compounding value, and being ready to monetize them when we get the appropriate window.

Operator: Thank you. I am showing no further questions. With that, I will hand the call back over to CEO Anuj Ranjan for any closing remarks.

Anuj Ranjan: Thank you all for being here this quarter. I look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for participating. This does conclude today's program. You may now disconnect.

#3201. I just tried Apple’s new iMac with M6 and this sleek all-in-one is so seamless I’m ready to ditch my Mac mini

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The iMac with M6 pairs a noticeable 2nm performance leap and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity with Apple’s iconic, minimalist hardware. While a higher starting price and the lack of a height-adjustable stand hold it back from perfection, its sharp 4.5K display and seamless setup make it a worthwhile upgrade for anyone holding on to an older Apple all-in-one.

Sleek, colorful design with color-matched accessories

Big performance boost thanks to Apple’s M6 and N1 chips

Surprisingly punchy speakers and solid built-in webcam

Sharp, vibrant 4.5K Retina display (with optional nano-texture glass)

Price hike on an already premium base model

Still lacks an optional height-adjustable stand

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Apple’s new iMac with M6 might look identical to its predecessor at first glance, but it’s the extra power and improved connectivity under the hood that make this upgraded all-in-one desktop continue to stand out.

Instead of drastically altering the iMac, Apple has kept more or less the same design since 2021 when the 24-inch model first debuted. Just like with the iMac M4, you’re still getting a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage webcam, and two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports at the back depending on which configuration of the new M6 chip you choose.

Similarly to the Mac mini M6 I reviewed, Apple’s M6 chip and its N1 wireless chip are the big upgrades here. While I wish there were other changes to its design — like an optional height-adjustable stand or a larger screen size — the iMac with M6 is a reliable and powerful desktop that’s incredibly simple to set up thanks to its one-cable solution. Also, unlike Apple's Studio Display monitors, the power cable is detachable, which makes cable management a breeze.

Besides being one of the best all-in-one computers, it’s also the only one that can be configured with a matte finish thanks to Apple’s optional nano-texture glass. However, is it worth upgrading from an older Mac or ditching your existing desktop setup for something more seamless? Find out in my full Apple iMac with M6 review.

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

4 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet built into power adapter

Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, Magic Mouse

The iMac with M6 is an elegant desktop that’s sleek and compact enough to fit into almost any space. What truly makes it shine, though, is the added muscle from Apple's M6 chip and the upgraded connectivity of the N1 — along with the fact that it remains the only all-in-one computer you can buy with an optional matte display.

The iMac with M6 that Apple sent over for review arrived in a single large box, complete with a blue fabric handle to match the desktop’s light blue colorway. Along with the computer itself, you get everything you need to start using it right away as it comes with a Magic Keyboard and a Magic Mouse.

Besides the color-matched USB-C to USB-C cable and power adapter with an Ethernet port built in that comes with the higher tier model, I really appreciated the fact that Apple includes a microfiber cloth in the box for keeping its screen fingerprint and smudge free.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The iMac with M6’s stand comes pre-attached, so there’s nothing to put together. There’s a white .5-inch border that wraps all the way around its 24-inch display along with a larger, 2-inch chin at the bottom. On the very top of the device, there’s a 12MP webcam with microphone holes on the back.

Then on the backside of the iMac with M6, there’s a hole at the top of the stand to route its power cable through along with two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left side depending on which configuration you choose.

Around the corner from the power button on the back right, there’s a 3.5mm audio jack on the edge for connecting wired headphones. When you're sitting in front of the iMac, that puts the jack on your front-left — a small detail, but I really like that the cable from my headphones didn’t get in the way when using the included Magic Mouse. Though if you’re left-handed, this could be an issue if you frequently use wired headphones.

Unlike the Mac mini M4 or Mac mini M6 I’ve used previously, I just had to plug in that single power cable and power the iMac with M6 on to get started. From there, I used the included USB-C cable to pair the keyboard and mouse and I was good to go.

Although this is the first Apple all-in-one I’ve tested, the iMac with M6 felt incredibly fast and responsive right from the get go. In fact, it was a very similar experience to how it felt to upgrade from the previous Mac mini to the new Mac mini M6 and as you might have guessed, this is all thanks to Apple’s new M6 chip.

As you can see in our benchmark testing below, the change from using a 3nm process on the M4 to a 2nm process on the M6 — though literally small — makes a huge difference in terms of performance. For instance, in our Geekbench tests, we saw almost a 1,000 point single-core increase while multi-core performance jumped more than 5,000 points.

Apple has also upgraded the SSD storage in this new iMac, resulting in significantly faster read and write speeds. For those interested in video editing on the iMac with M6, this will save you a ton of time as our Handbrake encoding test (which measures how long it takes the computer to transcode a 4K video file down to 1080p) dropped by nearly two minutes, down from 5:03 on the iMac M4 to just 3:20 on the iMac M6.

The new M6 chip isn’t the only upgrade under the hood though, as this is also the first iMac with Apple’s proprietary N1 networking chip built in. Alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, it also adds native Thread support so your iMac can act as a Thread border router and directly communicate with your smart home gear.

These are all big upgrades you’ll notice in your day-to-day experience with the iMac M6 and you can read more about them in my Mac mini M6 review. However, with one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 7 support, I saw gigabit speeds over Wi-Fi when running a few speed tests.

I could take that even further by running an Ethernet cable from my router to the iMac with M6’s power adapter as my review unit has a 2.5 GbE port built-in. It’s worth noting that while the base model doesn’t come with one, you can pay an extra $30 for the iMac power adapter with an Ethernet jack if you prefer the reliability and added speeds you get over a wired connection.

As we saw with the iMac M4 a few years ago, Apple has made serious progress when it comes to gaming on Mac and this is even more evident with the new iMac with M6. While the base model has a 10-core GPU, the upgraded one has a 12-core GPU, but both are great for gaming if you keep your expectations in check.

Given that I previously played Control on the Mac mini with M6 on Apple’s Studio Display XDR at the office, I wanted to see how Remedy’s third-person supernatural shooter played on the iMac with M6’s 4.5K Retina display at home.

Just like before, I did have to drop the resolution down to 1440p, but the game looked crisp and ran smoothly on Apple’s M6 chip. If you don’t mind sacrificing even more resolution, scaling down to 1080p gives you an even bigger performance boost across a wide variety of titles compared to the M4 chip.

In the time since I tested the Mac mini with M6, I picked up Stray on sale specifically to see how it runs on macOS. After booting up the game and playing through the intro, I’d say the iMac with M6 handled it surprisingly well.

While these are both somewhat newer titles, if you have a large backlog of Steam games you haven’t gotten around to finishing yet, the iMac with M6 could be the perfect way to play them. Even with the in-game resolution turned down, its display looks fantastic and the six-speaker system — with two pairs of force-cancelling woofers and two high-performance tweeters — helps bring the action to life too.

When the iMac with M6 was first revealed and I found out that Apple wasn’t going to bump up its screen size from 24 inches to 27 or even 32 inches, I was slightly disappointed. With the release of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, I think we might finally see a screen size bump to accommodate touch support in the next iMac — but that will be at least a few years away.

Now back to the iMac with M6, though I was initially disappointed it still had a smaller, 24-inch screen, it ended up taking me completely by surprise. Given that I do most of my work in a web browser with two side-by-side Chrome windows (each with dozens of tabs open simultaneously), I thought I wouldn’t be able to multitask the way I’m used to on the iMac with M6. Thanks to its higher 4.5K resolution though, I had more than enough screen real estate to do so quite easily.

The iMac with M6 is also slightly brighter than the older M4 variant based on our display tests. Colors are vibrant and both pictures and video appear very sharp too. I had no trouble at all editing photos in GIMP and all of my pics were color accurate on its display as well.

Since the iMac with M6’s speakers are so punchy, I decided to test its display further by watching The Wild Robot and a bit of Godzilla vs. Kong. In DreamWorks’ animated film, the robot Roz’s metallic body looked clean and crisp while Brightbill’s yellow feathers and the rest of the island’s foliage really popped.

Now if you’re partial to matte displays like I am and can’t stand seeing glare on a glossy screen, the iMac is the only all-in-one with this option available. This upgrade will set you back an extra $200 — but if you plan on using the iMac with M6 in a room with a lot of ambient light or near a window, it’s absolutely worth it.

Even though its design remains unchanged, the iMac with M6 packs in enough extra power to make it a worthwhile upgrade, especially from an older iMac with an M1 or M2 chip. Still, it does have its downsides — including a fixed-height stand that still can't be adjusted and a higher starting price over the previous model.

Let’s face it, there’s no computer or all-in-one that looks as good and features a design as iconic as Apple’s iMac. However, looks aren’t everything — and this is especially true coming from someone who also reviews home office furniture for a living.

Although you can tilt the display about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back, when it comes to ergonomics, this isn’t ideal. Instead, just like on Apple’s Studio Display, I’d love to see an optional height-adjustable stand for the iMac M6 too.

Sure, you can easily use a desk shelf or monitor stand to rectify this issue, but one of the main reasons someone buys an iMac over another all-in-one or a Mac mini is for the aesthetics. As I’m using one of the best standing desks from Uplift Desk for my Mac mini M6 setup, I was able to raise the desk itself to get the screen at a more ergonomic height. However, doing so makes typing on the included Magic Keyboard worse, since my forearms were tilted up instead of resting straight.

There’s something about seeing the color-matched accessories and stand together on a completely clutter-free desk that’s just really striking with an iMac. Having to ruin that look with an extra stand — or buy another accessory just to fix basic neck strain — stings even more when you take into account the other big downside with the iMac M6.

With its gorgeous display and simple setup, Apple’s iMac has always made an excellent family computer. You could set one up in a home office or even out in the living room and the entire household could use it for checking emails, managing calendars, watching videos, browsing the web or even playing games.

Thanks to RAMageddon though, the iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 — which puts a big dent in any family’s budget. Similar to the Mac mini M6, this new iMac is $200 more than its predecessor, and that’s without factoring in the additional cost of extra memory and storage. Upgrading from the base model’s 16GB of unified memory up to 24GB is an extra $200, and it’s the same story when you go from 256GB to 512GB of storage.

Add in the power adapter with Ethernet, a Magic Trackpad instead of a mouse, and a Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and the iMac becomes a premium purchase quite quickly. Granted, it’s a machine you will be able to use for years to come with its appliance-like reliability — but still, foregoing yet another price hike would have been nice for the iMac with M6.

The iMac with M6 remains the sleekest and easiest-to-set-up all-in-one desktop you can get. There’s no other Mac or Windows machine like it, and if you want a computer that looks as good as it performs, you won’t be disappointed. The new M6 chip and the inclusion of the N1 chip give the iMac M6 a significant power and connectivity boost that make it an easy upgrade to recommend for anyone holding on to an older iMac.

Even then, I would have liked to see some tweaks to its now five-year-old design — like a larger screen or, more practically, the option to configure it with a height-adjustable stand. Still, if you don’t want to fuss with an external monitor, webcam, and loose cables, and just want a machine that works straight out of the box, the iMac with M6 is an iterative but worthwhile upgrade.

#3200. Cult Phone-Maker Nothing’s Mystery Screenless AI Device Is Coming Next Month

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Nothing CEO Carl Pei believes your work tools can be cool too. He's building one to prove it.

In the introduction to the essay published on X by Nothing CEO Carl Pei on Wednesday, it almost sounds like he’s arguing against the premise of standalone AI devices.

In Pei’s post, he suggests AI’s “iPhone moment” is still several years away. This could read as though Nothing is holding its horses rather than diving into the fray right now. But that isn’t the case; in fact, it’s quite the opposite.

“Our first AI-native product ships next month,” Pei says. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”

Pei is playing it characteristically coy. He’s dropping clues, and you can bet there will be more to come in the ensuing days and weeks up until the official launch of this mystery product.

Standalone AI devices are a burgeoning industry, even if they’re yet to result in a hugely compelling, must-have consumer product. Whether it be pins, pendants, glasses, headphones or tabletop devices, tech companies are flooding the market with new native AI devices. Some companies, such as OpenAI, are working on ideas behind closed doors, whereas others, such as AI note-taking experts Plaud, are already establishing a strong and loyal customer base.

British startup Nothing is predominantly known for its retro-inspired audio products and cool smartphones, around which the company is building a cult following as an alternative to more mainstream, generic phone companies. It’s more closely aligned with lifestyle and fashion brands than most of its tech brethren. In spite of this, it sounds like its first AI device will be more work than play.

Just like computers, AI will need to prove itself in the realm of productivity — the workplace — before it spills over into being truly useful and appreciated in our personal lives, writes Pei. And so, Nothing is building a tool for the workplace, albeit one with the company’s customary design-forward approach.

“We were taught that seriousness and beauty could not share a room,” says Pei. But he wants you to know that work tools can be beautiful, and he promises Nothing’s will be.

This is all very mysterious — perhaps more so because the image accompanying Pei’s post actually looks like it could be a snapshot of one of many different smartphones from the past decade or more. The simple black rectangle with one rounded corner looks distinctly unlike a Nothing device, and something a less imaginative tech company might produce.

We shouldn’t be fooled by this, though. Nothing has yet to bore us with a design, and it seems unlikely to start now — especially after Pei’s treatise on the subject. No doubt there will be more hints forthcoming, as Nothing gears up to persuade you that its products belong just as much in your office as at a warehouse rave in Berlin, and that its approach to AI is essential to your workflow above and beyond the offerings of its strait-laced competitors.

#3199. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

#3198. Bread as a Sponge for Oil Is the Best Kitchen Hack I Learned All Year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.
