#3197. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Home Entertainment > Speakers

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

Sonos’ promise to release its AI-upgraded voice assistant is nearing its “Fall 2026” deadline, and before fans can use the highly anticipated update, the company continues to make small improvements to its app and player features.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3196. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3195. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

#3193. Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes – up to $500

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some GPUs will see bigger increases than others, while Intel and AMD remain mum on their pricing plans

Graphics are handled by an Nvidia Quadro M4000 card.

As the AI-driven global memory shortage rages on, Nvidia is notifying users that its RTX 50 series of graphics cards will see yet another significant price hike this week.

Also: I switched from Intel to AMD – here’s why I’m never going back

In August, Nvidia gave gamers and content creators fair warning that the company’s entire line of RTX 50 Series GPUs would get price increases of up to a 15%. The flagship 5090 is getting the highest: a nearly $500 increase on an already eye-watering $6,000 price tag at Best Buy. The lower-end 5050 and 5060 will get much more modest, if still grumble-worthy, $50-60 bumps, which puts the squeeze on consumers already caught between market hype and failed expectations.

Earlier iterations of the brand’s graphics cards, like the RTX 40 and RTX 30 series, won’t be directly affected by this decision. However, don’t be surprised if you see some resellers take advantage of the situation by adding their own price increases or snapping up stock to sell at a markup on the second-hand market.

Intel and AMD have been quiet about the possibility of a price hike on their own graphics cards, and neither company plans any immediate changes in response to Nvidia’s decision. Not yet, anyway. As companies like Nvidia continue to snap up the raw resources needed to manufacture AI chips and pledge their GPUs and motherboards to future AI data centers rather than the consumer market, it’s likely both companies will eventually follow suit with their own hefty increases.

#3192. Data Center Backers Suffer Near-Total Midterm Defeats Across the Country

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

More than 40 voting initiatives yielded almost nothing but resistance to data-center projects.

The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry.

But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts.

In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions.

Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting.

Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions.

Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful.

Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting.

The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches.

“I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night.

USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers.

The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny.

“Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico.

Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close.

“Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

#3191. HomeView with an arm? Apple reportedly plans $1,000 swiveling smart panel

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The HomeView Ultra is expected to feature a robotic arm and 9-inch display. Shades of Amazon's discontinued Echo Show 10?

The Apple HomeView is the company’s first dedicated smart home display, and new reports of how Apple plans to improve the product are already circulating. Apple is reportedly planning to announce a HomeView with a robotic arm as early as next year. The dynamic display is expected to cost up to $1,000.

Also: Apple’s HomeView may double as security camera

The HomeView isn’t even on the market yet — it will be available for purchase next week, starting at $299. This 7-inch smart panel features a speaker that doubles as a stand, and Apple will also sell a wall-mounted option.

As a smart home device, the HomeView is designed to serve as a platform for interacting with your Apple ecosystem, including Apple Home and Siri. It’s a smart dashboard that lets you view all your smart home devices and security cameras, as well as your calendar, messages, and other integrated apps.

The Information reported that Apple is rumored to be working on a higher-end smart display for 2027, with shipments starting in 2028. The new device, codenamed J595, may be branded HomeView Ultra and feature a robotic arm and a 9-inch display.

The new HomeView’s screen would be mounted on an articulated mechanical arm to swivel the display, tracking users during FaceTime calls to keep them on-screen. The device could feature proactive smart home automations, such as turning on devices or triggering a room scene when someone walks into the room.

Also: Google’s latest Home updates just fixed my biggest annoyances

The same report indicates that the hardware has been complete for a couple of years, but launch delays are attributed to software development issues. Integrating advanced AI features and proactive automation has, according to The Information, been a challenge for Apple.

A swiveling smart home display isn’t entirely new. Amazon used to sell an Echo Show 10 with a display that tracked users to keep them in the camera’s view during video calls, though this model has been discontinued.

However, one that works within the Apple ecosystem could change how users interact with their home interfaces, given the popularity of FaceTime calls and the prevalence of iPhone users.

Also: 4 big Amazon smart home announcements

A HomeView Ultra could even anticipate users’ needs by tracking people’s movements and automatically executing routines and scenes depending on where they are in the home.

While there’s reason to doubt whether most smart home users would welcome such technology in their homes or consider it too invasive, premium robotic smart displays indicate that companies are standardizing interactive central hubs for the home.

#3190. ‘You Can See Everything’ … in Space? A24 Sends Elizabeth Holmes Doc to ISS

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Nathan Fielder's documentary about the former Theranos CEO will screen for astronauts in outer space.

The popularity of You Can See Everything has apparently surpassed Earthly measures. Nearly three weeks after the nearly 3-hour documentary about disgraced former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes premiered in theaters domestically, studio A24 is screening it in outer space.

The studio said in an A24 Instagram post that it has granted NASA’s request to screen the film for astronauts aboard the International Space Station.

A representative for A24 didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

I’d say this was surprising news, yet after I saw the impact the movie had on Halloween, it makes perfect sense. You Can See Everything is a phenomenon.

At my daughter’s school, I saw a toddler dressed as Holmes, which certainly was a choice. People all over my social feeds were costumed as the infamous scrambled-egg bowl from the movie (IYKYK). Heck, the friend I saw the movie with took my idea and dressed in all black, wearing old-school headphones and an emo hairstyle, and carried a laptop to channel Nathan Fielder.

You Can See Everything, co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was initially slated for a limited theatrical release in the US. After three weeks, the documentary hit No. 1 at the box office last weekend, beating DC’s Clayface for the top spot.

Now, audiences around the world are clamoring to get a taste of the movie.

They still have to wait, though. UK moviegoers won’t be able to see it until Nov. 20. It’s coming to France on Dec. 30, and while Sony Pictures acquired the rights to release You Can See Everything in countries like Germany, South Korea and Latin America, no dates have been announced yet.

That said, those lucky astronauts in low Earth orbit will soon be side-eyeing yellow mixing bowls, questioning every move made by Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, and simply wanting more Amanda Seyfried in their lives.

For a movie that is already super disorienting, one has to assume that removing gravity from the equation will make watching You Can See Everything a next-level viewing experience.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

#3187. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3186. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

#3185. T-Mobile Is Throwing One More Phone Plan Into the T-Mix for Budget Subscribers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The T-Mix Saver plan rounds out the carrier’s new lineup, which is now live.

T-Mobile announced last week that T-Mix — a new suite of unlimited data phone plans — is replacing the Experience 2.0 and Essentials 2.0 plans. The core plans — Standard, More and Loaded — come with a perks system called Picks, which can be used toward streaming services and devices.

While the Experience era’s tenure was relatively short-lived, not all of it is going away: T-Mobile has kept a budget option for customers who want the basics at a lower monthly price. With T-Mix now live, the new T-Mix Saver plan joins the main lineup.

T-Mobile’s T-Mix Saver replaces the Essentials Saver 2.0 plan (which we’ve featured on a few of our best phone plans lists). According to the updated T-Mobile website, the new plan costs $55 a month for one line or $100 for two lines (the maximum allowed); those prices are without AutoPay. However, when you apply the AutoPay discount, that becomes $45 a month for a single line and $80 for two lines, according to a T-Mobile spokesperson. (The website is currently confusing on this point, because the other T-Mix plan prices are listed with AutoPlay applied, but T-Mix Saver is not.)

To compare with Essentials Saver 2.0, that’s a $5 savings for a single line with T-Mix Saver using AutoPay. You can get the new plan even cheaper if you transfer your existing number from another carrier, lowering it to $30 for one line or $65 for two. All prices exclude taxes and fees.

The plan is bare-bones, with zero Picks. Customers who want to add perks, such as Apple TV or DashPass by DoorDash, have to upgrade to the Standard plan for $55 (single) or $85 (two lines) per month. The Standard plan includes one Pick for a single line and two Picks for two lines.

Like the Standard plan, T-Mix Saver includes 50GB of high-speed data, followed by unlimited data at slower speeds. It also offers unlimited hotspot use at 3G speeds and SD (480p) video streaming.

“For a small percentage of customers, all they want is the best 5G network,” said Allan Samson, chief marketing officer at T-Mobile. “For them, we created the simple T-Mix Saver plan with exceptional customer service and all the perks of T-Mobile membership.”

#3184. LSI Industries (LYTS) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Royston drove 44% growth, but lighting and QSR softness persisted.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

LSI Industries Inc. (LYTS -16.83%) reported total revenue growth driven by the integration of the Royston Group acquisition despite weakness in the broader non-residential lighting and quick-serve restaurant markets. The company reported a shift in focus from the acquisition of its current platform toward the realization of potential through increased customer share of wallet and improved operational efficiency across its 23 manufacturing facilities. Management reported progress in high-demand verticals like grocery and refueling while navigating project timing delays and budget-driven pushouts from customers. Strategic efforts are currently focused on identifying procurement synergies and consolidating manufacturing footprints to enhance the margin profile and reach multiyear financial targets.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the LSI Industries Fiscal 2027 First Quarter Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Mr. Jim Galeese, Chief Financial Officer. Thank you, sir. You may begin.

James Galeese: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining today's call. We issued a press release before the market opened this morning, detailing our fiscal '27 first quarter results. In addition to this release, we posted a conference call presentation in the Investor Relations section of our corporate website. Information contained in this presentation will be referenced throughout today's conference call, included are certain non-GAAP measures for improved transparency of our operating results. A complete reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP results is contained in our press release and 10-Q. Please note that management's commentary and responses to questions on today's conference call may include forward-looking statements about our business outlook. Such statements involve risks and opportunities, and actual results could differ materially.

I refer you to our safe harbor statement, which appears in this morning's press release for more details. Today's call will begin with remarks summarizing our fiscal first quarter results. At the conclusion of these prepared remarks, we will open the line for questions. With that, I'll turn the call over to LSI President and Chief Executive Officer, Jim Clark.

James Clark: Thank you, Jim, and good morning, everyone. I appreciate you joining us today. Today, we're reviewing our first quarter results for fiscal '27. As you saw in our earnings release, we reported revenue of approximately $226 million, which is an increase of 44% over the prior year, reflecting the addition of Royston to our business. Adjusted EBITDA increased 41% to $22.2 million, and we generated nearly $14 million in free cash flow. Overall, I would characterize the quarter as one where we made good progress on a number of important initiatives while continuing to work through some challenging marketing conditions. Jim Galeese will cover the financial details in a few minutes. So let me start with Royston.

We are now several months into the integration, and I'm very pleased with the progress we're making. Royston delivered a solid quarter with sequential sales growth of 8% and a 100 basis point improvement in adjusted EBITDA margin. We're beginning to see the benefits of initiatives focused on improving operating efficiency and strengthening commercial execution. As I've said before, we didn't acquire Royston simply to become a larger company. We acquired Royston because it fits directly into our vertical market strategy that we've been executing for the past 7 years. Our strategy hasn't changed. What's changed is our ability to serve those markets. With Royston, we've significantly expanded the products, services and manufacturing capabilities we can bring to our customers.

And we're beginning to see the benefits of that expanded platform in the conversations we're having across our customer base. A few weeks ago, we formally introduced our Category of One initiative at NACS Convention. NACS is the National Association of Convenience Stores, and it's one of our largest trade shows. This was an opportunity to bring together a full scope of LSI's capabilities and present them to many of the largest convenience stores and refueling customers in North America. The response was extremely positive. I think many of our customers are just beginning to appreciate the breadth of what we can now offer.

And while these opportunities take time to develop, the conversations we're having today are broader and more strategic than they were just a few years ago. Turning to our vertical markets. Refueling and convenience stores continue to perform well. Sales increased approximately 5% during the quarter, supported by activity across several of our largest customers. The 2,500-site renovation program we discussed last quarter continues to progress as planned with activity expected to build through fiscal '27 and into fiscal 2028. We're also working with another major convenience store chain on a potentially significant renovation program, beginning with store concept developments right now.

As we've discussed on previous calls, the competitive environment in the convenience store market continues to drive investment in new locations, remodels and the overall customer experience. We love it. We believe this is a long-term trend and one that aligns very well with our capabilities. Grocery also remains healthy. We're seeing continued investment across broad customer base and order activity in that vertical increased 12% during the quarter. Across Display Solutions, overall orders increased 4%, and our pro forma backlog also improved. These are encouraging indicators, particularly given the broader economic environment. Quick-serve restaurants remain a more challenging market. We've talked about the uneven investment patterns in QSR over the last several quarters, and those conditions have continued.

Some customers are moving forward with their programs, others are delaying investment decisions. The softness has affected both our sales and margin. However, we recently received some very encouraging news from one of our larger QSR customers. They approved a 3,000-store interior renovation program that we've been working on for some time and selected LSI as 1 of 3 providers. The program is expected to begin late in our third quarter fiscal 2027 and continue over approximately 3 years. It's another example of the opportunities developing within our existing customer base, and we're thrilled to be part of it. Turning to Lighting. The broader market remains soft.

Sales for LSI declined approximately 6% during the quarter, reflecting weaker demand across several key commercial and industrial applications. We did see growth in refueling, sports and banking, but that was offset by weakness in parking, smaller retail, warehousing and automotive. Despite the lower volume, our Lighting team improved gross margin during the quarter, reflecting continued discipline around pricing and cost management. Order activity was relatively stable, and we continue to invest in new product development, training and customer engagement. We've built a very competitive Lighting business over the last several years, and I believe we're well positioned when the broader market recovers. I also want to touch briefly on operational efficiency.

We spent the last several years building a broader and more capable organization. Now we're focused on bringing those capabilities together and identifying opportunities to operate more efficiently. One example is the consolidation of our Collingwood, Ontario manufacturing operation. We're bringing that into our existing Canada's best facility near Toronto. We expect to complete that transition through the end of this fiscal year, and we'll generate more than $1 million in annual savings through this move. This is the type of work we'll continue to pursue across LSI, not simply reducing costs, but improving the way our businesses operate together, making better use of our facilities and our equipment and creating a more effective organization.

Looking ahead, I want to be realistic about our near-term. We're seeing positive order activity and a number of encouraging customer developments, but the timing of that opportunities doesn't always align neatly with our fiscal quarters. We're also dealing with continued softness in Lighting and QSR, as I just spoke of a minute ago. Inflationary pressures and the normal seasonal slowdown in our retail renovation activity as we move into the holiday period is something else we need to consider. At the end of the day, I feel very good about where we're positioned as a company. Over the past several years, we've been focused on building a broader and more capable organization.

Through a combination of our organic growth activities and strategic acquisitions, we've assembled a platform that I believe is unique in the market that we serve today. As we look ahead, our focus is increasingly shifting from building that platform to realizing its full potential. That means expanding our share of wallet with existing customers, introducing those new products and capabilities and continuing to improve the efficiency and profitability of our operations. And importantly, many of these opportunities are within our control. We don't need to rely entirely on improving economy or others to continue to make this progress. We're approaching an important milestone in our strategic planning process.

In December, we expect to share our next multiyear strategic plan with the investment community, outlining how we intend to build on the progress we've made under the Fast Forward plan and continue to create long-term shareholder value. We've always placed a great deal of emphasis on our high say-do ratio, setting expectations carefully and delivering against them. That discipline will remain central to how we approach this next chapter. As always, I want to thank our entire team for their continued hard work and commitment. There's a lot going on across LSI right now, and I'm pleased with the progress we're making.

I'm encouraged by what we see ahead, and I'm looking forward to sharing more about our future plans in December. With that, I'm going to turn the call back over to Jim Galeese for a more detailed review of our financial results.

James Galeese: Good morning, all. LSI delivered $226 million in sales, over $22 million in adjusted EBITDA and just under $14 million in cash flow in Q1, and I'll comment on all 3 areas. Starting with sales, the year-to-year 44% increase was led by Display Solutions segment, which includes the incremental impact of the Royston acquisition. Excluding the acquisition, Display Solutions sales increased 1% versus prior year, with significant fluctuation realized across key vertical markets. For Display, both C-store and grocery generated mid-single-digit growth rates, sustaining a high level of customer project activity, while QSR and banking were soft, both down double digits.

In C-store, our largest customer generated double-digit growth in the quarter as we completed renovation work on additional pilot sites. The multiyear renovation program proposed by this customer has different renovation package options depending on the site, and we're working closely with their team on finalizing content and overall project planning. Also in the quarter, we began renovation work for the 2,500-site award we announced last quarter in the refueling vertical. The initial award did not include Royston, but now includes signage, representing an early cross-selling win. For grocery, demand also remains favorable, led by sales to large chains.

Notably, the nation's largest retailer completed their line reviews for the next calendar year, and the result is, LSI will be awarded additional share of product. As projected, the QSR vertical remains very soft as chains respond to inflation-driven lower consumer traffic. However, as Jim mentioned, a large QSR chain selected LSI as a supplier for renovation of 3,000 stores over the next 3-plus years. Separately, we continue to make progress on the Royston acquisition. Sales improved sequentially, and all 3 businesses realized pro forma sales growth versus the prior year quarter. Looking forward, Display segment orders and backlog both increased 4% compared to the prior year quarter as project release activity continues in our 2 largest verticals.

The operating environment has become more challenging with the number of customer schedule changes and pushouts increasing. Reschedules range from several weeks to several months. There's multiple reasons driving this, one being the status of project budgets as we near the end of the calendar year. Another is job sites lagging behind schedule and skilled labor availability is also an issue. We continue to collaborate closely with customers on scheduling, particularly as we enter the slower seasonality period as customers limit renovation activity ahead of the holiday, high sales and consumer traffic period. Shifting to the Lighting segment. Lighting sales were 6% below prior year, the result of ongoing softness in the broader commercial and industrial market.

While the near-term outlook remains soft, we remain focused on margin management, where alignment of selling price to current cost supported a 10 basis point improvement in the year-to-year gross margin rate. Lighting quote activity continues to exceed orders with quotes for the last 3 months increasing 5% over last year, while orders increased 1%, reflecting the ongoing delayed quote-to-order conversion process. Next, several comments on adjusted EBITDA. LSI generated adjusted EBITDA of $22 million in the first quarter or 41% above prior year.

To summarize, EBITDA and EBITDA margin was favorably impacted by the incremental impact of Royston and C-store and grocery volumes, all being unfavorably impacted by lower volume in Lighting, and vertical customer mix in Display Solutions and the continued cycling through the lower margin backlog in the SignResource business. Progress was achieved in multiple margin improvement initiatives in the quarter. Royston EBITDA margin, which is accretive to LSI, increased 100 basis points sequentially from the fourth quarter. All 3 brands realized improved margins, including the SignResource business. We expect SignResource margin improvements to continue, targeting a 200-plus basis point increase for fiscal Q2 over Q1.

In addition, processes have been implemented to ensure pricing on all Royston project quotes and orders are aligned with current costs and provide for changes in key commodity costs. Further, we remain focused on identifying and implementing synergy savings across the business. We have already identified and in process of implementing $1 million in incremental procurement savings across the company. Also, we recently announced the closure of the Collingwood, Ontario manufacturing facility and consolidation of production into the Toronto area, Canada's best facility. The consolidation will be completed by the end of the fiscal year and generate over $1 million of annual cost savings.

Our first quarter sales and EBITDA performance generated solid free cash flow of $13.8 million, serving to reduce net debt by $14 million. In the 6 months since the acquisition of Royston, LSI has reduced net debt by over $23 million, resulting in a net debt to pro forma TTM adjusted EBITDA of 2.6x. To conclude, we are encouraged by the increasing level of program interactions with our customers as well as the progress on our key performance improvement initiatives. While we may continue to incur timing fluctuations in our projects and markets, we are confident in our direction and path and will accelerate our execution throughout fiscal 2027.

I will now turn the call back to the moderator for the question-and-answer session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Aaron Spychalla with Craig-Hallum.

Aaron Spychalla: Maybe first for us on the C-store vertical. In the release, you mentioned a pilot program with an existing customer kind of early in the large-scale renovation. And then earlier on the call, I heard about kind of store concept developments with another chain. So I just want to kind of confirm or just understand, are those one and the same? Are those 2 separate? And then just any other color on kind of timing or size potential for number of sites and pull-through on the Royston side of things as you look to expand wallet share with those opportunities?

James Clark: Yes. And so, first of all, just to answer your question, the 3,000-store is a program we've been awarded and that will bridge out through the third quarter -- late third quarter, early Q4 of '27 here and then go into 2028. As you remember, with our -- some of our other programs, this isn't unusual for us to come in where there's multiple suppliers, but we've been very effective at capturing a bigger share of the initial award as we go forward, and we're hopeful we'll be able to do the same here.

The development is another separate customer, and we're in the early stages of that right now, but it's very encouraging, and we've just moved on through some actual field deployments. So it's always an encouraging sign because it usually indicates a final decision and a go forward. And then lastly, separate, but we still have the 2,500-site program that we talked about last quarter. And this is on top of our normal rhythm of business. So these are kind of newer projects that are rolling in and ones that we thought were worth mentioning.

Aaron Spychalla: And then can you just provide a little bit more detail on some of the significant opportunities to drive operating leverage? You talked a little bit about the facility consolidation, some on procurement. But just any other details there as you kind of balance that with just some of the other kind of macro issues that you're navigating as well?

James Clark: Yes. I mean, I look at them as all as opportunities, right? We're -- we've got 23 facilities spread out across the U.S. right now. There are locations where we could consolidate some things, we could make better utilization of equipment and time we have. So we're looking at all of those things. We've always said we were going to kind of commit back and do this. And I think this is really all about that focus to getting to our 12.5% EBITDA. This is where this efficiency comes from. Better asset utilization.

If we're using a piece of equipment right now on a single shift, 8 hours a day, we've got 16 hours we could be using that piece of equipment or at least a portion of that. Those are all opportunities for us. We've got -- we're moving product between 1 or 2 facilities, partial here, partial there to get a completed product. If we can get that all under one roof, that creates a tremendous opportunity for us. So I think over the next 2 years, you're going to see us really kind of invest in that. The Collingwood facility is a good example.

Taking that and creating a center of excellence for Canada in Canada has always been our idea, and it has shielded us from the tariffs and the cross-border communication and the issues going on there. Those may improve. Those may stay like they are, they may get worse. But when we have a business that's fully capable of supplying almost everything we can do in Canada, that's a big plus for us. And then the additional plus is bringing it all under one roof. So I think you're going to see us continue to execute on a lot of all the operational opportunities, and that's going to go right towards our margin profile and our effectiveness in running the company.

James Galeese: Aaron, I would -- Jim Galeese here. I would just add to Jim's comments. So as you know, we've talked before, quality of earnings is very important to LSI for a number of reasons. And so we take both our business improvement initiatives and synergies associated with the acquisition very seriously, and we have quite a road map of items to build on. Jim mentioned a few, and I'll just mention a couple more. I think I mentioned in my comments how we've identified and in the process of implementing $1 million of procurement savings in key commodity areas. And that's just a start.

And our alignment, our ability to continue to align selling price to current cost is -- continues to get better. That's something LSI has always had a pretty good competency in, and we're expanding that into the Royston product areas. And you're seeing that, and Jim commented on it, and I did as well, the sequential improvement we've seen there and the sequential improvement we continue to expect moving forward and we'll realize moving forward. So quality of earnings and margin management, margin realization is a high priority for us, Aaron.

James Clark: And last quarter, we talked about a little bit of softness in margin around some of the SignResources projects that rolled forward after the acquisition. We've already been able to go in there and make significant improvement. I mean, we've still got a ways to go. We said that it would take us through the remainder of the calendar year to kind of get us on par, but I'm very happy with some of the progress we've made there and the team has done. And that's just that pricing discipline that we've always been very good at.

Aaron Spychalla: Good. And then maybe one last one, if I could sneak in. Just on the balance sheet. Can you talk about the time line and kind of confidence in continued EBITDA to free cash flow conversion to get that leverage down below. I think the target has been 2x.

James Galeese: Yes. I think we've been very clear about our timetable in terms of driving our leverage ratio to 2x and lower. And we expect that we continue to expect that to happen within the next 12 to 18 months. We see no reason that our free cash flow will continue the pattern that it is and in fact, should improve once we see a little more uplift and release on some of these larger releases on some of these programs.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Brent Thielman with Oppenheimer.

Brent Thielman: I guess first question, there was a comment just around customer discussions becoming more kind of broader, more strategic than a few years ago. Jim, if you wouldn't mind just expanding upon that and to what degree that gives you visibility here even as it seems like we're working through kind of a dynamic macro right now?

James Clark: I never want to get the cart before the horse, but NACS is a big trade show for us. It's probably the biggest, and it's a concentration of very large customers, both from the Royston perspective and from LSI, and that's been historical. The -- I think that there was an epiphany, a realization, kind of a finger snap of I get it now from a customer perspective. And I just felt like there was a lot of energy about that realization. And it still takes time to mature because in every one of these cases, our customers are currently buying from some incumbent.

And we're going to make the assumption that, that incumbent is doing a good job for them. We need to continue to articulate that the benefits that we're bringing, the Category of One we're developing under one roof as a manufacturer and as the integration partner to help our customers get it installed has real value. And what I was commenting to is, coming off of NACS where you get a high density of customers in one location in a short amount of time, you get a lot of input rapidly. And the realization of I get it, that connection with what we can do across their stores was clear and apparent and the energy level was very high.

And so, I just come off of that whole trade show very kind of excited. It's nice to see the program, the dream that we've kind of built and sketched out connect with these customers. And now it's just realizing that forward momentum and creating it into something that we are able to capture more of that wallet share, and we are able to move from 2 or 3 solutions to 5 or 6 solutions. And I feel like there was a lot of connection at the show about that capability. And in individual conversations.

I'm just mentioning that when you're there for 3 days and you can connect it one after another, it really is -- it really creates some energy.

Brent Thielman: Appreciate that, Jim. I guess as a follow-up, on Lighting. Are you seeing a market that's starting to stabilize? I don't think it's been especially good for you in the last few quarters? Or is some of what you're seeing in the quarter suggest it's getting a little bit worse?

James Clark: Well, I think that if you look at from an industry perspective, I think we've been outpacing in Lighting for multiple quarters, particularly if you go back 2, 3 quarters, we were consistently outpacing the market. We were showing that growth. Most of our Lighting, as I said, we've got high activity in some segments, and we've got lower activity in others. And I think that lower is just a little bit more advanced than the higher stuff right now. So you're seeing that decline, that 6% decline. With that said, though, I mean, all these customers we're talking to, and it's kind of segment-driven, are talking about projects they have in the queue, but they're just being pushed out.

They're being pushed. We usually see a little bit of accelerated activity. We call this -- we actually call this our lighting season. The time right before the fall hits, people start recognizing, "Oh, I've got to get this building lighting done. I've got maintenance work to do. We want to button things up before the cold weather hits. There's a little bit of activity, a little bit of increased activity that didn't occur this year. And I think some of that is where capital budgets, dollars associated with things that were improvements and putting budgets at the beginning of the year.

Some of the companies are saying, wait a minute, hold on, we're going to roll that into the beginning of next year. So I don't see any of the projects going away, but I do see an increased amount of customers kicking things down the road. And that's what we're experiencing.

James Galeese: Brent, the proof point on that is, in my comments where I said, in the last 3 months, our quote activity is actually up 5%, right? But yet our sales and our orders up 1%. So that shows then that the delayed quote-to-order conversion cycle. So they're frustrating. But when we get into it, there's reasons for that and a lot of it is around what you just said, how things are rolling up and how things are rolling up to their budgets. And if they're over, then they have to go in and look at -- make some changes, reengineer some things and not just lighting, by the way, but other finishing elements as well.

So that's just created an elongated cycle that's -- but that pipeline is there. It's just backing up.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Min Cho with Texas Capital Securities.

Min Cho: Congratulations on your QSR award. Jim, you did mention that you were 1 of 3 on this award and that you had gained some share. Just want to know if this included -- if this contract included some Royston products? And are the other 2 vendors, are they providing products that you cannot provide? Or is this just a diversification strategy by the customer? And then a final question on that, are you providing the project management on this contract?

James Clark: Okay. Min, thanks for the question. This is an LSI project. This is not -- doesn't include any Royston at this point. And a lot of that is because I think we've been involved in this project almost 3 years. We've talked before about these -- the way these cycles work, you sit down, you have design discussions, you do material selection, what's your objective? How much do you want to do this? You put the designs to the materials, you show samples, there's adjustments made. So we're just at that point where we went out and did some actual test stores.

They -- the customer kind of committed a direction, but this was all way in advance of the Royston project coming on board with LSI. So this is an LSI-only project. Because it's an LSI-only project, our competitive forces are a little bit more stable and mature. And so those competitors, those other people that are providing it, they provide the same category that we do. They don't provide anything else that we don't. In fact, we provide more than they do. It's just that this project doesn't require that yet. We are providing project management resources.

And it's yet to be seen, but it's not uncommon for us to walk into a project like this with 1/3 of the project, but take more of it as we move along. And that's all based on our execution capability. So I'm encouraged. I'm happy with what we've got, and I want more. And hopefully, we'll get more as we move through the project.

Min Cho: Something that you highlighted, Jim, during your Royston tour in October was the importance of your adapt services kind of leading with the program management and such. Can you provide just a little more information around that? Like how large is this? How large is the opportunity? And what does it really provide you in terms of the actual product rollouts?

James Clark: Yes. I mean, I always talk about it like it's catch-up for our fries, right? It doesn't necessarily independently drive business, but it does help quite a bit add to the desire for us to provide more services. And that -- having that very discussion is germane to our whole thesis, right, which is one stop, you can come in and we can really offload that customer from the burdens and the capability. Our capabilities really shine through there. So if you go back 3 years ago, it was a $10 million business. Today, it's a $30 million-plus business, but it really enables kind of the sales that we do.

And that becomes even more important as we bring Royston in. And I would also mention that Royston has a similar service capability in their business, not quite as mature as LSIs, but we've already started the work of integrating those 2 and leveraging off of a couple of things they do that we don't and then leveraging off of more things that we do that they don't. And just for clarity, those services are not -- we don't dispatch trucks to a location. And a lot of that is because if you think of -- I'll just take electrical licenses, for example. State by state, they vary quite a bit.

So if you're in Ohio and you're in Indiana, you've got to have an electrical license in Ohio, you've got to have an electrical license in Indiana. And then county by county, the rules and the standards can vary and even by city by city. So local resources are important to us. What we provide is the overall management of those resources, the permitting, the insurance discussions, the scheduling, all of that, that's what our ADAPT Services group provides.

Min Cho: Great. And then just finally, any update in terms of progress that you're making on your partnership with Carter? Is there anything in backlog yet?

James Clark: There is a lot of -- there's transfer work that Carter already had in the works. There have been a lot of discussions bringing them into -- bringing Carter and the services into what LSI has right now in our customer base. I would say that we're still in the early stages of that. When we signed the agreement with Carter, we explained that, again, this is project cycle timing, and that project cycle is usually 12 to 18 months. So I think I'm encouraged by what we're doing. We've had some great wins already where we've been able to differentiate ourselves in our installation capabilities and coordinated schedules better, and the customers have seen that.

And I'm encouraged by the conversations we're in. But there's -- I wouldn't say there's any tangible momentum in new business quite yet.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Amit Dayal with H.C. Wainwright.

Amit Dayal: So, Jim, just from the recent acquisitions, et cetera, and the size of the company now, how much risk to quarterly variance is there from any customer scheduling changes or pushouts?

James Clark: I mean, I think that's -- and we've been dealing with this since COVID. I mean, if we're speaking historically, I think that we've talked about this before that disruption in schedule and timing, and there's a lot of things that have driven it. Coming out of COVID, I remember just getting permits through local offices, city offices and things like that were a major impact. Today, I think it's budgets. It is almost 100% budgeting.

And where they went in an initial budget said, "Hey, we're going to have $100,000 for each store, and we're going to do 10 stores, and we're going to spend $1 million." All of a sudden, by August or September time frame, they're saying, wait a minute, we're still going to spend $1 million, but we may only get 7 stores done. And so we're going to push these other 3 stores down the road because we don't have the budget for it. But the good news there is that, usually when you're doing one of these rebranding programs, that work is not going away.

They're not going to rebrand 10 of their stores and leave 40 of them in the old format. So I don't really have a lot of concern about the business being there and their commitment to getting the business done. But that inflationary pressure on a whole build-out and broadly across an organization is just putting pressure on their ability to meet their original commitments. So I'll just use that kind of 10 stores as an example. They're just not able to get 10 stores across the finish line with the same budget. Most of the businesses aren't making additional capital available.

So they adjust, we push these projects down the road a bit, and we're pretty confident that they're going to come back around.

Amit Dayal: And then with all the focus on integration and trying to create these synergies, does that take away any resources from product development in the near-term?

James Clark: It's certainly not product development. Product development for the most part, is a dedicated committed team across our organization. We've always -- and one of my marketing folks kind of hit me up the other day on it, Jim, you don't talk about new products as much as you used to on the calls. And I would like to just take a moment to say our commitment to new products is still -- is a vital part of our strategy going forward. And we're still very committed to it. We're still releasing 20-plus new products a year in Lighting. We're looking for all kinds of new materials and new ways of doing things in our Display Solutions.

We have technology upgrades and efficiencies we've been able to put into our refrigerated products. All of that activity is still going on. The integration activities, does it slow it a bit? I'd say Lighting is pretty much untouched. Lighting continues at the same pace it always has. I'd say some of the Display Solutions, minimal impact. Maybe a little bit more on the refrigerated product side because we're making big decisions with Southern Case Arts and JSI and EMI's refrigerated products, and we might have a greater slowdown there because we need to make sure we're making the right decision that spreads across all of them.

But I would also say that our speed and our commitment and our focus on getting some of this operational benefits out of the organization has definitely increased as of late. We've brought on Royston. I think we've got a good rhythm going with Royston. Now we're taking our operations teams, and we're saying, "Okay, let's focus on this efficiency. How do we get more out of this equipment?" Like I was saying earlier, having a great piece of equipment that we're only running 8 hours a day, there's a huge opportunity there, right? How do we bring more in-house where we might be subcontracting some work through an external partner?

How do we move that in-house because we know we can improve the margins. We have better control of our whole supply chain. So all of those activities are things we've been working on over the last, I'd say, in earnest over the last 3 months by program, more than a year. So we've already identified where we want to work. That work was done a year ago. I talked about our July meeting. We really kind of put a finer point on things. And then by September, we were really starting to execute and Collingwood is kind of a first visible piece of that. But there's other activities we're doing.

And I'm very encouraged by them because I think that's the last part of the equation on getting us to that 12.5% under that Fast Forward 2028 plan.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the call back over to Jim Clark for any closing remarks.

James Clark: I want to just say that I'm encouraged by a lot of what's ahead of us, right? We're dealing with an inflationary environment, macro trends in the economic environment. And I think that as a team, as a company, we're doing a very good job of kind of adjusting. I mentioned in my comments that I wish everything fell into a 90-day cycle, and I think you're seeing some of that exposure right now where we're not able to control some of the things we're not able to control We've got good plans going forward to go back and get this operational efficiency. We put together all the pieces, all the ingredients for this opportunity that's in front of us.

Now it's going about measuring things out correctly and making sure we're mixing them correctly to get that recipe just right. And I'm encouraged by the work that we're doing. It was a smaller piece of my comments, but we are going to roll out an updated Fast Forward plan. We'll be doing that. We will be sure to give everybody notice, but it will be kind of mid-December, let's say, 12, 15, 16, somewhere in that bracket, and we will give plenty of notice to everybody. And it's not an abandonment of our 2028 plan. It's just a fine point on it, and it extends it out to 2032. And I'm encouraged by that.

We have in front of us the plans to get there. We have in front of us the opportunities to get there. And the overall economic environment can be a headwind or a tailwind for us, but it's not going to stop us from getting there. The most encouraging thing is, a lot of these activities we'll do are under our control. So there are things that we're able to do internal in the business. And so they should be a little bit more resistant to the economic swings. But obviously, there's things we need to do that still rely on an economy that's moving forward. But we have a little bit more control over it.

So I feel encouraged by our ability to kind of execute against those things. There's still a lot of good runway left in front of us. I still feel like we're in the early innings of this whole story. And I see a clarity and an acceptance by our customer base and an execution by our team that is -- that continues to just gain momentum, and I'm very encouraged by what we have in front of us. So with that, I'll just say thank you for joining us. And I know it's a little early, but we may not have an opportunity to talk too much directly. Happy holidays to all of you and your families. So take care.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation, and have a wonderful day.
