November 2026 is officially underway, and Paramount+ is kicking off the month with a fresh batch of titles ready to headline your weekend watchlist. As the weather turns and the holiday rush approaches, the streamer has cooked up an eclectic mix of bingeworthy arrivals designed to help you kick back, unplug, and ease into the season.

Whether you crave chaotic laughs or high-stakes drama, there is plenty on tap. Reality fans can dive headfirst into “Big John’s Bosh! Family,” which throws open the doors to the viral Fisher clan led by internet sensation “Big John” and his boxer son Johnny “The Romford Bull.” If you prefer a darker comedic edge, look no further than “It Gets Worse,” a new Showtime comedy from British comedian Leo Reich that follows three broke Londoners scrambling to survive an eviction notice. Meanwhile, drama lovers get the ultimate primetime spectacle with a two-hour “Sheriff Country” and “Fire Country” crossover event, uniting Max Thieriot’s firefighters and Morena Baccarin’s deputies against one massive emergency.

That lineup should keep you plenty busy as November hits its stride. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn — here are three newly added Paramount+ shows you need to add to your watchlist this weekend.

What is it about? Paramount+ is inviting you to check out the chaotic world of one of the internet’s most beloved families. “Big John’s Bosh! Family” follows John “Big John” Fisher, the booming viral sensation behind the catchphrase, and his wife Charlotte, as they live their big, colorful lives. They've got a big family to match, with rising professional boxer son Johnny “The Romford Bull” Fisher, their “city boy” son William, their daughter Hetty, and a pair of grandmas affectionately known as “Fat Nan” and “Skinny Nan.” Each episode is a look at their family's world and how they're living.

Why you should watch it: If you’ve ever followed the Fishers’ feel-good videos online, this is an unfiltered look at the chaos and comedy that turned them into a global sensation. And even if you haven’t heard of the family, this is fun reality TV with a whole lot of heart.

Watch "Big John's Bosh! Family" on Paramount+ from Nov. 5

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What is it about? Created, written by and starring British comedian Leo Reich, “It Gets Worse” is a dark sitcom about being young and broke. Reich plays Ethan, one of three university best friends, alongside Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray), who share a flat together in London. When an eviction notice threatens to change everything for them, these friends scramble to keep their lives, and their bond together, from completely falling apart. But as the show's title suggests, things rarely go their way.

Why you should watch it: Leo Reich is a fresh young voice in British comedy, and this six-episode Showtime series gives him a lot of room to breathe and showcase his acerbic tongue. If you like your comedies a little bleak and a lot clever, this is a quick and enjoyable binge you'll want to add to your watchlist.

Watch "It Gets Worse" on Paramount+ from Nov. 6

What is it about? Two of CBS’s hit dramas collide in this special two-hour crossover event. “Fire Country” follows Bode Donovan (Max Thieriot), a young convict who joins a prison firefighting program to serve out his sentence in his Northern California hometown, while its spinoff “Sheriff Country” centers on no-nonsense sheriff Mickey Fox (Morena Baccarin), who keeps the peace in the same county. This event brings the firefighters and the sheriff’s department together as both work to tackle an emergency bigger than the two of them.

Why you should watch it: This crossover lets the worlds of “Fire Country” and “Sheriff Country” fully overlap. That means a bigger, badder dose of life-or-death action the franchises do so well for the loyal fans. It also makes a great jumping-on point if you’ve been meaning to check out either show.

Watch the "Sheriff Country" and "Fire Country" crossover event on Paramount+ from Nov. 6

#3182. Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The iPhone Duo likely won't make it into Santa's sleigh this year. Here's what Apple had to say about it.

Apple is unsure when it will have more of its foldable iPhone Duo in stock for customers to purchase ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

During Apple’s earnings call on Monday, Nov. 2, Apple’s chief operating officer, Sabih Khan, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo would catch up with current demand.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: Some magical touches

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today … We’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan told investors.

The stock and shipping delays were among the broader concerns on an earnings call riddled with questions about rising memory chip costs driven by the AI industry, according to reports from TechCrunch.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

Last month, the iPhone Duo (Apple’s priciest smartphone to date) sold out shortly after its official launch on Oct. 23. Apple told the Financial Times that demand for the new Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary” after the smashing sell-outs, though veteran techies like Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman posited that Apple knew it would encounter supply chain issues, yet it was still the plan all along.

Those who didn’t initially jump to preorder the new device or wait in line at an Apple store are still facing shipping times that extend into 2027. Some outlets are even reporting that carriers like Verizon have offered gift cards as apologies for the extended delays.

Apple CEO John Ternus signaled the company’s effort to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, announcing that Apple will be “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer supplying pieces for the device.

Also: iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Ternus said during his opening remarks on the earnings call.

While the iPhone Duo snafu is a rare event for Apple, which traditionally has a strong reputation for a smooth supply chain, rising demand for memory chips is raising hardware costs across the industry, and it’s something Apple can’t circumvent. On the call, Khan noted that Apple has had to increase prices on numerous products, though he said those decisions were made rather “reluctantly.”

Back in June, MacBooks and iPads saw price increases of up to 25% due to rising hardware and chip costs.

As Apple works to iron out its kinks, customers may be looking elsewhere. Reports from Korea indicate that Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales jumped 20% in the week after the iPhone Duo became available, and recent reports of cracked displays are another strike for Apple.

So, Santa may not be able to deliver the iPhone Duo this year, but Samsung’s foldables may make it onto Christmas lists across the globe instead.

#3181. Tomato Paste, Mayo and 5 More Foods You Can Use for Cleaning

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A potato to lift rust from cast iron, plus more edibles that do double duty as cleaning agents.

For every spill, splatter or spot, there seems to be a specific product promoted to make you believe nothing else could possibly handle the job. We already know that’s false, right? Pantry heroes such as white vinegar, baking soda and club soda are already staples in our regular rotation when we’re not sure which of the dozens of bottles under the sink to grab.

Many other kitchen staples, however, can also handle certain types of dirty work. None of these are exactly an all-purpose cleaner (as may be obvious with staples such as tomato paste, below), but for specific jobs, in the absence of the perfect product, or to spite the industrial cleaning complex that would have you believe there is a perfect product, the solution or anecdote may already be lurking in your cupboards.

Using that which you already have on hand is a win-win-win. You’ll feel like a mastermind, save money and avoid the tyranny of more and more plastic. “The most sustainable cleaner is usually the one already in your kitchen, says Julian Silva, founder of Plastno nontoxic cleaners, “because you skip buying another single-purpose bottle.”

To use pantry products for cleaning and polishing, “It’s helpful to figure out why a certain product or method works in order to better determine other applications,” says Sofia Martinez, cleaning expert and owner of Sparkly Maid Austin. She also cautions, however, “Disinfecting is not the same as cleaning. Just because a product or method removes soil, provides shine or covers up odor doesn’t mean that the surface has been properly disinfected.”

Silva, Martinez and other cleaning experts below explain why and share seven kitchen staples you probably already have on hand that can clean or polish.

Polishing and disinfecting are far from the same thing, but the kitchen staple you might have sitting right next to your stove can also add shine.

“Olive oil can make fingerprints on stainless-steel appliances much less noticeable, because it creates an ultra-thin coating that changes how light reflects off the surface and disguises smudges,” says Raquel Perez, owner of Karen’s Green Maids in Chicago.

You’re not going to want to use large quantities of oil to clean up the oil and other foodstuffs that spatter during cooking, obviously. “Only use a tiny drop,” Perez advises. “Rub it onto a microfiber cloth, and always test on a small, hidden area first. Too much will make it feel greasy.”

Tomato paste isn’t exactly something like baking soda, where you might confidently apply it to whatever and see if it works. “I would describe tomato paste as a very limited tarnish removal option, not an all-purpose cleaner,” says Martinez. In other words, don’t rub deeply colored, concentrated tomatoes on your cutting boards and countertops.

However, it might do the trick for polishing stainless steel, copper pots and pans, or brass fixtures. “Its acidity can help loosen some oxidation,” she says, “while its thick consistency helps the paste stay in contact with the surface.” As with just about everything here, try a small amount on an out-of-the-way spot first.

Soaking up excess oil with bread is the kind of hack that deserves its own headline. (See here.) You can also use it in place of a broom when something shatters.

“Soft bread is great for broken glass because the crumb grabs the tiny shards a broom misses,” says Silva. “Carefully pick up the big pieces first, then press a slice over the area and toss it right after.” Make sure to press, not rub, as rubbing can cause bigger problems and small scratches. Disposing of it right away, and deep in the trash, is also crucial so nobody (including pets) mistakes it for something they could eat as a snack or croutons.

Your sink may be the basin you use for rinsing and cleaning, but grime and soap residue can build up in certain places and require cleaning. For a quick fix that requires less elbow grease and leaves your stainless steel sink shiny, turn to your baking supplies.

“Sprinkle a little flour over a clean, dry sink and rub it around with a soft, dry cloth or paper towel to remove residual grime and give it a polished look,” says Sham Zemichael, owner and operations manager of Costina Cleaning Services. Conditions must be right in order to begin here, though. “Note that this can backfire if you do it over a damp sink,” he says. “You’ll be left with a flour slurry and more grime than there was before. I use it as a finishing touch on washed and completely dried sinks, and I also recommend keeping the flour away from the drain to avoid it clumping in there.”

Cream of tartar might be one of those baking supplies that sits in the back of your cabinet for years (decades?) because it’s used only for highly specific baking projects. If you’re not regularly stabilizing egg whites in your kitchen or using it as a baking soda sidekick, try using it up before the best-by date by giving it another purpose.

“Most of those gray ‘scratches’ on ceramic plates and sinks are actually metal left behind by forks and knives, since the glaze is harder than the cutlery,” says Silva. “Cream of tartar mixed into a paste with a little water is a gentle, mildly acidic abrasive, so it rubs that metal off without hurting the glaze.” It won’t fix a true scratch, but it will give old ceramics a smart look when they just need a little glow-up.

Seasoning cast iron is a process unto itself, giving its heavyweight, heat-retaining base what is essentially a nonstick surface. Even if you consistently give your cast iron the white-glove treatment in care and cleaning, little rust spots can still appear here and there. You don’t always have to start over with the full seasoning process when this happens, however.

“My favorite way of cleaning light surface rust on cast iron is dipping a half-cut potato in baking soda and rubbing it over the rusty patches,” Zemichael says. “The small amounts of oxalic acid inside potatoes help loosen rust buildup, and the baking soda acts as a mild abrasive for a cleaner finish,” he says. “It doesn’t work for stubborn rust, though. I simply use it for new spots when they appear.”

For kitchen tables or coffee tables that have been begging you to use coasters, you may be able to minimize water rings with what you have on hand for sandwiches. “Mayonnaise can help with water ring stains in some types of wood,” says Perez. “Before trying this solution, find out what type of wood finish your table has and how deep the water-ring stain goes,” she says, whether it’s just in the finish or goes deeper. “That will affect how you should try to remove it and avoid making the situation worse.”

The vegetable oil in full-fat mayonnaise can help displace the moisture that’s locked inside the finish. Apply a thin coating to the ring and let it sit for at least 15 minutes or overnight, covered with plastic wrap. Wipe with a clean, dry cloth after the mayo has absorbed the moisture.

White or hazy rings are worth trying this on, but darker rings might be beyond help. “The mayo can affect the appearance of the stain, as opposed to removing it,” says Perez, and you could be left with a greasy area around the stain if it’s not completely removed.

#3179. Crypto Market Today, Nov. 5: Bitcoin Erases Post-Election Rally as Wall Street Suffers Worst Day in 18 Months

Wednesday's crypto recovery proved short-lived as a widespread tech sell-off spilled into digital assets.

Cryptocurrency markets suffered steep losses on Thursday as a broad sell-off across Wall Street spilled into digital assets, triggering renewed selling pressure. Bitcoin (BTC -6.20%) dropped 5.65% to $75,880.60, while Ethereum (ETH -8.93%) tumbled 7.80% to $2,233.79. Solana (SOL -7.18%) declined 6.22% to $89.55, as investors retreated from riskier assets and erased much of Wednesday's post-election recovery.

Thursday's cryptocurrency sell-off was driven by a sharp deterioration in risk appetite across global financial markets. U.S. technology stocks led Wall Street lower as investors grew increasingly concerned about elevated valuations and the sustainability of massive artificial intelligence infrastructure investments. The Nasdaq (^IXIC -5.52%) saw a 5.5% decline which intensified selling across speculative assets, with cryptocurrencies particularly vulnerable to the sudden shift in sentiment.

Meanwhile, leveraged trading amplified the downturn. As Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies declined, liquidations created additional selling pressure, accelerating losses across the market. The reversal was especially striking given Wednesday's brief recovery, illustrating how quickly market momentum can shift when financial conditions tighten and investors reduce exposure to higher-risk assets.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have also faced considerable selling pressure, recording more than $1.1 billion in net outflows over three consecutive trading sessions before posting a modest inflow on Wednesday. Thursday's broader market sell-off raises concerns that institutional withdrawals could resume.

Of the key funds, iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (NASDAQ: IBIT) fell 5.07%, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (NYSEMKT: FBTC) fell 4.93%, and iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (NASDAQ: ETHA) fell 7.25% as crypto ETF pricing tracked the broad decline in the underlying coins.

Zooming in, Bitcoin's ability to defend the $75,000 to $76,000 region is becoming increasingly important. Bulls will want to see this level held or Bitcoin risks a deeper correction. The broader altcoin market faces a similar test. Ethereum, XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana have surrendered much of their earlier gains, leaving investors watching whether key support levels can hold.

The outlook for cryptocurrencies will depend heavily on developments in traditional markets. If selling pressure across technology and AI stocks persists, digital assets may struggle to establish a meaningful recovery. One key signal to watch is whether Bitcoin and the broader crypto market can hold support even as the Nasdaq and semiconductor stocks continue to weaken.

Until that divergence develops, or the sell off in tech and AI tapers off, investors should remain cautious about interpreting short-lived rebounds as evidence of a sustained recovery.

#3176. A New Water Heater Technology Kills Bacteria Right in the Tank

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I asked the inventor about his design and when consumers might see the tech in their homes.

One challenge of current water heater designs is staying hot enough to kill harmful bacteria like Legionella pneumophila, which can cause Legionnaires’ disease. A new water heater design, developed and patented by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, aims to raise tank temperatures to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, which spells instant doom for Legionella bacteria.

Legionella bacteria love warm water, so while they struggle to survive in a water heater tank set to 120 F, they’re more than comfortable elsewhere in a home’s hot water pipes. It’s technically possible to achieve sufficient temperatures with existing water heaters, but those temperatures are also likely to scald human skin whenever you turn on the faucet.

The biggest innovation of this new design is how it finds a new use for heat exchangers, the same technology behind air conditioners, heat pumps, furnaces and refrigerators. I wanted to know more, so I reached out to David Yashar, a NIST mechanical engineer behind the new design.

As Yashar and his team researched ways to kill Legionella bacteria, they needed to figure out how to make tank temperatures around 160 F safe and practical for humans. They ultimately landed on the concept of using cold water entering the water heater to cool the hot water leaving the tank with an unmixed heat exchanger that contains the water inlet and outlet.

The principle behind unmixed heat exchangers—where the fluids don’t mix—is that incoming cold water gets a heating boost from the hot-water outlet while cooling the water to safe levels for people. As a result, the tank can maintain the high temperatures required to prevent pathogen growth behind illnesses like Legionnaires’ disease, which has a fatality rate of around 10%, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Beyond the safety benefits, the process recaptures some waste heat and can improve heating efficiency for the cold water, since it enters the tank warmer.

I’ve covered various heating, ventilation and air conditioning tech over the years, so I immediately recognized similarities between the new design’s unmixed heat exchanger and those used in HVAC and refrigerators. For example, air conditioners use a heat exchanger for the refrigeration cycle (also called the Carnot cycle) to pull heat from air inside your home (evaporator coil) and push it outside (condenser coil) without pulling in outside air. Additionally, heat pumps may use a heat exchanger for defrosting ice buildup when in heating mode.

When I asked about the similarities, Yashar noted that it wasn’t a coincidence that his patent took inspiration from HVAC and refrigeration tech. Yashar said, “My background is in HVAC&R, and it is very common to use unmixed heat exchangers like this to manipulate the bounds of the Carnot cycle to achieve some specific condition. I came up with the idea when I first learned about Legionella and the existing mitigation strategies.” He goes on to explain that using an unmixed heat exchanger “across the inlet and outlet was a very simple, effective, and inexpensive way to push the water temperature up to that condition and back down.”

It’s fitting that Yashar discovered better ways for heat exchangers not only to kill pathogens, but also to improve energy efficiency. Finding new applications for existing technology is certainly an underrated aspect of invention.

As exciting as this tech is, a patent doesn’t necessarily mean it will hit the market immediately. Yashar notes that while his research “proved the concept using a 60-gallon tank,” it depends on when manufacturers license the technology and get their engineers working on designing consumer products suitable for homes. This process could happen quickly or take several years.

It may be years before we see consumer heaters that use the promising new technology.

Because Yashar’s concept essentially modified an existing water heater, I asked if it would be possible to retrofit products in people’s homes. He notes that NIST’s project started with the intention of modifying the tank’s hardware and controls. “The steps we took might not be simple tasks for an existing application,” said Yashar. “It really depends on a lot of things, so it is best if people learn how this works and understand how to achieve it within their existing application.”

He brings up one important consideration: Retrofit tanks will need extra insulation to be worth it. It’s “absolutely necessary for a retrofit because the tank temperature will be about 40 degrees hotter than what the existing system was designed for. If this isn’t done, the standby losses would be very large.” Without appropriate insulation, any efficiency gained by the heat exchanger would be lost to heat loss in standby mode.

So, while a retrofit might be possible, it seems more likely to engineer a product from the ground up based on this design, especially if consumers want to keep utility costs manageable.

For more tips, see the best temperature to set your thermostat this winter and learn how to find air leaks in your home for more efficient heating.

#3174. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3173. Safari finally gets 3 popular browser features – and I can’t wait to try them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New developer beta release notes point to deeper Siri AI integration and more Safari customization.

Developer betas for MacOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and iOS 27.3 are here, with a few major upgrades to the Safari browser. Vertical tabs, adaptive dark mode, and deeper Siri AI integration are on the way to the public, but are first in beta for testing.

Also: Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Siri AI is expected to be further woven into Music, Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Safari. Adaptive dark mode will allow for any website to be viewed in dark mode, even if the site doesn’t support it. Finally, vertical tabs are pretty straightforward, enabling vertical navigation and drag-and-drop tab reorganization.

Here’s what you can expect when the software goes public in mid-December.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Siri AI gains more access to your Apple devices, allowing more cross-app functionality and the ability to execute complex, multi-step tasks within your apps.

According to 9to5Mac, you can ask Siri AI to create a playlist in Music and save it to your library, request messages to be scheduled for a later send, organize and label photos, and create a detailed calendar invite — all with your voice.

The same reporting also states that Siri AI features will appear in Maps, Weather, Shortcuts, and Notes, signaling that an AI-supercharged Siri will live in every crevice of your Apple devices.

Also: iOS 27 will organize your open Safari tabs now

I’m not one to complete tasks like the ones mentioned above on my iPhone — I’m far more likely to do them on my MacBook Air, since I associate the laptop with productivity. Every blue moon I’ll rearrange my entire Apple Music catalog, every month I fill out my calendar, and sometimes I’ll go through Photos and try to organize it. I can see myself automating certain steps in these tasks, and I’m excited to try it.

A WebKit blog post details that adaptive dark mode is coming to Safari, how it will work, and what users can expect. According to the post, 40% of web page loads are from dark mode users, but only 10% of web pages natively support it.

I’m particularly excited about this feature, as I set my Apple devices to automatically enable dark mode at 7 p.m. to encourage a more relaxing evening scrolling vibe, especially while reading. I read a lot on my MacBook, and in a dark room, a bright page can feel too bright, but dimming my laptop’s display doesn’t quite do the trick.

Also: Your AirPods got better in iOS 27 – three new ways I’m using them

The WebKit blog post states that adaptive dark mode uses “a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue” and distinguishes between when a page’s color is purely decorative and when it carries substantial meaning, to ensure the user experience remains consistent between light and dark modes.

Vertical browser tabs aren’t a new concept, but they’ll soon be new to Safari. I see the value in vertical tabs: a list view is easier to scan, web page titles aren’t smushed when several tabs are open, and they’re particularly useful when you’re working on a widescreen monitor.

Many people who spend hours using their Mac or MacBook may find this upcoming feature useful. I do believe that Safari is the superior browser for personal use, given its integration with your Apple devices, especially with features like Handoff.

Also: 7 AI-free iOS 27 features that make old iPhones exciting again

However, I do have one major gripe with vertical tabs: they’re usually locked to the left panel, and I prefer the right. If Safari allows this customization, I’ll seriously consider switching from horizontal tabs.

Military and space applications declined in the quarter by $9 million with lower production on radars and other miscellaneous platforms. Our industrials business also grew $0.8 million during Q3 to timing of production orders. Electronic Systems operating income for the third quarter was $28.7 million or 22.2% of revenue. versus $23.3 million or 18.6% of revenue in the prior year period.

Excluding restructuring charges and other adjustments in both years, segment operating margin was 22.5% in Q3 26, versus 18.9% in Q3 25. The year over year increase was driven by higher manufacturing volume and our value based pricing approach. Turning now to liquidity and capital resources. In Q3 2026, we generated $32.7 million in cash flow from operating activities compared to $18.1 million in Q3 of last year. Our strong cash generation was driven by higher net income partially offset by higher working capital during the quarter.

Year to date cash flow from operating activities is $77.5 million and year to date free cash flow was $65.2 million, representing year to date free cash flow conversion of 103% to 134% of adjusted net income. In Q4 of last year, the company amended its credit agreement, which now includes a $200 million term loan and a $450 million revolver. The new $650 million facility lowered our cost of capital gives us incremental capacity to execute on our acquisition strategy. As of the end of the third quarter, we have available liquidity of $434 million, comprising of the unutilized portion of our revolver and cash on hand.

Interest expense in Q3 was $3.1 million compared to $2.9 million in Q3 of 25. The year over year increase in interest cost was primarily due to higher debt balances, offset by lower interest rates on our debt due to more favorable terms in our new credit agreements. Also, as a reminder, in November 2021, we put in place an interest rate hedge that went into effect for a 3-year to 7-year period starting January 2024 and picks the 1 month term SOFR at a 170 basis points $150 million of our debt. The hedge is still in place and will continue to drive significant interest cost savings for the rest of 2026 and beyond.

To conclude the financial review, I would like to say that the third quarter results continue to affirm our Vision 2027 strategy is working and we are not only on track to achieve those targets, but well positioned to deliver on our new vision 2032 strategy as well. I will now turn it back to Steve for his closing remarks. Steve?

Stephen G. Oswald: Okay. Thanks, Suman. Just in closing, a few things. First, Q3 was another record quarter for DCO. And frankly, I could not be happier This year, we achieved record revenues, record EBITDA margins, record bookings, and strong cash generation. The strong book to bill will also be a tailwind for us going into 2027. It was also our sixth consecutive quarter of revenue of $200 million and gross margins and adjusted EBITDA margins of 28.9% and 17.5%, respectively and ahead of schedule to meet our vision 2027 goals. In addition, the company's engineered product revenue revenues were at 24% in Q3 as we drive higher OEM and aftermarket product through the P&L.

As everyone knows, driving this percentage as high as possible is our number 1 strategic focus with 100% commitment. Finally, let me again go back to the beginning of my remarks. And thank you all again for your strong support for the vision 2032. It means a lot to us at Ducommun. We all look forward to a great future for our company and shareholders, with the finishing of Vision 2027 and the launching of Vision 2032 in January 2028. #3171. I Took the iPhone 18 Pro Max to Japan and Its New Camera System Brought Out My Creative Side

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The iPhone 18 Pro got fun new camera features and they made my bucketlist travel destination more memorable.

Apple gave its pro iPhones a crucial camera and battery boost this year. As a frequent traveler, these upgrades had me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so I took it with me to Japan. Going vintage watch hunting through the streets of Tokyo to 6 a.m. hikes in Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari and the Shinto shrines, I used the new phone as my main camera. It made me rethink my shots, pushed me to experiment more with my perspective and surprised me in the most unexpected ways.

The variable aperture, manual camera controls and new Photographic Styles make the iPhone 18 Pro the most fun camera system from Apple, even if they are just minor upgrades from the 16 Pro and 17 Pro. The starburst effect in f4, grain in Photographic Styles and adjustable shutter speeds add drama, depth and more personality to even the most mundane shots.

From my time landing in Osaka to landing back in Delhi, the iPhone 18 Pro Max had me experimenting for two weeks. Here’s what I shot and how the new upgrades made an impact on my first trip to Japan.

The iPhone 18 Pro has manual controls baked into the Camera app. I can adjust the focus, choose the lens aperture from four stops, pick a shutter speed and select the white balance without needing to install a third-party app. The variable aperture is the main attraction here, letting me experiment with lighting as I visited various shrines.

You can go from f/1.48 to f/4 on iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera to adjust the amount of light hitting the sensor. Apple has programmed the f/4 (its narrowest) setting to give you a starburst effect with bright light sources, which showed up as light blobs on older iPhones. I used f/4 to get starbursts from the reflections of sunlight hitting a shrine:

Not every photo needs this effect, but starbursts add a unique style that you won’t find on any other phone. I was busy framing my shots to get the most reflections and the cameras didn’t disappoint.

Combine this with adjustable shutter speeds (takes a bit getting used to) and it leads to endless new possibilities. On the night I landed in Osaka, I went out for a stroll near my hotel, and took about 250 shots at a red light. I only got a few decent light trails, but it forced me to get more creative with my photography

After a few days I finally got the shot of a moving car stabilized with a blurred background. The trick? Finding the right shutter speed (1/15 in this case) through trial and error and moving my iPhone at the same speed as the car. At night, I stuck to 1/2s for moving vehicles with handheld stabilization. I’m happy with the results.

From light trails at night to a speeding car in daylight, the iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras create an effect that was previously only possible through third-party apps. This is different from simply taking a live photo and tapping Long Exposure in edits. You can track a subject to focus and the rest of the movement creates visual effects like the ones in my photos.

Apple’s manual controls are all about getting creative with your frames. You can then personalize these with the new film look and grain in Photographic Styles. These are like simulations that you’d find on the Fujifilm X100 series or Ricoh GR cameras.

For example, I edited this cyclist shot in the Photos app. I used the Dramatic + Film Style because I liked the blue tint in the sky and background, while keeping the skin tone intact. It gave my shot a moody look without editing the colors on my subject, like a regular filter would.

For these two nature shots, I brought all three aspects: adjustable shutter speed, f4 aperture and new Photographic Styles into a single frame. I love the grain, film and glow effects on the iPhone 18 Pro this year. They make the iPhone cameras exciting again.

However, there are a few things I’d like to change about this software.

The grain and film look are nice additions but I’d have loved to adjust the intensity of grain, much like my Vivo X300 Ultra. The current look is good for photos shot in bright light, but anything dim starts looking too artificial. The grain is too aggressive for most situations.

As much as I appreciate the new manual controls, I’m not fond of their placement in the Camera app. I missed a slow shutter shot of the Shinkansen because I was busy finding the manual control. These bullet trains are just too fast!

The new manual controls can be added to the top of the viewfinder or accessed through the six-dot settings menu at the bottom-right corner. In both positions, they aren’t made for one-handed use. It’d also be nice if I could adjust the position of certain toggles in the six-dot menu on the viewfinder. I need the aperture and shutter speed on the rightmost side, but I can’t edit it. The two icons aren’t instantly recognizable up on top. I believe that if I could change their positions in the bottom menu, I’d recognize them faster and remember their positions for a more reliable shooting experience.

Then comes the Camera Control. It doesn’t support any of the new manual controls. So, you can’t adjust the shutter speed or choose an aperture. If I have an extra button dedicated to the camera, I’d ideally like to use it for manual controls. It’d allow faster access to the new features.

In my opinion, Apple should also let us assign two separate Photographic Styles on the front and back cameras. On my trip, I had set a Fuji-like look for street photography, which seemed great for my surroundings but not for my selfies. You can always edit these photos in post, but if I’m out with new friends and sharing these photos with them, it’d be easier if I could set two different Photographic Styles for the front and back cameras.

During my trip, I didn’t have to top up my iPhone 18 Pro Max more than once a day. I left it on charge overnight as my mornings were reserved for breakfast and figuring out the train connectivity through Google Maps. (Seriously, I don’t know how I’d travel without this app.)

Japan is a unique mix of next-gen technology and decades-old systems. While it has a Suica card for public transport, I couldn’t add it to my Apple Wallet. Most stations don’t accept Visa contactless payments. I had to run to the nearest 7/11 to get cash and purchase train tickets. Some markets are also cash-only, so my iPhone was constantly running Maps, Music and Camera for a healthy 6 hours a day.

It lasted me through long photography sessions and constant navigation without any issues. In my experience, this is a huge upgrade over my iPhone 17 Pro Max, which required two charging instances if I was pushing it with Camera and Maps usage. The new model also doesn’t get as warm as its predecessor. I noticed the heat dissipates quicker when using the iPhone 18 Pro Max without a case. I’ve tried three cases so far and each one traps heat, making it warm to touch. If you can, going caseless is a good idea on the new pro iPhones.

The added battery life is a fantastic addition to this year’s model, and will be appreciated by anyone who travels regularly. This is in line with CNET’s tests, where the iPhone 18 Pro Max emerged as the longest-lasting battery life of any iPhone Apple has ever made. I just wish it was lighter. At 248 grams, it is one of the heaviest phones on the market and if you put a case on it, the iPhone 18 Pro Max becomes bulky and hard to use with one hand. I hope Apple finds a way to give us an even better battery life in a lighter form next year.

On the front, you also get a smaller Dynamic Island, which can expand to show up to three live activities (up from two) simultaneously. However, some apps aren’t yet fine-tuned to accommodate the change. On one occasion, when I ordered food through Uber, while running Spotify and Maps navigation, the Live Activity cut the “2” in 27-minute ETA for the order. So I had the next direction, music and an incorrect ETA as glanceable info on top of my screen.

Japan was one of my bucket-list locations and I’m glad I took the iPhone 18 Pro Max with me. This is the most fun I’ve had with an Apple camera system in a long time. From the shrines in Kyoto to the riverside walk along the Sumida River in Tokyo, these cameras invited me to get more experimental. The film-like Photographic Styles, new manual controls and variable aperture helped me get more creative with my perspectives.

It took me more than 250 shots at a crossing in Osaka before I figured out which shutter speed was ideal for what occasion. Similarly, I experimented with my frames to find the best angles for the starburst effect in f/4. Then came the film simulations in Photographic Styles to stylize my shots within the Photos app. All of these new iPhone camera features give me a more analog feel, and I’m here for it.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max, thankfully, has the battery life to support my curiosity and slow learning pace. Through my trips last year, I had to carry a power bank with me, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max changed that. I’m more confident it will last through the day. While none of those camera features would appeal to casual users, the battery life enhancements and improved heat dissipation are tangible upgrades that would benefit everyone.

I’ve tested my fair share of smart and color-changing light bulbs over the years, but I wasn’t quite sure about one that doubles as a Bluetooth speaker. After trying out the GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb for a month, I was surprised by how well this combination works.

Currently, you can get the GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb for $22 at Amazon. This LED bulb normally retails for $32, but Amazon is offering an instant $10 discount that drops the price to $22. Given the long-term energy savings of LED bulbs compared to conventional incandescent and fluorescent options, it might be worth grabbing a couple. Here’s why.

The GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb Color Changing Bluetooth Speaker lets you play music directly from your phone to it, making it the perfect bedside companion when you're trying to wind down. In addition, it comes with a remote that easily lets you change its colors, intensity, and even set up a multi-unit system for stereo sound.

What really sold me on this setup is that it’s not trying to compete with all the other speakers I have around, including the two Apple HomePods in my bedroom that I use with my TV. While the sound isn’t mind-blowing, it’s more than enough to help me wind down before bedtime. Since the bulb sits in a lamp right next to my bed, it’s perfect for playing ambient noise or an audiobook to help me fall asleep. That same balance also makes it a solid upgrade for a home office, delivering background music while working.

It’s also worth highlighting that despite its color-changing abilities, this isn’t technically a "smart" bulb that relies on Wi-Fi — and you don’t need to download another app. Instead, it pairs with a simple remote that lets me cycle through colors, tweak brightness, and adjust audio playback with the click of a physical button. This plug-and-play simplicity makes it super easy to use and ideal for older adults or elderly family members who don’t want the hassle of complicated tech.

The reason I suggest getting a pair isn’t just the extra savings — it’s that you can link multiple bulbs together completely wire-free. I’ve set it up so the two light bulbs sit on opposite sides of my bed, assigning one as the left channel and the other as the right. Effectively, I get a true stereo pair that makes listening far more immersive. There’s also a Party Mode that syncs the bulbs to change colors and pulse to the beat of the music.

Between its simple remote controls, clutter-free audio, and wire-free stereo pairing, this two-in-one bulb convinced me it’s no gimmick — especially while you can grab it for just $22 for a limited time.

#3169. Want an AI job? Deployment engineers are earning executive-level pay – up to $1.45M a year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AI has ushered in new jobs, and some of them are paying handsomely, according to a new study.

AI engineers are making well over six figures in salary — and plenty more in bonuses and equity, according to data from a new report by executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Enterprises now pay “elite” AI deployment engineers between $586,000 and $1.45 million annually in total compensation, with senior leaders in the field earning up to $2.25 million, according to the report. This figure approaches the median compensation of executive officers of public companies, the authors note.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

Christian & Timbers is an AI executive search and leadership advisory firm, recruiting CEOs, board members, technology executives, and AI engineers for enterprises. The new report draws on more than 550 interviews with engineers, deployment leaders, and executives conducted from January through June 2026, along with closed and current open offers. The compensation bands are Christian & Timbers’ estimates and represent ranges rather than statistical averages.

“Enterprise CEOs are under pressure to deliver returns for their AI investments. The most important decision is how to build the team that delivers on that goal,” said Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of Christian & Timbers, in a press release.

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

The report noted that the staggering salary range includes base salary, bonus, and annualized equity. Christian & Timbers said it defines an “elite” forward deployment engineer (FDE) as “a senior AI-native deployment builder, typically with 7 to 15 years of experience, including at least two years building and deploying agentic automated workflows that deliver measurable ROI with a documented enterprise impact of $10M or more,” who has also led a team of other forward deployment engineers.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

The large salary ranges reflect increasing enterprise investments in AI talent and employee development. Microsoft, AWS, and OpenAI have announced more than $7.5 billion in corporate and partner investment in AI deployment over the past six months, Christian & Timbers noted in the release.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

There’s an increasing need to fill roles such as Senior Principal AI Engineer, AI Solutions Engineer, and Head of Deployment — but there is a limited pool of qualified candidates. The firm estimates that only 2,000 of the most senior deployment leaders exist in the US market, according to a previous Christian & Timbers study, which does not meet demand — so companies are competing for the same small group of professionals, hence the increasing salaries.

While the report underscores lucrative yields for certain engineering roles, the firm said that public job titles make comparisons more challenging.

“Christian & Timbers’ elite category spans several titles, while advertised FDE roles cover a broader range of experience and responsibilities. Experienced deployment engineers may be recruited directly or promoted into the work under titles such as staff software engineer or principal AI engineer,” the study said.

Plus, equity and bonus make up 52% to 66% of senior engineer pay, and most job postings don’t include that value in the salary, the report noted.

Motorola's new Signature 27 has one of the fastest wired charging speeds we've seen for a US phone.

After teasing it during Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September, Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 phone will be unveiled on Thursday, and it clearly wants to make a big impression for that high starting price.

Even with the ongoing RAM shortage leading to higher prices for most phones, it would be understandable to think a $1,600 candybar-style phone sounds extravagant. It is. But it’s actually priced competitively against the 512GB model of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (also now $1,600 following its own fall price increase).

The Signature 27’s biggest feature could be its 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera, which is capable of a 3x optical zoom and what Motorola calls a 100x Super Zoom Pro. That camera is joined by a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel front camera. An Event-Based Vision action sensor will also be included to assist with photographing fast-moving subjects.

But particularly eye-opening to me — as someone who’s constantly tracking how quickly phones can recharge — is that the Signature 27 will have 90-watt wired charging. For context, the Galaxy S26 Ultra and the iPhone 18 Pro Max charge at 60-watt speeds, with both phones being among the fastest we’ve tested. The Signature includes a 7,000-mAh silicon carbon battery, which is a newer battery technology that’s able to pack more capacity into less space.

The phone will have a 6.8-inch 1.5K-resolution display that runs at a 120Hz refresh rate, but has an absurdly high 12,000-nit peak brightness. By comparison, many phones we’ve tested lately have included 2,000- and 3,000-nit brightness levels that make it easy to see the screen in sunny environments.

Powering it will be Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, which Qualcomm says will be particularly helpful for gaming at high-graphics settings, recording video at 8K resolution as well as 4K at 60 frames per second and for on-device AI tasks. The phone’s audio system is created with a partnership with Bang and Olufsen, which we’ll have to hear but should help tune the phone well for music and movies.

The Signature also gets several Android 17 features that debuted on Google’s Pixel 11 series, including Rambler for voice transcription that uses AI to remove “umm”s from the text as well as understanding commands. There will also be a Create My Widget feature for having Gemini create personalized homescreen widgets, and the ability to use American Sign Language for texting. Motorola’s own Qira AI assistant will also be available on the Signature 27, which Motorola says will work across Lenovo devices.

Like the Razr Fold, the Signature 27 will get seven years of software and security updates — which brings Motorola firmly in line with what Google and Samsung provide to their flagship Pixel and Galaxy phones. The Signature will come in two Pantone colors: the dark coal smoke and the green capulet olive. I am interested in feeling both phones because the coal smoke model is described as having a “tactical weave finish” akin to materials used for cars while the olive is said to have a textile-inspired finish that may be closer to the vegan leather backings we’ve seen on the Razr line.

The Signature 27 may be expensive, but I do see where there may be an audience. With the recent retreat of OnePlus from the US phone market, fans of that brand may be looking for a new gamer-friendly phone alternative with both a high-end processor and fast phone charging. The Signature 27 is also arriving after years of growth for Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones, which itself has included a number of luxury-minded variants such as Razr phones that include Swarovski crystals.

The Signature 27 will release first in the US, going on preorder on Nov. 19 before going on open sale Nov. 26. Both the coal smoke and capulet olive models will come with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory.

#3165. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

#3164. It’s Possible You’ve Been Making Coffee All Wrong: 6 Mistakes a Pro Says to Avoid

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Avoid these brewing blunders for coffee that tastes like the stuff baristas make.

I make coffee every morning, almost without fail. I haven’t always used the same method, and because I bounce between processes to test and experiment with coffee makers, beans and, yes, even K-Cups, I’m open to the idea that I might not always get it right.

According to Sarina Prabasi, the founder of Buunni micro-roastery in New York City, I’m in good company.

Prabasi serves on the board of the Specialty Coffee Association and assures me I’m probably making one or two common coffee-brewing mistakes, like everyone else. Coffee is nuanced; it’s easy to fall into habits—often passed down from family, and often bad.

Whether you brew your morning coffee with a pour-over, French press or espresso machine, here are six coffee mistakes to avoid.

Even the slightest film of soap residue can taint your next cup.

Ditching the soap for your coffee pot and pour-over immersion brewer might seem like dubious advice. In reality, your coffee equipment doesn’t need a scrub down every time you use it. Even small amounts of residue from fragrant dish soap detergent will leave you with a sudsy, subpar pot of coffee.

“It really stays in there; it can mess with the flavor, and so, usually, a good rinse with super hot water is enough for black coffee,” Prabasi said. Oils from the beans may build up over time, so fragrance-free dish soap comes in handy for occasional deep cleaning. A simple rinse with hot water will more than suffice for daily use, however. Save yourself time and avoid any unwanted “soap scum” notes that might interrupt the notes of your single-origin Sidama natural roast.

Coffee beans are one pantry staple you shouldn’t buy in bulk.

Buying in bulk can save time and money at the grocery store, but it can disappoint coffee drinkers. Buying smaller quantities of beans helps you avoid stale, flat coffee, especially for average drinkers and households with one or two people. Probasi told us that you’ll know coffee has gone stale because it “can taste like a shadow of itself.”

The roaster recommends checking the coffee label for a roast date within one month, ideally within two weeks. (Keep in mind, the “best buy” date is different and isn’t an indicator of freshness.) If you don’t like grinding at home, the roast date should be on the fresher side.

But you needn’t panic about the declining flavor in your cupboard like a ticking time bomb. “Every day post-roast doesn’t mean it’s losing freshness, but after two weeks, I’d say it starts to go down,” Prabasi said. Store coffee in an airtight container but avoid the humid fridge with its plethora of smells that can stick to the beans.

You can find tutorials online recommending brewers, scales, tampers, water filters, grinders and miscellaneous techniques to make the perfect cup. Experimentation is key to crafting your favorite brew but only if you start with the basics. “So just adjust only the water in the beginning,” Prabasi said.

If you don’t have a kitchen scale, the roaster told us the rule of thumb is to start with two tablespoons of ground coffee per cup of water. The finer the grind, the stronger your coffee will taste, so adjust the grounds-to-water ratio accordingly. If that seems too weak or too strong, then adjust by adding more or less coffee at the same grind level.

Beyond the basics, you can get creative. “If your coffee is too sour, it’s maybe that you prefer a dark roast,” Prabasi said. Coffee too bitter? You can adjust the roast type by buying a level down, such as dark to medium or medium to light. “ If you got a coffee from East Africa, maybe try one from South America, you know, like switch [it] around,” she said. Changing one element at a time ensures you know which step affected the result, for better or worse.

Filling your coffee pot with tap water will yield less-than-ideal flavors. For most of us, filtered water will make a big difference in your coffee’s final flavor. Tap water often contains by-products that a home water filtration system can easily remove.

Almost all tap water in the US is disinfected with low levels of chlorine. This chemical helps keep drinking water safe as it leaves treatment centers but can alter the taste and smell of tap water. Chloramines can also strip lead and copper from pipes, by-products that can affect even the most carefully prepared coffee.

Smell can be a dead giveaway that your coffee has gone stale. Prabasi explains that you should immediately open a bag of beans or ground coffee and smell the roasted coffee scent. Aroma is a key indicator of flavor. No aroma means a serious lack of taste.

Prabasi said stale coffee can taste muddy or flat and lack any complex tasting notes that a bag might list on its label. “ That’s why I think for in the coffee profession, so much of what we do is tasting coffee,” she said. “From the farm to the coffee shop, every step of the way coffee gets tasted or cupped, in our vernacular.”

Old coffee isn’t likely to make you sick, so there’s no need to toss it. You might, however, want to shift from taking your coffee black. Making iced coffee is a simple way to mask the lack of tasting notes. An immersion brewer also lets you steep the grounds longer to add a bit more flavor after the coffee has dulled.

Don’t skimp on organic coffee even if it costs a few bucks more.

The multitude of coffee brands at the grocery store can feel overwhelming. To help sift through the masses, Prabasi explains the organic coffee label is a sign of quality that’s important for coffee.

“If you can, then I think for coffee and tea, organic is really important because coffee and tea crops, especially from large farms, tend to get really over-sprayed,” Prabasi said. Pesticides are sprayed right onto the coffee cherries, and coffee is unlike an apple that you can wash or a banana that you peel before eating. Tea leaves go through a similar process, and anything left on the leaves then steeps into your mug.

The coffeehouse owner made it clear that she doesn’t believe coffee needs to be expensive to be considered “good.” Great coffee comes in a variety of price points. ” I think the care that goes into sourcing it, to roasting it, or just serving it, I would be looking for those things,” Prabasi said. The organic label is a helpful place to start.

For more coffee intel, here’s how to read coffee labels and the best travel mugs of 2026, tested by CNET.

#3162. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3161. Is Chrome’s settings menu getting a search bar? What we know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chrome might receive a much-needed addition.

I’m a longtime Chrome user, but I’ve never been a fan of the browser’s user settings menu, which has grown into a dense collection of nesting submenus that can be difficult to navigate. That may be changing soon.

Also: How Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

X (formerly Twitter) user, Leopeva64, posted a short video and several still images showcasing a potential new feature in Chrome Canary, which Google uses to test new Chrome web tools and features. The posts show the search bar pinned to the top of the settings menu for instant access. By entering the name of the submenu or feature you want to access, the new search bar could save a lot of time normally spent clicking around, trying to remember exactly where it’s located.

In Chrome Canary, Google is testing removing the scroll arrows that let you automatically scroll to reveal hidden items when you hover over them in the 3-dot menu. They also added a scrollbar, and the search box at the top and the footer are now pinned so they are always visible: https://t.co/Plx6BgKfJN pic.twitter.com/D7TxDkCtmP

According to Leopeva64, other possible new features include a visual update that groups similar menu options into tiles for faster navigation of your most-accessed settings, as well as pinning the menu footer to keep it visible as you click through.

Chrome Extensions is also up for a possible refresh with a move to a dedicated submenu called Manage Skills to help keep all of your installed extensions organized and make it easier to remove ones that are no longer needed.

Also: How to take full-page screenshots in Chrome on any device – it’s easy and free

Google Lens may get a new submenu, called “Ask Google about this page,” for searching for items you see across an entire page, not just in a single image.

There’s no official word yet on when these features will leave Canary’s testing environment and become available in the regular Chrome menu. I’ve reached out to Google for a comment, but at the time of writing, I have not received a response.
