#3160. Dorian LPG (LPG) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Peak freight rates and Panama Canal bottlenecks drove record results this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dorian LPG Ltd. (LPG -6.78%) reported record quarterly financial results, characterized by peak freight rates and significant gains from opportunistic vessel sales. Management reported that the freight market hit new highs due to geopolitical conflict and logistical bottlenecks at the Panama Canal, which effectively shortened the global shipping supply. The company strengthened its balance sheet through a $368.4 million refinancing and the sale of four vessels since July 2026, generating substantial cash for fleet renewal and shareholder distributions. While Middle East exports have declined, management stated that U.S. production growth continues to absorb new tonnage, maintaining a constructive outlook for the VLGC sector.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Dorian LPG Second Quarter 2027 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A brief question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. Additionally, a live audio webcast of today's conference call is available on Dorian LPG's website, which is www.dorianlpg.com. I would now like to turn the conference over to Ted Young, Chief Financial Officer. Thank you, Mr. Young. Please go ahead.

Ted Young: Thank you, Chelsea. Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for joining us for our Second Quarter 2027 Results Conference Call. With me this morning today are John Hadjipateras, Chairman, President, and CEO of Dorian LPG Limited, John Lycouris, Head of Energy Transition, and Taro Rasmussen, Vice President of Chartering. As a reminder, this conference call webcast and a replay of this call will be available through November 12, 2026. Many of our remarks today contain forward-looking statements based on current expectations. These statements may often be identified with words such as expect, anticipate, believe, or similar indications of future expectations.

Although we believe that such forward-looking statements are reasonable, we cannot assure you that any forward-looking statements will prove to be correct. These forward-looking statements are subject to known and unknown risks and uncertainties and other factors, as well as general economic conditions. Should one or more of these risks or uncertainties materialize, or should underlying assumptions or estimates prove to be incorrect, actual results may vary materially from those we express today. Additionally, let me refer you to our unaudited results for the quarterly period ended September 30, 2026, that were filed this morning on Form 10-Q.

In addition, please refer to our previous filings on Form 10-Q, where you'll find risk factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those forward-looking statements. Finally, I would encourage you to review the investor highlight slides posted this morning on our website. With that, I'll turn over the call to John Hadjipateras.

John Hadjipateras: Thank you, Ted. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on a busy morning. We're proud to be following in the footsteps of Maersk, Genco, International Seaways, and last but not least. So before my colleagues provide you with detailed comments on our financial results and an interesting market overview, as well as progress of our operation, I'd like to provide some strategic perspective. The freight market, which hit new highs, as well as gains on sales, are reflected in the record earnings that we are reporting today. After the $1.25 per share dividend, irregular dividend declared by our board last week, the total return to our shareholders since our 2014 IPO will amount to over $1.1 billion.

We're confident in the sector's dynamics for the foreseeable future. With the refinancings completed in September, we feel that we have a balanced capital structure with capacity to support growth and withstand headwinds that may arise. Our fleet investment and reinvestment strategy has always been measured and deliberate. The ships we have on order will have improved technical and operational features, which will add to their earning potential. In market cycles where bigger investments are warranted, as was the case with our expansion in 2013, we will aim to be ready to take them on.

While in the last quarter, the strong rates stole the show, we found the fact that U.S. export facilities did not operate at maximum capacity to be the most interesting development, because it showed that the sector is currently short shipping. In the 12 years since our IPO, not only has U.S. production and exports been growing, but their growth has also surprised on the upside, absorbing with new building books, which at time had seemed excessive. We believe in LPG fundamentals, and we hope that together with potential growth in ammonia carried down the line, demand will continue to expand, as has been the case to date.

Having said that, we also believe that the order book is adequate and the restraint will be rewarded. Going back to the present, the Iran conflict and its recent developments effectively put a stranglehold on exports out of the Straits of Hormuz and out of the Red Sea, and highlighted the critical role that the U.S. plays in global LPG supply. The Panama Canal is once again heavily congested, pushing more VLGCs to ballast around the Cape of Good Hope. With the dry season approaching, we do not anticipate near-term relief.

While it's impossible to predict the outcome and implications of the Middle East conflict on our trade, we believe that peace is not a threat, as some have predicted, but rather it will restore and expand trade, replenish stocks, and potentially clear the dark fleet when it comes. I will now pass over to Ted, who will present our quarterly financial review.

Ted Young: Thanks, John. My comments this morning will focus on capital allocation, our financial position, liquidity, and our unaudited second quarter results. We've continued to opportunistically monetize our fleet since our last earnings call. In October, we completed the sale of both Clermont, which we had discussed on our last call, as well as the Captain John NP, the oldest ship in our fleet. The two sales generated proceeds of approximately $167.4 million net of commission. We also paid down debt associated with the Clermont of $16 million.

On September 2, we entered into a new seven-year, $368.4 million credit facility to refinance several credit facilities, including the 2023 amended and restated facility, the Cougar and Crest Japanese financings, and the Commander tranche of the BALCAP Facility. The new facility carries a margin of 140 basis points over SOFR, which is an improvement of around 60 points compared to the 2023 A&R Facility, and also has an age-adjusted profile of 22 years. The facility also has a revolving credit facility, which currently has a capacity of $154 million and a $200 million accordion facility, both of which give us financial flexibility and support our future growth.

We've also managed to keep in place an existing interest rate swap, which means that about 58.5% of the current term loan balance is currently fixed at 2.85%. We'd also note that the syndicate of banks includes all those previously part of the 2023 A&R Facility, in addition to three new banks. In September, we also announced that we entered into an agreement with Hanwha Ocean to build three 90,000 CBM dual-fuel Neo-Panamax VLGCs for delivery in 2030 for a price of approximately $338 million. This brings our total number of newbuildings to four. We made the 10% down payments on those vessels during the September quarter.

At September 30, 2026, we reported $578.8 million of free cash, an increase of $236.6 million, or nearly 70% from the previous quarter. Since September 30, we've received sale proceeds from Clermont and Captain John NP, and enjoyed continued strong freight markets as reflected in distributions from our Helios Pool, leading to our current cash balance of almost $785 million. Our debt balance of $484.8 million at quarter end was reduced following the sale of the Clermont and repayment of $16 million of debt, therefore bringing our pro forma debt balance at the 30th of September to $469 million.

Based on our stated quarter-end book debt at $484.8 million, our debt to total book capitalization stood at 25.6%, and our net debt to total capitalization at negative 5%. Using the pro forma sale proceeds, the debt repayment, and our current cash balance, we currently have net cash of about $320 million, and a current all-in debt cost of 4.94%, and our undrawn revolver of 154.8 million. Coupled with our healthy cash balance, we clearly have a comfortable measure of financial flexibility to support growth or whatever may come. We expect our cash cost per day for the coming year to be approximately $27,000 per day.

The slight increase versus our previous guidance is largely a function of the reduced number of vessel days following the vessel sales. For the discussion of our second quarter results, you may find it useful to refer to the investor highlights slides posted this morning on our website. For the second quarter, the Helios Pool earned a TCE for its spot and COA voyages of $115,163, and an overall TCE result of $99,915, reflecting the very strong rate environment. On page four of our investor highlights materials, you can see that we have seven Dorian vessels on time charter within the pool, indicating spot exposure of just over 73% for the 26 vessels in the Helios Pool.

Dorian's reported TCE revenue per available day for the quarter was just shy of $97,000, which, for the third quarter in a row, was the highest TCE rate we have earned in our corporate existence. The favorable variance versus our forward guidance is due to demurrage booked in September and favorable mark-to-market adjustments on our COAs. We plan to issue our forward booking information in the near future. Daily OPEX for the quarter was $10,273, excluding dry docking-related expenses, which was a modest decrease over the prior quarter due mainly to lower maintenance and repair costs. Our gross time charter-in expense for the five TCIN vessels came in at $18.2 million, or $36,635 per TCIN day.

Those vessels contributed positively to our quarterly profits. As we redelivered one vessel during the quarter, we note that we expect our TCIN expense to decrease to about $29,954 per TCIN day going forward, or about $13.8 million quarterly in aggregate. Total G&A for the quarter was $14 million, and cash G&A, that's G&A excluding non-cash comp expense, was about $8.2 million. The $8.2 million included about $1.3 million of incentive compensation expense accruals, which leaves our core G&A around $7 million. Our reported adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was $242 million, which is also a record, and included $63.6 million of gains on sale from the sales of the Corsair and the Constellation.

We will reflect the gains on the sales of the Clermont and the Captain John NP next quarter, and expect those to amount to in excess of $88 million. But for this quarter just ended, excluding the gains on the Corsair and the Constellation, EBITDA was $178.4 million. Total cash interest expense for the quarter was $5.7 million, which is down sequentially from the prior quarter, and principal amortization for the quarter was $9.9 million.

For the coming quarter ending December 31, after taking into account the changes in our financing structure, we expect cash interest expense to come in around $6.1 million and principal amortization to be about $9.8 million, excluding the $16 million we already paid in conjunction with the sale of the Clermont. The regular cash dividend declared at the beginning of the month of $1.25 per share is our 20th consecutive and 21st in total, and brings the total to $20.90 per share in regular dividends that we have paid since September of 2021.

Including that regular dividend to be paid this month, we have paid nearly $865 million of total dividends and have generated net income of $1.2 billion, including about $100 million of gains on sale over the same time period. As we've explained, our board weighs current earnings, our near-term cash flow forecast, fleet investment needs, and the overall market environment among a number of factors in making its determination the appropriate level, if any, for our dividends. Our sector can be a volatile one, and our dividend policy needs to reflect that. I would note, however, that the $1.25 per share dividend reflects a constructive market outlook while also allowing the company financial flexibility for future fleet reinvestment.

We continue to be on the lookout for fleet renewal opportunities and will be judicious with our free cash flow. With that, I'll pass it over to Taro Rasmussen.

Taro Rasmussen: Thank you, Ted. The quarter ending September 30, 2026, has three headlines: escalating conflict in the Middle East, congestion at the Panama Canal, and record highs in the VLGC freight market. There are several aspects of the conflict in the Middle East that have had significant impacts on shipping and arbitrage economics, whether the initial collapse of the MOU, Houthi advances to the Red Sea coast, or the successful attack on the Saudi East-West pipeline. These aspects combine to create a backdrop for energy markets solving a shortage crunch for importing regions and explains energy markets acting with urgency. Meanwhile, the Panama Canal's critical role in U.S.-Asia trade cannot be ignored.

Record-high Panama Canal auction prices and severe delays were witnessed during the quarter amidst meteorologists concluding the coming El Niño season could be one of the most severe on record. These are the leading explanations for how the Baltic Exchange's BLPG3 calculated TCE climbed from about $82,000 per day on July 1 to about $198,000 per day on September 30. This nominal TCE is based on a roughly 60-day round trip rather than about 80 days if the ballast length is around the Cape of Good Hope, which increases the denominator for getting per-day earnings. Furthermore, the assessed TCE does not account for weather factors, delays, and other costs.

Increased delivered product prices after the MOU ceasefire and increasing freight rates incentivize solutions to increasing exports from the Arabian Gulf and vessels to chance transits through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably on oil tankers and VLGCs, Middle East exporters turned to own tonnage or willing ship owners to load at Arabian Gulf terminals and discharge to waiting vessels outside the Arabian Gulf. Additional seaborne tons of oil products and LPGs gave some relief to shortage-stricken countries in Asia and drove rates up.

However, because of irregular availability of vessels willing to transit the Strait of Hormuz, irregular scheduling to ensure a transit with least risk, and irregular supply of vessels to receive cargo in the Indian Ocean, sometimes with little notice, it is a logistically inefficient operation. Freight markets benefited from the inefficiencies, increasing vessel utilization. The requisite premiums for ship owners to take the risk of transiting the Strait of Hormuz acted as a locomotive on the reported rates. It should also be noted that while the shuttle services through the Strait of Hormuz have increased Middle East exports compared to the prior quarter, presently available data suggests export volumes are about half of pre-conflict levels.

The secondhand tonnage markets also benefited from the new trade, as Middle East exporting countries and risk-willing companies turned to purchase prompt tonnage to outright own vessels and secure a regular supply of vessels able to attempt transits through the Strait of Hormuz. The successful attack on the Saudi East-West pipeline to Yanbu by pro-Iranian interests had a significant impact on widening the arbitrage, as crude oil and LPG export capabilities were severely restricted. The Houthi alliance's capture of Mocha and Perim Island during September 10, 11 has further expanded their capacity to attack vessels in the Red Sea and drove up delivered prices in Asia.

Whereas several container alliances have committed to Red Sea transits, Bab-el-Mandeb is de facto closed to tankers and VLGCs because of expressed threats to Saudi origin cargo, as would be the case for Yanbu exports. The Houthi alliance's advance to the Red Sea coast happened immediately after a period of rising, record-setting auction prices at the Panama Canal. In August, there were 25 Neo-Panamax auctions with an average winning bid of about $2 million, with winning auction prices rising above $4 million five times. In July, there were 45 auctions with winning bids averaging about $1 million.

The reduced number of auctions reflected the reduced transit capacity and water management implemented by the Panama Canal authorities in preparation for El Niño. Through August and mid-September, the canal authorities issued multiple notices to the restrictions, adding planning uncertainty for ship owners and adding congestion when demand was peaking due to the elevated commodity markets. The new records set during this calendar quarter were primarily due to high demand from all shipping sectors, as seen the quarter prior, but it was the reduced transit capacity and ever-changing restrictions that made non-auction transits nearly impossible to accomplish. It should be noticed that the drought season in Panama has not yet commenced.

The additional costs associated with Panama Canal congestion translates to higher freight levels, and higher barriers to smooth canal transits incentivize sailings around the Cape of Good Hope. The longer transits from the U.S. to Asia absorbing vessel supply explain why VLGC loadings in the U.S. Gulf for this calendar quarter averaged about 102 a month, compared to about 113 a month the quarter prior, because North American production continues to grow. The Middle East conflict is therefore not the only point of attention for the VLGC market. The quarter ending September 30, 2026, mimics the prior quarter in that the Iran conflict has instilled urgency into worldwide commodity markets and exacerbated existing logistical inefficiencies.

Even with the VLGC market contributing to solutions for providing energy from the Arabian Gulf, knock-on inefficiencies have presented itself. While there are no obvious silver bullets to address congestion at the Panama Canal, past experiences and the company's flexible fleet will help overcoming those obstacles in the coming quarter, and we remain well-positioned to capture arising opportunities. Thank you. I will now pass on to Mr. John Lycouris.

John Lycouris: Thank you, Taro. At Dorian LPG, we remain committed to continually enhancing energy efficiency and promoting the sustainability of our business at sea and onshore. Of the 22 vessels we commercially operate, 14 are scrubber-fitted and five are dual-fuel LPG. The high oil prices driven by the ongoing Middle East conflict and frequent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz has caused bunker price differentials to remain elevated, underscoring the value of our fuel efficiency initiatives and installation of scrubbers on our vessels.

For the second fiscal quarter of 2027, scrubber vessel savings were higher than the previous 11 quarters, amounting to approximately $4,174 per calendar day per vessel, net of all scrubber operating expenses, and has benefited our vessels with improved voyage economics. Fuel differentials between high-sulfur fuel oil and very low-sulfur fuel oil averaged $174 per metric ton, while that of LPG as fuel versus the very low-sulfur fuel oil stood at about $314 per metric ton, making LPG economically attractive for our dual-fuel vessels. We remain committed to being at the forefront of energy efficiency advancements.

Our participation in the MIT Maritime Consortium continues to support and sharpen our focus on future sustainability and operational efficiency across several areas of maritime research. One topic that has received particular attention in a recent meeting was nuclear propulsion. A panel featuring representatives from the Maritime Administration, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Coast Guard, the American Bureau of Shipping, and the West P&I, which was moderated by a Dorian LPG board member and ex-American Bureau of Shipping CEO, Christopher Wiernicki, explored the potential of nuclear power in commercial shipping, particularly its ability to reduce emissions and enhance energy security.

Ongoing research into reactor and port safety has yielded encouraging results, with floating nuclear power plants potentially paving the way for broader adoption in commercial shipping. We continue to closely monitor developments at the IMO, particularly the ongoing discussions around the Net-Zero Framework ahead of the MEPC 85 in late November and early December of 2026. While the final regulatory framework and implementation timeline remain uncertain, we believe a practical and globally consistent approach is important to support long-term investment decisions rather than the fragmented regional regulations. In the meantime, our focus remains on improving fleet energy efficiency, reducing emissions, and maintaining flexibility in our future fuel strategy.

We have also developed an emissions simulation model to assess different regulatory scenarios and their potential financial implications for our fleet, allowing us to remain well-prepared as the regulatory landscape evolves. We are confident that the Dorian LPG fleet will be prepared to meet regulatory changes in the future. I would like to pass it over to John Hadjipateras for his final comments.

John Hadjipateras: Thank you very much, John. Chelsea, we are ready to take questions.

Operator: Thank you. At this time, if you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. To leave the queue at any time, please press star two. Once again, that is star one to ask a question. Our first question will come from Omar Nokta with Clarksons Securities. Please go ahead.

Omar Nokta: Thanks. Thanks, operator. Good morning. Obviously nice results. Congrats on the record earnings and record achieved rates. The business is clearly, and the market, clearly are in a strong position. You did discuss a good amount of the Panama Canal dynamic here in your remarks. Clearly there were a lot of log jams definitely throughout the year, but I did want to ask about what we've seen here recently. It seems at least that over the past several weeks, there's been maybe an easing in the congestion levels there. It's been going on, it feels like maybe, call it for past six to eight weeks.

It doesn't appear that there's as much of a delay dynamic as there was before, and yet, VLGC spot rates remain at exceptionally high levels, if not still at the near record figures. Just want to get from your perspective, are we perhaps maybe overplaying the impact of the Panama Canal dynamic? Are spot rates maybe structurally supported by something else beyond just the congestion that we have been seeing there? Thank you. If you're able to answer that, I appreciate it.

John Hadjipateras: I think, like I said in my remarks, but also Taro more completely, there are several factors, and Panama is just one of them. I think that I'd let Taro give you a more complete explanation, but I think that the Panama effect, you don't get it until you get it, and when it comes, it exasperates, and then it unwinds slowly. But, Taro, you can tell Omar a little more about why it seems to linger in the freight market, or whether you think other factors are more influencing the freight market more than the Panama effect.

Taro Rasmussen: Sure. Thank you for the question, Omar. The quick answer is that a lot of the decisions about ballasting were made weeks before, several weeks before. That reduces some of the immediate congestion and adds to the ton miles. It also is a reflection that what I mentioned about changing rules and transit advisories, that causes a lot of unease because you need to make your ballasting decisions a month before your laycans. That is a reflection of that.

Also, we know some will try to predict the weather way too far in advance, but we are very aware of the fact that October, November is typically the wet season in the area, and the drought season starts around the new year. We just have to look at mitigating potential risks here, and I do not think we are alone because otherwise we would see more congestion. I think it is a perfectly fair reflection, the spot market of where we are vis-a-vis Panama.

Omar Nokta: Okay. Thank you. Appreciate that.

John Hadjipateras: In addition to the Panama effect, the ton mile effect, do not forget also the inefficiency. The 50% of the volumes that are coming out of the Middle East do not travel efficiently. There is transshipment that delays both at the loading and the crossing of Hormuz and the transshipment, and then the delay and then the reloading. That whole system also creates a shortage.

Omar Nokta: Yeah. Thanks, John. Maybe just as a quick follow-up to that point, are you able to give a sense of the volumes coming out of the Middle East? What portion are coming out of, say, the Hormuz via the STS and what's coming out of the Red Sea?

Taro Rasmussen: We don't have the most recent figures. I think most are scrambling to put that data together. What you will see is, for many VLGCs, to answer your point about the proportion coming out of the Red Sea, they might have loaded around now, but you would not see the data until much later because those vessels are presently heading north into the Mediterranean around Africa, so you'll have a delay in data. Unfortunately, I don't have the best answer for you right now. I'm sure we'll all get more clarity later on.

Omar Nokta: Thank you. Okay. Yeah, that certainly makes sense. I appreciate it. Just one more, and maybe on kind of Dorian-specific. Certainly, you've been taking advantage of the strong market, especially the run-up in asset values to monetize for the older VLGCs, and you've been basically rolling the proceeds effectively into the newbuildings. How are you thinking about the capital allocation from here that I know you've mentioned in your comments, looking at modern tonnage? But, should we expect you maybe to continue this approach of monetizing some of the older vessels in this environment and perhaps replacing them with newbuildings? Or do you maybe look for on-the-water tonnage?

John Hadjipateras: We sold five ships this year, and the average age of those ships was almost 13 years, and the average price that we got for them was about $83 million. The market has continued to advance, and it reflects abnormal conditions. So, I'm not going to say that we won't sell anymore, but I will say that we're not, at the moment, actively seeking to sell. On the newbuilding front, yes, we're content with where we are at the moment, and we're not in a rush to go add to the order book. But a natural replacement cycle would require us to do more newbuildings in the next few years.

But whether we do them in the next year or beyond that is still up in the air. We're content to wait and see how the prices develop.

Omar Nokta: Got it. Thank you, John, for that. That is it for me. I will pass it back.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question will come from Stephanie Moore with Jefferies.

Stephanie Moore: Hi, good morning. Thank you. I think you noted today that U.S. terminals still did not run at full capacity because ships were effectively short. How much spare terminal capacity is there? When do the new export projects come online? Is the constraint now shipping rather than actually terminals? My second question, just to put it all together at once here, is, we always think it is important to know, if we do see some kind of normalization in the Middle East and Gulf cargoes return, how quickly would you expect to see rates adjust? I know that is a pretty complicated question, but would just love to get your thoughts on that dynamic too. Just those two. Thank you.

John Hadjipateras: Not too complicated for Taro, but it is a very interesting question. Thanks, Stephanie. Taro?

Taro Rasmussen: Thanks for the question, Stephanie. The way we see it right now is that the main constraint is indeed the availability of tonnage, short and sweet. In terms of the capacity or the utilization rate, I do not have the percentage off the top of my head here. Refer to what I mentioned that compared to what we saw last quarter, we are down about 10 loadings just in the U.S. Gulf a month. So, you are 10% inefficiencies, plus or minus. I forgot, what was the third question, sorry? Or maybe it is difficult to do the follow-up. I hope that addressed it. Oh, there you are.

Stephanie Moore: The first question was just about terminal capacity.

Stephanie Moore: The second was just on the Hormuz and how fast, if we were to see some form of peace, when we would start to see rates move.

Taro Rasmussen: Excellent question. I hope my previous remarks covered the capacity there. About Hormuz, I think, as with anything geopolitical, the initial wave is one of sentiment, then comes the realignment of the trade. So it's probably going to be in two phases. In terms of the normalization of rates, we certainly, as Mr. Hadjipateras mentioned, peace is an attractive enabler of trade, so may that happen. With regards to answering your question properly, I think it's difficult to start making predictions about when peace happens, also a key consideration is what kind of peace.

I think there's many options up in the air right now, whether it's the discussed tolls or whether it is a ceasefire or a permanent peace, I think that's a few too many scenarios for me to digest right now. I think that's a question for everybody to consider, what peace actually means.

John Hadjipateras: Yeah. No, Stephanie, you also asked how fast. It could be very fast. The market may react, very fast, but I don't believe that in the medium to long term, we're looking at a net negative. So you saw when the MOU was signed, the market went down, then within days, it bounced again. The volumes are still there to be shipped, if the Hormuz opens, there'll be more volumes to be shipped. It takes time for the market to rebalance, for tonnage to get into an efficient mode. So I really find, as I said before, that when the threat of peace is viewed as a negative, it's a little bit silly.

I don't view it as a negative in the long run. Thank you anyway. I thought it was a nice, challenging question. Also, the first part of it about the capacity, the capacity, it's difficult to pinpoint when you don't know, when it's a new situation. It's a wonderful situation to find yourself in when you're on the supply side, where the demand exceeds supply. We haven't had that too often in shipping until recently. So, it's kind of in play, let's see how it goes. Thank you, Stephanie. I think, Chelsea-

John Hadjipateras: We're done with the questions, right?

Taro Rasmussen: She's saying yes from Stephanie.

Operator: This does conclude the Q&A portion of the call, so I'd like to turn it back to John Hadjipateras for any additional or closing remarks.

John Hadjipateras: Thank you, Chelsea. Yes, indeed. Thank you very much, Omar. Thank you, Stephanie, for your participation, and everyone else.

John Hadjipateras: Have a good fall, and see you in January. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you, ladies and gentlemen. This brings us to the end of today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation, and you may now disconnect.

#3159. The Clock Is Running on Apple’s Siri Settlement. How to File Before Dec. 21

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model between June 2024 and March 2025 is eligible to file a claim.

Dec. 21 is the last day to file a claim in Apple’s $250 million settlement over delayed Siri features, and payouts could reach $95 per eligible iPhone.

The class covers anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or any iPhone 16 model between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, the stretch when Apple was promoting a more personal Siri that hadn’t arrived yet. Filing takes a few minutes online, and each qualifying phone gets its own claim.

The iPhone 16 went on sale in September 2024 with Apple Intelligence at the center of its marketing. However, the first AI features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, several weeks later, and the most heavily promoted one, a Siri that could pull personal context from your apps, was further delayed in March 2025.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The opt-in form is available only for a limited time, so get your name in the pool before it closes. Eligible buyers have until Dec. 21 to file, and each qualifying iPhone gets its own claim.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. Apple denies all of the lawsuit’s allegations and denies that it did anything unlawful or improper.

If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme.

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

#3157. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3156. Lyft and DoorDash Have a New Subscription. Why You Should Read the Fine Print First

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Online > Online Services

Two memberships for the price of one sounds good — until your credits expire.

Lyft and DoorDash are teaming up for a new plan that essentially gives you two subscriptions for the price of one. But is it worth it?

Lyft announced the Lyft Go with DashPass subscription Thursday. Lyft says you’ll earn 8% back in credits to use toward your next Lyft ride or DoorDash order. Lyft Go with DashPass includes DashPass, DoorDash’s $10 monthly subscription — which includes no delivery fees and additional savings on select DoorDash orders.

Lyft is accounting for common mishaps. Lyft Go allows three trip cancellations per month and unlimited use of the Lost Item Fee Waiver in case you leave something behind in somebody’s car. Lyft currently charges $20 for drivers to make the return trip. And if you opt in to Lyft’s Round Up and Donate feature, Lyft will match 100% of your charitable donation.

Since Lyft Go with DashPass is $10 per month, you’ll basically get DashPass and Lyft Go for one price.

Lyft also has Lyft Go Core, a lower-tier monthly subscription that’s $5 per month. It won’t include DashPass, and you’ll earn 5% instead of 8% in credits. You’ll still get three ride cancellations and donation matching.

There are some caveats that may make you think twice. You won’t be able to earn credits through DoorDash orders and then redeem them with Lyft. And credits expire after 60 days. If you cancel your Lyft Go subscription, those credits may also expire sooner or become unavailable. And these subscriptions only work in the US. Lyft and DoorDash didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

So if you earn credits within your free trial, you may want to use them before the trial ends if you’re considering canceling before your card is charged.

The new subscriptions give me pause given what we already know about US adults and subscriptions. CNET’s annual subscription survey found that only 10% of US adults are paying for meal and food delivery subscriptions and even fewer (3%) for automotive subscriptions.

However, subscription spending is up 23% compared to last year’s average of $1,080. Now, US adults are spending an average of $1,332 annually on subscriptions. However, most are paying for streaming services (61%), retail platforms (48%) and music (35%). If this isn’t a subscription you’ll use regularly enough to redeem the credits, it could be another subscription that sucks $10 out of your monthly budget. And you’ll need to do the math to see if the savings add up enough to justify paying for the rides, your DoorDash orders and the monthly subscription.

Both Lyft Go with DashPass and Lyft Go Core are now available in the Lyft app nationwide, and a one-month free trial is available. However, if you already have DashPass, you can link your account with Lyft to have Lyft Go with DashPass at no extra cost. And if you have Lyft Pink, you’ll automatically be transitioned to Lyft Go with DashPass at no extra cost to the current price. However, Lyft Pink All-Access and Lyft Business Travel Rewards aren’t changing.

#3154. Northwest Natural (NWN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management lifted full-year guidance but flagged a housing slowdown tied to elevated mortgage rates.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Northwest Natural Holding Company (NWN +0.97%) reported results for the third quarter and first nine months of 2026. Management increased full-year earnings guidance based on year-to-date performance and constructive regulatory developments in several jurisdictions. The company executed multiyear rate plans and settlement agreements in Washington, Oregon, and Texas while continuing to invest in utility infrastructure. Strategic initiatives focused on expanding the natural gas storage footprint and integrating water utility services into existing growth markets. Financial results for the period included the effects of customer additions across all utility segments and disciplined operations and maintenance spending.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us and welcome to the Northwest Natural Holding Company Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. After today's prepared remarks, we will host a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star 1 to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star-1 again. I will now hand the conference over to Nikki Sparley director of investor relations. Please go ahead.

Nikki Sparley: Thank you. Good morning, and welcome to our third quarter 2026 earnings call. In addition to the press release, a supplemental presentation is available on our Investor Relations website at ir.nwnaturalholdings.com. And following this call, a recording will also be available on our website. As a reminder, some things that will be said this morning contain forward-looking statements. They are based on management's assumptions, which may or may not occur. For a complete list of cautionary statements, refer to the language in our press release. Additionally, our risk factors are provided in our 10-Q and 10-K filings. We will also refer to certain non GAAP financial measures.

For additional disclosures about these non GAAP measures, including reconciliations to comparable GAAP measures, please see our press release and the slides that accompany today's call. Which are available on the Investor Relations page of our website. Please note our guidance assumes continued customer growth, average weather conditions, and no significant changes in prevailing regulatory mechanisms, or assumed outcomes or significant changes in local, state, or federal laws, legislation, or regulations. We expect to file our 10-Q later today. With us today are Justin Palfreyman, president and chief executive officer, and Raymond J. Kaszuba, senior vice president and chief financial officer. Justin will provide highlights from the quarter, a regulatory update, and a look forward.

Raymond will walk through our financial results and guidance. After Justin and Raymond's prepared remarks, we will host a question and answer session. With that, I will turn the call over to Justin.

Justin Palfreyman: Thanks, Nikki. Good morning, welcome, everyone. I am pleased to report another quarter of strong financial results. Earnings per share for both the quarter and year to date exceeded our expectations. Driven by disciplined cost management, solid operational execution, and continued customer growth. Given the strength of our business through the first 9 months, our visibility into the remainder of 2026, and we are raising our annual earnings guidance. With the heating season still ahead, we are confident in our position today and the momentum we are building into 2027. Importantly, we achieved these results while prioritizing customer affordability.

At a time when inflation and energy costs are top of mind, our objective is to invest prudently in growth, reliability, and the safety of our systems. While carefully managing costs on behalf of our customers. That mindset is embedded across our organization. A central tenet of our long term strategy is collaborating with regulators to align customer needs with utility investment requirements Across our service territories, we continue to find that timely recovery of investments is important for both customers and utilities. We have long been proponents of multiyear rate making and its benefits. Customers benefit from more gradual and predictable rate adjustments, and utilities gain greater visibility and certainty to invest in critical infrastructure.

With this in mind, let me provide an update on our regulatory dockets. Starting in Texas, settled our SiEnergy rate case on September 1st under our ownership. The settlement provides an $8.6 million revenue requirement increase a 9.8% authorized ROE, and a nearly 60% equity ratio. We also received the factors necessary to file for the gas reliability infrastructure program or GRIP which provides accelerated recovery of CapEx between rate cases. We expect new rates to take effect in November subject to commission approval. Even after the rate changes, still expect SiEnergy's customer bills to remain competitive with other Texas gas utilities.

SiEnergy is laying the foundation for future investment recovery through both GRIP and the established benefits provided under HB 4.38 thousand. Together, these mechanisms help reduce regulatory lag, support ongoing infrastructure investment, and contribute to more gradual customer bill impacts over time. Turning to Northwest Natural Water. Foothills, our largest water utility, continues to make progress on its Arizona rate proceeding. Including its request for formula rates. We believe formula rate structures can provide a more efficient path for recovering investments while maintaining transparency and regulatory oversight. We have 4 additional water rate cases underway that we expect to conclude in early 2027. We also continue to advance our rate consolidation strategy across our water utilities.

We have made progress in Idaho and Washington, and are pursuing further consolidation in Oregon, Arizona, and Texas, with the goal of simplifying regulatory administration and reducing costs for stakeholders. Turning to Northwest Natural's regulatory updates. As we mentioned last quarter, new rates in Washington became effective August 1st following approval of our multiyear rate plan settlement. In October, we received the final order for our Alternative Rate Mechanism or ARM, in Oregon. We are pleased with the outcome. The order provides for a $13 million increase in revenue requirement compared to the original ask of $15.6 million New rates were effective on October 31st.

We also received approval for our annual Purchased Gas Adjustments or PGAs in both Oregon and Washington. Even after taking into account the arm in Oregon, the recent Washington rate case, and gas costs from the PGA, the average Northwest Natural residential customer continues to pay about the same today for their natural gas service as they did 20 years ago. Over that same period, comparable electricity rates have more than doubled in our region. Entering the heating season, our gas supply and system readiness position us well to meet customer demand. This includes the addition of 2 new compressors at our Mist storage facility helping to support reliability during peak winter conditions.

In Oregon, we continue to engage constructively with stakeholders as the state advances the framework for multiyear rate making. Phase 2 is now underway, with conversations occurring across several work streams. While these discussions progress, our priority remains the same. Finding solutions that support customer affordability while ensuring utilities can continue to make the investments necessary to maintain safe and reliable service. Under the Oregon Commission's current schedule, we expect to file our first multiyear rate case in 2028 with new rates effective in 2029. Before our first multiyear rates go into effect, we are closely examining additional options. Such as a general rate case to ensure timely recovery of our investments and costs.

By 2029, once multiyear rates are in place in Oregon, we expect over 95% of our overall rate base to have some form of forward looking rate plan or mechanism. These mechanisms support more timely recovery of investments help to smooth out customer rate impacts, and provide longer term visibility into our financial results. With that, let me spend a few minutes on our major growth initiatives. Starting with SiEnergy. Customer growth remains strong, up approximately 13% for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026. Elevated mortgage rates have begun to moderate housing activity from peak levels in Texas.

While SiEnergy is not immune to these trends, we are still bullish on the Texas housing market long term and are still seeing healthy double digit customer growth and a robust development pipeline. Underscoring our confidence in the future, our backlog continues to grow and sits at nearly 265 thousand lots as of quarter end. Since acquiring SiEnergy less than 2 years ago, have added approximately 110 thousand new lots to the backlog which is quite a testament to the strength of SiEnergy's reputation and development team.

SiEnergy continues to be 1 of the fastest growing gas LDCs in the country and the combination of continued customer growth, a constructive regulatory framework, recovery mechanisms in Texas support our confidence in SiEnergy's long term EPS growth. For our water utilities, we are making great progress on centralizing and consolidating the business. Our objective is to build a platform designed to scale efficiently over time. Customer growth at Northwest Natural Water was just over 2% for the 12 months ended September 30, Similar to SiEnergy, we are seeing a modest slowdown in housing activity in some of our markets due to higher mortgage rates.

Over the coming years, are still confident in our long term 2% to 3% customer growth target. Our teams are making significant progress on capital projects at our Foothills utilities, including tank projects that support anticipated and reliability of our water storage and distribution systems. Longer term, greenfield development remains an important incremental growth driver for our water utilities. I am excited to highlight that we recently began construction on the first community in Texas where we are serving gas, water, and wastewater through both sea energy and Northwest Natural Water.

The ability to offer multiple utility services through a single company is a differentiated value proposition for developers, and we see opportunities to expand this model in the years ahead. Finally, moving to MX3, As a reminder, MX3 is a $300 million FERC regulated gas storage expansion project that will add 4 to 5 BCF of capacity in our region. The project is fully contracted with 25 year agreements upon notice to proceed. 12.5% ROE, and a 50% equity layer. We continue to work through the permitting process and remain on track to receive notice to proceed by the end of 2027.

As discussed last quarter, we received unanimous approval of our conditional use permit from the Columbia County Board of Commissioners. As expected, an appeal was filed with the Land Use Board of Appeals, or LUBA, That process is underway, and our timeline for notice to proceed remains unchanged. MX3 represents an important opportunity to enhance energy reliability across the Pacific Northwest and, upon receiving notice to proceed, would support increased our long-term earnings growth target to 5% to 7%. In summary, the strategic work we have done over the past few years is starting to produce tangible results.

We serve growing service territories, are advancing key regulatory initiatives, and investing in critical infrastructure all while controlling costs and maintaining financial strength. Given our year to date results and expectations for the balance of the year, we are raising our 2026 earnings guidance, and remain confident in our long term growth. Additionally, we recently announced our largest dividend increase since 2012, which reflects that same confidence. The dividend remains an important component of our shareholder value proposition. And the increase highlights both the strength of our underlying business and our expectation that we will continue to drive sustainable earnings and dividend growth over time.

That confidence is grounded in our well established track record, For more than 167 years, Northwest Natural has successfully navigated a variety of economic environments, including periods of elevated inflation and higher interest rates. Throughout our history, we have consistently adapted to those conditions and delivered value to shareholders while staying committed to affordability and serving customers safely. With that, I will turn it over to Raymond for a more detailed financial update.

Raymond J. Kaszuba: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. As Justin mentioned, we are raising our EPS guidance range to $3.10 to $3.20 driven by our better than expected year to date performance constructive regulatory outcomes, the strong execution we are seeing across the company. A meaningful contributor has been our continued focus on cost management. We are seeing favorable O&M performance across several parts of the organization, reflecting both productivity improvements and disciplined spending decisions. We are also reaffirming our capital expenditure plan of $500 million to $550 million. Year to date CapEx is up 12% over last year, as we continue to invest in growth and reliability across our utility systems. Turning to a more detailed review of our financial results.

As a reminder, our gas utility earnings are seasonal with the majority of revenues and earnings generated in the first and fourth quarters during the winter heating months. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported a loss of $0.71 per share compared to a loss of $0.73 per share for the same period of 2025. Results were modestly improved year over year due to higher margin across all businesses and O&M expense management that was partially offset by higher depreciation and financing costs. For the first 9 months, we reported earnings per share of a $1.62 in 2026 up 6.6% compared to adjusted EPS of $1.52 for the same period in 2025.

The year to date increase in earnings per share reflected a higher contribution from SiEnergy, as well as new rates across our gas utilities in Oregon and Washington. These items were partially offset by higher O&M expenses at Northwest Natural Water. At Northwest Natural Gas, year to date net income was up $1.6 million but EPS was down roughly $0.02. Results were driven by new rates and continued cost discipline. At SiEnergy, year to date net income was up $4.4 million or $0.10 per share reflecting customer growth and a full period of contribution from the Pines acquisition.

At Northwest Natural Water, year to date net income was down $1.7 million or $0.04 per share reflecting higher O&M from continued operational centralization, and higher depreciation from several key infrastructure projects. Finally, our other segment's year to date net loss improved by $8.5 million driven by lower O&M, partially offset by higher financing costs. Overall, we are pleased with our execution and believe the guidance increase appropriately reflects the strength of our year to date performance while maintaining a prudent outlook as we start the 2026 to 2027 heating season. Turning now to shareholder returns. Last month, we announced an increase in our indicated annual dividend of $0.03 bringing it to $2 per share.

This marks our largest dividend increase since 2012, and extends our track record to 71 consecutive years of dividend growth. I am very pleased with the significant progress we have made over the past 2 years to bring the payout ratio down to our long term target range of 55% to 65%. Our dividend increase reflects the strength and stability of our underlying business. We continue to have strong organic growth opportunities across our regulated businesses and remain committed to investing in essential utility infrastructure and driving sustainable earnings growth. Maintaining a solid balance sheet and returning capital to shareholders.

As we have said previously, we expect dividend growth to be higher than it has been historically, and supported by continued earnings growth. Beginning in 2027, we will announce updates to our dividend approach in connection with our annual guidance updates on our fourth quarter earnings call in February. Before turning to questions, I wanted to briefly discuss how we are thinking about financing in the current environment. Given the recent interest rate volatility and broader inflation, we remain focused on a financing strategy that preserves flexibility and supports long term value creation. On the debt side, we have intentionally maintained a diversified maturity profile and avoided concentrations of refinancing risks.

Approximately 75% of our debt is at our regulated businesses, financing costs are generally recovered through rates. Northwest Natural Gas, which represents the largest portion of our needs, benefits from a predictable capital program that generally requires only modest debt financing each year. That allows us to remain flexible and opportunistic as we access capital markets. Across the company, we have maintained very limited exposure to floating rate debt. Our target remains 10% or less. Which helps reduce earnings volatility and provides greater predictability for customers and shareholders. For 2026, we have completed debt financings for the year. On the equity side, we believe the ATM provides sufficient flexibility to support our anticipated equity needs.

Continue to expect to need $40 million to $50 million in total for the whole year and we have already issued $26 million While equity needs may vary from year to year depending on our CapEx profile, we believe our current plan can be supported by our ATM. Stepping back, I want to emphasize the flexibility of our financing plan. We have multiple levers to execute our capital program and navigate changing market conditions. Combined with our regulatory strategy and disciplined approach to capital allocation, we believe we are well positioned to continue delivering value for both customers and shareholders across a wide range of economic environments. With that, we will open up the call for questions.

Operator: You will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star 1 to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star-1 again. We ask that you pick up your handset when asking a question to allow for optimum sound quality. If you are muted locally, please remember to unmute your device. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Your first question comes from Konstantin Lednev with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Analyst: Hi team. Good morning and congrats on a great quarter.

Yeah. I appreciate the question. We are evaluating options for bridging the period between 2026 and when we will file our first multiyear, rate case in 2028. And just in terms of timing or maybe accelerating some of that No. I do not think so, Konstantin. Okay. And just with the, I guess, with the Oregon election behind us, some of the policy shifts in Oregon enable further gas generation just to back up renewables or coal retirement or the data center uncertainty kind of complicate some of these incremental gas demand needs just as we think in the context of MX3 and any further kind of missed expansion Yeah. No. it is a great question. The gas fired generation is difficult in Oregon.

We would expect that you would see more of that happening in surrounding states just because of some of the, restrictions in the state of Oregon. All of that, though, and the dynamics that you are referring to bode well for future gas storage expansion because there is a very significant need, especially on peak during the winter, for additional, energy resources, whether that is whether that is generation on the electric side or even on the gas grid itself. And so we still see strong long term demand beyond even MX3 for gas storage in our region. Okay. Got it. And then just maybe a quick regulatory follow-up on the SiEnergy kind of settlement.

Just in terms of what is embedded in the current plan and just going forward, assuming approval, what would you look for in terms of timing of the GRIP filings going forward on a more cyclical basis? Yeah. We have the factors in place now for Grip and assuming we get the final order here in the next few weeks, we would expect that our first grip filing would be in 2027.

Raymond J. Kaszuba: So and similar to other utilities who have leveraged this mechanism, we have up to 5 years of leveraging grip before a general rate case will be required again.

Analyst: Okay. Got it. that is finally clear. Appreciate your time today. Congrats again.

And we continue to be bullish on our outlook in terms of housing growth in Texas, but I think that the peak from maybe 2 or 3 years ago as. #3153. What to Know About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent keeps a running profile of everyone who uses it. Yes, even if you deny it permission to do so. And by doing so, it’s effectively made Jolly, its “cute and cuddly” mascot, a harbinger of concerning security architecture.

Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

#3152. The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta today

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The wait is over for trying Siri AI on iOS 27. Here's what you need to know to get started.

Enabling Siri AI, Apple’s new generative AI-powered virtual assistant, on a compatible Apple device running iOS 27 used to prompt a message informing the user that the device would be added to a waitlist with varying wait times. Now, you can download Siri AI automatically as soon as you enable it on your compatible iPhone, Mac, or iPad. The one exception is that, if there is unusually high demand, Apple could temporarily reinstate its waitlist.

You’ll need a compatible device that runs Apple Intelligence, like an iPhone (15 Pro or newer), iPad (Mini A17 Pro or newer or an M-series chip), Mac (MacBook Neo or M-series chip), Apple Watch (Series 9 and Ultra 2 or newer), or Apple Vision Pro.

Instead of adding you to a waitlist, Siri AI will begin downloading right away.

Siri AI is Apple’s upgraded virtual assistant, now powered by generative AI. Instead of giving you canned responses to your questions, Siri AI will be able to answer complex questions, understand more natural-sounding phrases, and maintain context throughout conversations and across your Apple ecosystem.

ZDNET’s Lance Whitney recommends using Siri AI’s onscreen awareness feature to ask it for directions, explain something you see on your phone’s screen, or to add items from your screen to a list. He also uses Siri AI to edit his photos simply by asking for the changes he wants. But that’s just skimming the surface. You can read more about Whitney’s experiences using Siri AI here.

Also: I thought I had Siri AI in iOS 27 – until I found it hidden in my settings

For years, Apple has been working to gain relevance in AI to compete with major players like OpenAI and Google. While Apple Intelligence features like Writing Tools, Genmoji, and Image Playground have helped, Apple has lagged far behind in upgrading its signature voice assistant to generative AI.

iOS 27 delivered Siri AI in beta this fall, along with iPadOS 27, MacOS 27 Golden Gate, VisionOS 27, and WatchOS 27.

You need a compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro to use Apple Intelligence features like Siri AI. Not all Apple devices that support the latest iOS 27 (or other OS 27) will support Siri AI.

Here are the Apple devices that support Siri AI:

You also need to have your device in a supported language (English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, or Spanish) and to reside in a supported region (not available in mainland China or in iOS, iPadOS, or WatchOS in the European Union).

The United Kingdom is joining a growing list of countries looking to potentially restrict or outright ban smart glasses, especially in public spaces. Satvir Kaur, the country's Safeguarding minister, said in a Guardian report, "The government is looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users."

Kaur added that the benefits of smart glasses have to be weighed against their harms. In England and Wales, Meta glasses were recently banned in courtrooms, much like a similar ban in New York state. The courts promised to confiscate the glasses if they were worn into the courtroom (and returned after upon leaving).

According to Kaur, England's National Health Service and Department for Education are separately looking into policies regarding smart glasses.

In the last few months, smart glasses, like the Ray-Ban Meta, have faced a public backlash, even earning the moniker "pervert glasses."

In a debate about the glasses, MP Anne Sabina said, "Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses."

Whether or not a ban is enacted, Britain is adding to a growing chorus of governments and agencies looking at restricting smart glasses.

Australia's government announced in September that it was barring the use of camera-equipped glasses in government workspaces. The EU is scrutinizing glasses, though nothing official has been pursued yet.

Even Kaur pointed out that built-in cameras and displays could be beneficial for visually impaired individuals. "Smart glasses have been a game-changer, helping them navigate the world around them," Kaur said.

However, smart glasses don't necessarily need cameras to be beneficial.

Meta claims it was working on its camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio for years before their debut at Meta Connect 2026. Perhaps the company was, but at the time it seemed to launch in time to combat some of the pervert glasses criticisms.

Several Tom's Guide writers have tried the Audio-only Meta glasses, and we've all come away with the same praise: it was the right call.

"Taking out the camera has made me an even bigger fan of Ray Ban Meta glasses," AI editor Amanda Caswell said after 72 hours with the glasses.

There is a way for smart glasses to gain traction, and perhaps ditching the camera could help.

What are your thoughts? Should smart glasses with cameras be banned, or do they have their uses?
